Conservation used to mean stopping time. A painting was a patient; varnish was a bandage; the ideal was to return the object to a single authentic hour and then prevent further hours from occurring. That ideal had a hidden historiography. It assumed the authentic hour was already known, usually as the artist’s last brushstroke, and that later repairs, soot, liturgy, and even damage were noise.

A newer conservation talk prefers verbs. To museum an object is to keep choosing which traces will remain legible. Cleaning is not the removal of history; it is the promotion of one history over another. The nineteenth-century restorer who “completed” a medieval panel was not more ideological than the twenty-first-century restorer who leaves the lacuna as a paler mute. Both are editors. They differ in which audience they imagine and in how proudly they sign the edit.

Critics of reversible methods sometimes complain that visible fills and honest seams break the spell. They want the old miracle: an untouched past that happens to hang at eye level under LEDs. The complaint is aesthetically sincere and philosophically confused. The spell was always produced with scaffolding, attributions, and lighting. Reversibility is not a refusal of beauty. It is a refusal to trap the next generation inside today’s certainty about what the object “really” was.

There is a colonial edge. Objects that arrived by seizure were often cleaned into a style that made them readable as art in the receiving capital, which is to say, cleaned of the uses that had made them un-museumlike. To restore the pigment without restoring the right of refusal is to complete the seizure in a gentler font. Some institutions now consult source communities about smoke, wear, and whether an object should be seen at all. Consultation is slow and can be theater. It is still a different verb from rescue.

If this sounds like relativism, notice what it does not say. It does not say that all edits are equal, or that pigment chemistry is a matter of taste. It says that technical competence cannot supply the missing decision about which past is being kept available. The decision will be made. Calling it science does not make it less a decision. Calling it care does not either. The more honest museum is the one that can show its verbs.

items.stem: Transection of the pituitary stalk rapidly lowers circulating ADH and produces diabetes insipidus, while prolactin often rises because hypothalamic dopamine can no longer reach the anterior lobe. These findings are consistent with ADH being:

choices.text: Synthesized by anterior-pituitary gonadotrophs and released into the cavernous sinus
A steroid produced by the adrenal cortex under ACTH control only
Synthesized in hypothalamic nuclei and axonally transported to the posterior pituitary for release
Made by ovarian granulosa cells as the primary osmoregulatory hormone

items.explanation: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are peptides synthesized in hypothalamic magnocellular neurons (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei). Axons of the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract terminate in the posterior pituitary, so cutting the stalk disconnects those endings from their somata and ADH falls. Anterior-lobe hormones are made by pituitary cells under hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting factors delivered by the portal system; loss of dopamine inhibition explains the prolactin rise and shows the stalk lesion is not a generic shutdown of every pituitary cell. ADH is not an adrenal steroid or an ovarian product.

distractorRationales.A: Gonadotrophs secrete LH/FSH, not ADH; ADH is posterior-pituitary/hypothalamic.
distractorRationales.B: Adrenal steroids are cortisol/aldosterone/androgens, not ADH.
distractorRationales.D: The ovary does not secrete the physiologic antidiuretic hormone.

items.stem: The same acetic acid sample (25.0 mL of 0.10 M; pKa = 4.74) is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. After 12.5 mL of NaOH has been added, the pH is closest to:
items.explanation: Initial millimoles of acetic acid = 2.50. After 12.5 mL of 0.10 M NaOH, 1.25 mmol of HA has been converted to acetate, leaving 1.25 mmol HA. That is the half-equivalence point, where [HA] = [A−] (volumes cancel in the ratio). Henderson–Hasselbalch then gives pH = pKa = 4.74. 2.87 is the approximate starting pH of 0.10 M acetic acid before any base. 7.00 would be a strong-acid equivalence point. 8.72 is the ballpark equivalence pH after a full 25.0 mL of NaOH, not after half that volume.

distractorRationales.B: 2.87 estimates the pH of untitrated 0.10 M acetic acid (√(Ka C)), not the half-neutralized buffer.
distractorRationales.C: pH 7 is not a special point on a weak-acid titration curve except by coincidence; half-equivalence is at pKa.
distractorRationales.D: ≈8.7 is the equivalence-point pH after 25.0 mL of NaOH, when the solute is acetate alone.

items.stem: Hydrogen is burned: 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. A closed bulb is charged with 4.0 g H2 (Mr = 2.0) and 16 g O2 (Mr = 32). Which reagent limits, and what mass of water can form?

choices.text: The reagents are stoichiometric; 20 g H2O forms (4 + 16)
O2 limits (0.50 mol); 9.0 g H2O forms
O2 limits (0.50 mol); 18 g H2O forms
H2 limits (2.0 mol); 36 g H2O forms

items.explanation: Moles: n(H2) = 4.0/2.0 = 2.0 mol; n(O2) = 16/32 = 0.50 mol. The equation consumes 2 mol H2 per 1 mol O2, so 0.50 mol O2 would need 1.0 mol H2 and is limiting; 1.0 mol H2 remains unused. Water produced is 2 mol H2O per mol O2, hence 1.0 mol = 18 g. Hydrogen is in excess, not limiting. Adding masses of H2 and O2 (20 g) ignores that 2.0 g of unused H2 stays uncombined. Half of 18 g would be appropriate for 0.25 mol O2, not 0.50 mol.

distractorRationales.A: The mole ratio is 2.0 : 0.50 = 4 : 1, not the stoichiometric 2 : 1, and unused H2 is not water.
distractorRationales.B: 0.50 mol O2 produces 1.0 mol H2O = 18 g, not 0.50 mol = 9 g.
distractorRationales.D: 2.0 mol H2 would require 1.0 mol O2; only 0.50 mol O2 is present, so H2 is excess.

items.stem: Acetone (CH3COCH3, bp 56 °C) and 2-propanol (CH3CH(OH)CH3, bp 82 °C) have similar molar masses. Why is the alcohol’s boiling point higher?

choices.text: Acetone is more polar, so it should boil higher; the alcohol’s higher boiling point is due to its slightly larger mass alone.
2-Propanol can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas acetone can only accept hydrogen bonds and otherwise relies on dipole–dipole and London forces between ketone molecules.
Acetone ionizes in the liquid, lowering its boiling point.
The C=O bond of acetone is stronger than the C–O bond of the alcohol, so acetone molecules are harder to separate.

items.explanation: Boiling separates molecules, so intermolecular forces—not intramolecular bond strengths—set the boiling point. 2-Propanol has an O–H group and therefore hydrogen-bonds to itself. Acetone is polar and can accept a hydrogen bond from a donor, but a pair of acetone molecules cannot form O–H···O hydrogen bonds. The extra cohesion in the alcohol raises its boiling point despite nearly identical molar mass. Acetone does not ionize as a bulk liquid, and the strong C=O covalent bond is not broken on vaporization.

distractorRationales.A: Acetone is polar but lacks an H-bond donor. The boiling-point gap is much larger than the tiny mass difference would suggest.
distractorRationales.C: Acetone is a molecular liquid; it does not dissociate into ions in the neat liquid in a way that would control boiling point.
distractorRationales.D: Vaporization does not break the carbonyl double bond. Intramolecular bond strength is the wrong comparison.

items.stem: A full-thickness burn destroys epidermis including the stratum corneum. Insensible water loss and infection risk both rise sharply. The most direct explanation is loss of:

choices.text: Dermal melanin production, which is the primary water-tight seal of skin
The cornified lipid-keratin barrier that limits transepidermal water loss and microbial invasion
Vitamin D photoproduction, which is what physically occludes bacteria
Eccrine overproduction of hypotonic fluid as the only change after a burn

items.explanation: The stratum corneum is a brick-and-mortar of keratinized corneocytes and intercellular lipids from lamellar bodies. That composite is the principal barrier to evaporative water loss and to many microbes. Destroying it in a full-thickness burn is why patients desiccate and become infected unless the surface is replaced or dressed. Melanin absorbs UV in deeper living layers; it is not the water seal. Cutaneous vitamin D synthesis is a photochemical reaction, not a mechanical lid on bacteria. Burned skin does not cool the patient by secreting extra sweat from destroyed glands; insensible loss is barrier failure, not eccrine overdrive.

distractorRationales.A: Melanin is a UV pigment transferred to keratinocytes, not the lipid-keratin water barrier.
distractorRationales.C: Vitamin D is a hormone precursor, not the physical occlusion that keeps water in and pathogens out.
distractorRationales.D: Full-thickness injury destroys sweat glands; the water loss is passive through a missing barrier.

items.stem:
Human red cells have an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm. Equal aliquots are placed in NaCl baths (NaCl treated as membrane-impermeant). Relative cell volume at 2 min is:
150 mOsm bath: 1.82; 300 mOsm: 1.00; 450 mOsm: 0.71; 600 mOsm: 0.58.
Which description matches the data and osmosis?

choices.text: Cells swell in the hypotonic 150 mOsm bath and shrink in the hypertonic 450 and 600 mOsm baths.
150 mOsm is hypertonic, because the volume 1.82 shows water leaving the cells.
Volume is independent of bath osmolarity, because 0.58 is not far from 1.82.
600 mOsm causes lysis; lysis would increase, not decrease, packed cell volume.

items.explanation: Water moves toward the higher osmolarity. At 150 mOsm the bath is hypotonic to 300 mOsm cytoplasm, so water enters and relative volume rises to 1.82 (less than the ideal 300/150 = 2 because of non-solvent cell solids). At 300 mOsm there is no net driving force (volume 1.00). At 450 and 600 mOsm the bath is hypertonic, water leaves, and volume falls to 0.71 and 0.58, near the ideal 300/450 = 0.67 and 300/600 = 0.50. A volume below 1 is shrinkage, not lysis.

distractorRationales.B: Volume 1.82 is swelling from water entry; 150 mOsm is hypotonic, not hypertonic.
distractorRationales.C: Volume falls monotonically from 1.82 to 0.58 as osmolarity rises from 150 to 600 mOsm.
distractorRationales.D: Lysis would burst cells and cannot explain a relative volume of 0.58; that is crenation in a hypertonic bath.

items.stem: Acetyl-CoA labeled in both carbon atoms of the acetyl group enters the citric acid cycle by condensing with unlabeled oxaloacetate. After one complete turn, regenerating a four-carbon intermediate, how many of those labeled carbons have been released as CO2?

choices.text: Zero; the two CO2 molecules lost in that turn come from carboxyl groups that were already on oxaloacetate.
One; isocitrate dehydrogenase always releases the methyl carbon of the newly added acetyl group.
Two; both acetyl carbons are fully oxidized to CO2 before succinate is formed.
Three; an extra CO2 is released at succinyl-CoA synthetase.

items.explanation: Citrate synthase adds the two carbons of acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. In the same turn, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase each release one CO2, but those carboxyl carbons originated in the oxaloacetate that accepted the acetyl group, not in the acetyl group just added. Both labeled carbons remain in succinate (and therefore in the regenerated four-carbon acids). Because succinate is symmetric, those labels scramble and a fraction of the label is lost in subsequent turns, but the first turn releases none of the acetyl carbons as CO2. Succinyl-CoA synthetase does not decarboxylate.

distractorRationales.B: Isocitrate dehydrogenase does not specifically release the methyl carbon of the acetyl group in the first turn; that methyl carbon remains in the four-carbon intermediates.
distractorRationales.C: Neither acetyl carbon is lost as CO2 in the first turn. Both are still present in succinate, so the ‘fully oxidized before succinate’ claim is false.
distractorRationales.D: Succinyl-CoA synthetase converts succinyl-CoA to succinate with formation of GTP; it does not release CO2, and three labeled CO2 molecules are not produced in one turn.

items.stem: A city fines an unlicensed drumming circle in a courtyard at 11 p.m. at the same measured level it permits from a ticketed waterfront concert with a corporate sponsor the same night. Applying the author's principle, which evaluation follows?

choices.text: The differential is automatically justified, because a ticketed event is by definition not noise.
The differential may be defensible, but only as a named political allocation of the scarce good of loudness, not as a mere meter reading.
Both events must be banned, because the author forbids all exemptions, including hospitals.
The courtyard drumming is dirt in the medical sense, so hygiene language is the only honest description.

items.explanation: The author's principle is that like sounds require like reasons and that exemptions should be named as political choices rather than as nature. A concert and a drumming circle at similar intensity, sorted by license and sponsorship, is the hymn-versus-brand structure applied to a new pair. The text allows that some exemptions (a hospital generator, perhaps a funeral) can be defended; it does not treat tickets as a natural solvent of noise, demand a total ban, or accept dirt-language as honest by default. Applying the principle therefore yields a demand for named reasons, which is B.

distractorRationales.A: Treating a ticket as a definitional escape from noise is the vitality-as-atmosphere move the walk-after-dark paragraph criticizes.
distractorRationales.C: The closing paragraph explicitly allows that a hospital generator may deserve its exemption; unlimited prohibition is refused in the fourth paragraph as well.
distractorRationales.D: Hygiene-as-dirt is the costume that lets preference skip justification; applying it here would repeat the trick, not follow the principle.

passage.title: Who may be loud
passage.body:
Noise ordinances are written as if they were thermometers. A number of decibels is named; a clock hour is named; a fine is attached. The language of public health does real work here: sleep is not a luxury, and a child whose window faces a compressor is not being precious. But the thermometer conceals a second instrument, which is a social sorting device. Cities do not merely suppress loudness. They decide which kinds of loudness will be classified as vitality and which as nuisance, and the decision tracks, with embarrassing regularity, the prestige of the people making the sound.

Walk a mixed street after dark and the taxonomy is audible. A licensed terrace with heaters and a playlist is "activation of the night-time economy." A storefront church whose singing lasts past the same hour is a complaint waiting to be logged. A terrace is a business; a congregation is a disturbance that happens to own a building. Street vendors packing ice and calling prices are "chaos"; a restaurant's Friday overflow onto the pavement is "vibrancy," provided the overflow has paid for a permit. The ear that writes the ordinance has already been trained to hear money as atmosphere and unpaid sound as aggression.

Defenders of the ordinances will say that the issue is volume, not culture. Sometimes it is. A speaker stack aimed at a bedroom is a harm whether the music is sacred or commercial. The author's claim is narrower and more awkward: when two sounds of similar intensity are sorted differently, the sorting is not acoustics. It is a theory of who belongs in the air. "Quiet" is then sold as a natural baseline, like clean water, when it is often an aesthetic associated with certain housing and certain hours of salaried rest. Night-shift workers returning at dawn, whose rest is real, rarely get to define the city's sonic morals. People who sleep when the ordinance writers sleep do.

None of this is a brief for unlimited noise, or for the romance of the unregulated street. A city that cannot protect sleep will punish the poorest first, because they cannot buy distance from compressors. The decent aim is not a louder city but a less hypocritical one: a city that admits that permission to be loud is a scarce good, distributed by licensing, policing, and taste, and that "quality of life" is never only a medical phrase. It is also a claim about whose life is the measure.

The rhetorical trick is hygiene. Once noise is framed as dirt, opposition to a particular sound can wear the costume of sanitation rather than of preference. Dirt, unlike preference, does not have to justify itself at a public meeting. It only has to be pointed at. That is why a campaign against a night market can speak the idiom of rats and refuse even when the photographs show swept stones, and why a campaign for a waterfront festival can speak the idiom of civic joy even when the sound spill is identical. The same wave-form, two moral uniforms.

If the argument holds, then reform is not a new app for logging complaints. It is a requirement that like sounds be given like reasons, and that exemptions be named as political choices rather than as nature. A hospital generator may deserve its exemption. So, perhaps, does a funeral that spills into a street. What cannot be defended is the pretense that the ordinance is only a meter reading. Meters do not know the difference between a hymn and a brand. Officials do, and they should have to say so.

items.stem:
Stereology of a hepatocyte with total volume 5000 µm³ gives these volume fractions and counts:
Cytosol 54%; mitochondria 22% (1400 organelles); rough ER 9%; nucleus 8% (1 nucleus); lysosomes 1% (250 organelles); other 6%.
Which numerical comparison is correct?

choices.text: The nucleus occupies 54% of the cell (2700 µm³).
A typical mitochondrion (0.79 µm³) is larger than the nucleus (400 µm³).
Lysosomes occupy more volume than all mitochondria combined (50 µm³ versus 1100 µm³).
Mitochondria together occupy 1100 µm³, which exceeds the 400 µm³ nucleus.

items.explanation: Nuclear volume is 0.08 × 5000 = 400 µm³. Combined mitochondrial volume is 0.22 × 5000 = 1100 µm³, so the mitochondrial population is larger than the nucleus even though each mitochondrion is small (1100/1400 ≈ 0.79 µm³). Cytosol, not the nucleus, is 54%. Lysosomes are only 0.01 × 5000 = 50 µm³, far below 1100 µm³. The arithmetic from the given fractions therefore shows mitochondria as a major volumetric compartment relative to the nucleus.

distractorRationales.A: 54% is the cytosol fraction; the nucleus is 8%, or 400 µm³.
distractorRationales.B: 0.79 µm³ per mitochondrion is much smaller than the 400 µm³ nucleus.
distractorRationales.C: Lysosomes are 50 µm³ versus 1100 µm³ of mitochondria; the inequality is reversed.

items.stem:
Ksp(AgCl) = 1.0 × 10−10 at 25 °C. Two experiments:
(1) AgCl(s) in pure water: Ksp = s2, s = [Ag+] = [Cl−].
(2) AgCl(s) in 0.10 M NaCl: Ksp = [Ag+](0.10).
What are [Ag+] in (1) and (2)?

choices.text: 1.0 × 10−10 M in both, equal to Ksp
1.0 × 10−5 M in both, because s is a constant
0.10 M in water; 1.0 × 10−10 M in NaCl

items.explanation: In pure water s2 = 1.0 × 10−10, so s = 1.0 × 10−5 M. With a common-ion chloride concentration of 0.10 M, [Ag+] = Ksp / 0.10 = 1.0 × 10−9 M, a ten-thousand-fold suppression. Ksp is the product, not the silver concentration. Solubility is not invariant once a common ion is added. [Ag+] cannot be 0.10 M in water; that would give Q = 0.01, vastly exceeding Ksp.

distractorRationales.B: Ksp is [Ag+][Cl−], so [Ag+] equals Ksp only if [Cl−] = 1.0 M, which is not the case in either experiment.
distractorRationales.C: The common-ion experiment is designed to change s; the two [Ag+] values differ by 104.
distractorRationales.D: 0.10 M is the added chloride, not the silver ion in water.

items.stem: The cartoon’s humour most depends on

choices.text: a mismatch between official claims about time and care and the pictured instruments of waiting, triage, and denial.
a scientific proof that wall clocks cannot have hands.
the price of fake plants in real hospitals.
Upper Shore’s bus timetable.

items.explanation: The panel sets a motto valuing time against handless public time, private mismatched clocks, a triage question about sitting up, a fake plant still tagged, and a caption that the system is coping. Satire is the collision of claim and apparatus. B is literal nonsense. C is a detail in service of fakery, not the engine. D is not in the image. Cartoon items should name the structural irony rather than a prop.

distractorRationales.B: The missing hands are symbolic of unmeasured public time, not a physics claim.
distractorRationales.C: The tag on a fake plant supports a theme of display, but the humour is the whole waiting system.
distractorRationales.D: No bus timetable appears; Upper Shore is the letter-writer’s suburb.

passage.title: Cartoon: Clinic time
passage.body:
A single-panel cartoon, unsigned, published on a letters page.

Foreground: a waiting-room bench. Four people sit. Above each head a small clock; the hands are at 1:10, 2:40, 4:15, and 9:50. None of the clocks match the large wall clock, which has no hands.

On the wall, a framed motto: WE VALUE YOUR TIME. The frame is gold. The glass is cracked.

To the right, a receptionist window. The receptionist smiles with many teeth and holds a clipboard titled TRIAGE (PRIVATE). On the clipboard the only visible line is: “Can they still sit up?” A potted plant on the sill is fake; its price tag remains.

Under the bench, a fifth clock, face-down.

Caption, in small type: “The system is coping.”

A letter printed beneath, from “Concerned, Upper Shore”: “Cartoons like this undermine dedicated staff. If people arrived on time and did not bring relatives, clocks would match.”

items.stem:
A 512 Hz tuning fork is used to measure wavelength in two media. Wave speed is v = f λ.

Medium | Frequency (Hz) | Measured wavelength (m)
Air | 512 | 0.670
Water | 512 | 2.90

What is the speed of sound in the air measurement?
items.explanation: The frequency is the fork frequency in both media; only wavelength and speed change. In air, v = 512 × 0.670. Compute 500 × 0.670 = 335 and 12 × 0.670 = 8.04, so v = 343 m s−1. The water row gives 512 × 2.90 = 1485 m s−1, which is a valid speed of sound in water but is not the air value. 219 m s−1 would be 512 × 0.427 or a mix-up of 0.670 with a two-way path. The frequency in hertz is not itself a speed. The table’s two rows illustrate that the same f produces a longer λ where v is larger.

distractorRationales.A: 219 m s−1 does not equal f λ for either row. It may come from using a halved wavelength or an incorrect product.
distractorRationales.C: 512 is the frequency in hertz, not a speed. Speed requires multiplying by the measured wavelength.
distractorRationales.D: 1485 m s−1 is f λ in water (512 × 2.90), not the air measurement asked for.

items.stem: Glutamine synthetase catalyzes glutamate + NH4+ + ATP → glutamine + ADP + Pi. The uncoupled condensation glutamate + NH4+ → glutamine + H2O has ΔG°′ ≈ +14 kJ/mol, whereas ATP hydrolysis has ΔG°′ ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol. Which statement is most accurate in the cell?

choices.text: The unfavorable glutamine-forming step cannot occur even when coupled, because ΔG°′ is a state function that forbids any positive partial reaction.
Coupling phosphoryl transfer from ATP makes the net standard free-energy change negative (≈ −16 kJ/mol), and a high [ATP]/[ADP][Pi] ratio further drives ΔG negative, allowing net glutamine synthesis.
Enzymes rewrite ΔG°′ of the uncoupled condensation to a negative value without chemical coupling to ATP.
Because ΔG°′ of ATP hydrolysis is negative, every ATP-dependent reaction runs to completion regardless of mass-action ratios.

items.explanation: Standard free energy is path-independent for a defined chemical change, but cells couple an unfavorable process to a favorable one so that the net reaction has negative ΔG°′. Adding +14 kJ/mol to −30.5 kJ/mol yields about −16 kJ/mol for glutamate + ATP + NH4+ → glutamine + ADP + Pi. Actual ΔG also depends on mass action; a high [ATP]/[ADP][Pi] ratio makes ΔG even more negative. Enzymes accelerate approach to equilibrium; they do not change ΔG°′ without changing the reaction stoichiometry, and they do not force every ATP-dependent reaction to completion independent of Q.

distractorRationales.A: A positive ΔG°′ for an isolated step is allowed if it is coupled into a net reaction with negative ΔG°′; metabolism routinely uses such coupling.
distractorRationales.C: Catalysts do not alter standard free-energy differences of a given reaction; coupling changes the reaction that is actually catalyzed.
distractorRationales.D: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q; mass action can reverse or stall ATP-dependent reactions when products accumulate or ATP is low.

items.stem: The speaker's attitude toward the clerk is best described as

choices.text: ironic contempt for a man who will not read
respectful attention that resists turning him into a moral mascot
clinical neutrality with no evaluative language
sentimental praise of his poverty

items.explanation: The narrator grants the clerk a serious ethics while refusing the commentator's saint-making. Evaluative language is present (“too clean,” “indecent”) but aimed at theory and curiosity, not at sneering at the clerk. There is no portrait of poverty, and the tone is not purely clinical.

distractorRationales.A: The clerk is defended, not held in contempt.
distractorRationales.C: Words like indecent and too clean are evaluative.
distractorRationales.D: Poverty is not a theme; the purse has little money, but that is not the praise.

passage.title: On keeping a promise to a stranger
passage.body:
When the magistrate asked why he had returned the purse, the clerk did not say honesty. He said habit. He had been taught, in a household that measured virtue by small repetitions, that a found object remains someone else's until the world has been given a fair chance to reclaim it. The purse contained little money and a letter, unsealed, beginning: I will not be there when you arrive. He did not finish it. To finish it, he thought, would convert a duty into a story, and stories have a way of making the finder important.

Philosophers like to treat this as a puzzle about property and knowledge. If he does not know the owner, is the duty weaker? If the letter would have saved a marriage, does withholding it become a harm? The clerk would have found the questions indecent. He was not refusing knowledge so much as refusing a role. The city had clerks for lost property; it did not have clerks for other people's farewells.

A later commentator, writing after the clerk was dead, praised him as a Kantian saint: he acted from a maxim he could will as universal. The praise is too clean. The clerk's maxim was local and slightly ashamed. He did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not universality, kept his eyes off the page. That is not a lesser ethics. It is an ethics that knows how quickly curiosity dresses itself as concern.

The owner collected the purse the next morning and did not thank him. In the commentary this becomes a test of whether virtue needs recognition. The clerk, if asked, would have said only that the counter was busy.

items.stem: Surgeons joke and drop formality in the lounge, then adopt a composed, technical demeanor as soon as a family enters the OR corridor. Goffman’s dramaturgical analysis treats this shift as which distinction?

choices.text: Back-stage versus front-stage regions of performance, with impression management tailored to the audience
Looking-glass self, which is about regions of a theater rather than imagined judgment
Deindividuation, which requires a mob and anonymity
Wernicke’s fluent speech as the only front-stage tool

items.explanation: Goffman’s Presentation of Self analogizes interaction to theater: front stage is the public performance maintained for an audience; back stage is where the performer can relax the role and prepare. Moving from lounge to family corridor is that regional shift, a core impression-management practice. Cooley’s looking-glass is reflected self-feeling, not theater regions. Deindividuation is crowd anonymity. Aphasia localization is unrelated to dramaturgy.

distractorRationales.B: Looking-glass self is Cooley’s imagined judgment, not Goffman’s front/back regions.
distractorRationales.C: A lounge-to-corridor shift is not a deindividuated mob.
distractorRationales.D: Language areas do not define dramaturgical regions.

items.stem:
A taut string is fixed at both ends. Standing-wave wave speed on the string is v = √(T/μ) and the fundamental frequency is f1 = v / (2L). Measured quantities are:

Quantity | Value
Length L | 0.80 m
Linear density μ | 5.0 × 10^−4 kg m−1
Tension T | 80 N

What is f1?

choices.text: 125 Hz
200 Hz
250 Hz
500 Hz

items.explanation: Wave speed is v = √(80 / 5.0 × 10^−4) = √(1.60 × 10^5) = 400 m s−1. The string is fixed at both ends, so the fundamental has λ/2 = L and f1 = v / (2L) = 400 / 1.60 = 250 Hz. Using 4L in the denominator (the closed-pipe formula) gives 125 Hz. Using L instead of 2L gives 500 Hz, which is actually the second harmonic. 200 Hz would require v = 320 m s−1 or L = 1.00 m, neither of which matches the table. The linear density must be in kg m−1; leaving μ in grams would collapse v by √1000 and is not one of the options.

distractorRationales.A: 125 Hz is v / (4L), the closed-pipe fundamental. A string fixed at both ends uses 2L, like an open pipe.
distractorRationales.B: 200 Hz does not follow from v = 400 m s−1 and L = 0.80 m. It would require a different tension or a 1.0 m string.
distractorRationales.D: 500 Hz is v / L, which is the second harmonic (n = 2) of this string, not the fundamental.

items.stem: From the seminar warmth to the outbox, the tone shifts toward

choices.text: unqualified triumph
a cooler self-accusation that still refuses melodrama
farce about plumbing
religious confession with a priest

items.explanation: Early beats are comic-uneasy (coat too large, laugh too quickly). The close names cowardice without a collapse into sermon, and the glass offering his mouth moving is dry rather than priestly. Triumph is what the friend wrongly heard. Plumbing and priests are not in the register. A tone shift question should hear the temperature drop from the nodded room to the unsent honest line, which is cooler and more exact, not louder.

distractorRationales.A: He deletes the self-flattering note; triumph is the friend's error.
distractorRationales.C: Bathroom is setting, not farce about pipes.
distractorRationales.D: The glass is a mirror, not a confessor.

passage.title: The borrowed coat
passage.body:
He wore other people's sentences the way some men wear coats: against weather, and with the labels left in. At the seminar he began, "One might argue," and then produced, almost unaltered, a paragraph his supervisor had emailed at midnight to save him. The room nodded. He felt the coat settle on his shoulders, warm and slightly too large in the sleeves.

Afterward a friend said, "That was the first time you sounded like yourself." He laughed too quickly. In the bathroom mirror the coat was still on. He tried to take it off by telling the truth to the glass: I do not know whether I think this. The glass, being a glass, offered his mouth moving.

Ethics talks as if authenticity were a mineral you either contain or fake. The evening suggested something cheaper and more ordinary. A borrowed argument can keep you from freezing. It can also teach your arms the wrong length. The crime, if there is one, is not the borrowing. It is the nod you collect as if the sleeves had always been yours.

He sent the supervisor a note: Thank you. I sounded like myself. He deleted it. He sent: Thank you. I used your paragraph. He left that one in the outbox until morning, which is a kind of cowardice that still knows the difference.

items.stem: The half-equivalence pH implies pKa nearest
items.explanation: At half-equivalence, [HA]≈[A−], so pH≈pKa. That volume is 12.50 mL on this design, pH 4.20. 2.88 is initial. 8.72 is equivalence. 12.15 is excess OH−. Interpolating the intended Henderson–Hasselbalch point is the skill; do not average endpoints. The data already include the half point; no extrapolation off the table is required.

distractorRationales.A: Initial pH of 0.100 M HA is not pKa (weak acid is not fully dissociated).
distractorRationales.C: Equivalence pH of A−(aq), not pKa.
distractorRationales.D: Strong-base excess region.

passage.title: Unknown weak acid titration
passage.body:
25.00 mL of monoprotic unknown HA (0.100 mol L−1 stated by the stockroom) is titrated with 0.100 mol L−1 NaOH at 25 °C. pH is measured with a probe calibrated at 4.00 and 10.00.

V(NaOH) / mL | pH
0.00 | 2.88
5.00 | 3.46
12.50 | 4.20
20.00 | 4.94
24.00 | 5.56
25.00 | 8.72
26.00 | 11.24
30.00 | 12.15

A classmate says the equivalence volume must be 12.50 mL because that is “half way on the page.” Another wants Ka from the initial pH alone, treating HA as if it were a strong acid.

items.stem:
A 0.10 M aqueous solution of the weak base B is prepared. The base-dissociation constant is Kb = 1.0 × 10^−5, with Kb = [HB+][OH−] / [B]. Analogous to a weak acid, [OH−] ≈ √(Kb × 0.10). Water at 25 °C has Kw = 1.0 × 10^−14 so pH + pOH = 14.00.

Quantity | Value
C of B | 0.10 mol L−1
Kb | 1.0 × 10^−5
[OH−] from √(Kb C) | 1.0 × 10^−3 mol L−1

What is the pH of the 0.10 M B solution?

choices.text: 2.00, treating B as if it were a 0.10 M strong acid.
5.00, equal to −log10(Kb).
13.00, treating B as a fully dissociated 0.10 M strong base.

items.explanation: [OH−] ≈ √(1.0 × 10^−5 × 0.10) = √(1.0 × 10^−6) = 1.0 × 10^−3 M, so pOH = 3.00 and pH = 11.00. Reporting pOH as if it were pH, or setting pH = −log Kb, are common slips. A strong 0.10 M base would have [OH−] = 0.10 M, pOH = 1.00 and pH = 13.00, which overestimates the basicity of this weak base. The solution is clearly basic (pH > 7), which already eliminates any answer near 2. The weak-base square-root step is the same algebra as for a weak acid, but the logarithm is of [OH−], not of [H+].

distractorRationales.A: pH 2.00 would describe a 0.010 M strong acid, not a weak base. The species B produces OH−, so the solution cannot be this acidic.
distractorRationales.B: −log10(Kb) = 5.00 is pKb, not pH. pH of a weak base is obtained from pOH = −log[OH−], then 14 − pOH.
distractorRationales.D: pH 13.00 is the strong-base result for 0.10 M OH−. Only a fraction of B is protonated, so [OH−] is 10^−3 M, not 0.10 M.

items.stem:
Two purified organelle enzymes are assayed versus pH (activity in the same arbitrary units):
pH 5.0: hydrolase L = 92, catalase P = 8.
pH 7.0: hydrolase L = 14, catalase P = 88.
pH 8.0: hydrolase L = 6, catalase P = 71.
Compartment L has a measured luminal pH of 5.0; compartment P has a luminal pH of 7.2.
Which assignment fits both the pH data and standard organelle chemistry?

choices.text: L is the mitochondrial matrix (pH near 8), because hydrolase L still has 6 units at pH 8.
L is lysosomal (acid-optimum hydrolase) and P is consistent with peroxisomal catalase.
Both enzymes are cytosolic, because cytosol is pH 7 and hydrolase L still has 14 units there.
P is lysosomal, because catalase destroys H2O2 most rapidly at pH 5 (activity 8).

items.explanation: Lysosomes maintain an acidic lumen so that acid hydrolases work at their pH optimum; hydrolase L is almost fully active at pH 5 (92 units) and nearly inactive at pH 7–8, matching that compartment. Peroxisomal catalase operates near neutrality; catalase P peaks at pH 7 (88 units) and is weak at pH 5 (8 units), matching lumen pH 7.2. Residual activity of L at pH 8 is only 6 units, far below its acid peak, so L is not a matrix enzyme. Catalase’s low activity at pH 5 rules out a lysosomal assignment for P.

distractorRationales.A: Activity 6 at pH 8 is a trough, not an optimum; the mitochondrial matrix would not house an acid hydrolase of this profile.
distractorRationales.C: Fourteen units at pH 7 is a small fraction of L’s pH-5 peak, so the enzyme is not tuned to the cytosol.
distractorRationales.D: Catalase P has only 8 units at pH 5 and 88 at pH 7, the opposite of a lysosomal acid optimum.

items.stem: Freshly dissolved α-D-glucopyranose mutarotates in water until [α]D reaches the equilibrium value of the anomeric mixture. Methyl α-D-glucopyranoside, dissolved in the same neutral water, shows a constant specific rotation for hours. Why?

choices.text: The methyl glycoside is an acetal at C1; the ring cannot open to the aldehyde without acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, so anomers cannot interconvert
Methyl glycosides are aldehydes that racemize instantly, so rotation is already zero
The methyl group inverts configuration at C5, destroying the D series and freezing rotation
Glycosides have no stereocenters, so they cannot be optically active in the first place

items.explanation: Mutarotation of glucose proceeds by reversible ring opening of the hemiacetal to the open-chain aldehyde, which can reclose to either the α or the β anomer. A methyl glycoside is a full acetal: the anomeric carbon bears two C–O bonds (the ring oxygen and OMe). Acetals are stable in neutral or basic water and open only when acid catalyzes hydrolysis. Without access to the aldehyde, the anomeric configuration is locked and [α] does not drift. The glycoside remains chiral (multiple stereocenters) and optically active; methylation does not invert C5 or erase stereochemistry.

distractorRationales.B: A glycoside is an acetal, not an aldehyde. Instant racemization to zero rotation is not observed; the rotation is simply constant.
distractorRationales.C: The methyl is attached to the anomeric oxygen at C1. C5, which defines the D/L series, is untouched.
distractorRationales.D: Methyl glucopyranoside has five stereocenters and a large specific rotation; it is optically active but configurationally locked at C1.

items.stem: The extract as historical commentary mainly suggests that the empty tram was

choices.text: a straightforward restoration of public transport.
a piece of staged lighting whose meaning split in the street and in the papers, while the timetable had already conceded the service.
proof that children always side with companies.
irrelevant to who owned the evening street.

items.explanation: Officials, strikers, two captions, the generator, and the clerk’s line about surrender in the timetable all treat the tram as theatre and argument, not as service. Children running are appropriated by rival headlines, not a bloc vote. The clerk is called more useful than the lengthen/shorten camps because he names illumination as the stake. That is historical commentary on a symbol, not a transport report.

distractorRationales.A: No passengers were permitted; “service” is the company’s word, ironised.
distractorRationales.C: The children are photographed and captioned two ways; they are not a corporate constituency.
distractorRationales.D: The clerk says what remained was who owned the look of the street.

passage.title: Note on a cancelled tram
passage.body:
In the third week of the lockout the company ran a single tram, brightly lit, along the route at dusk, with no passengers permitted. Officials called it a demonstration of service. Strikers called it a lantern on a coffin. Children ran beside it anyway, as they had when the cars were working, and were photographed. The photograph was printed in the morning paper under the heading NORMALITY RETURNS, and in an overseas paper under the heading CHILDREN MOCK THE DEAD LINE.

A clerk in the tram office, years later, wrote that he had been told to leave the lights on even if the generator complained, because darkness would look like surrender. He added, without apparent bitterness, that surrender had already occurred in the timetable. What remained was a moving argument about who owned the look of a street at evening.

Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

items.stem: Which comparison best tests whether hypotonicity is required for the scatter drop?

choices.text: B versus D at 10 s only, because both are hypotonic.
A versus B across time, because osmolarity is the intended difference and A does not drop.
C versus D, because mercury is a metal.
The s.d. column alone, without condition labels.

items.explanation: Independent variable for that claim is bath osmolarity; A is the isotonic control and stays near 1.00 while B falls. That isolates hypotonicity. B versus D confounds extra aquaporin. C versus D confounds block versus extra pores, both hypotonic. Error bars without labels cannot test the claim. Identifying variables means matching the student’s first clause to the control that actually holds osmolarity at 300.

distractorRationales.A: Both hypotonic; cannot show hypotonicity is required.
distractorRationales.C: Both 150 mOsmol; the difference is pores, not tonicity.
distractorRationales.D: Unlabelled uncertainty does not identify the independent variable.

passage.title: Vesicle swelling under osmotic load
passage.body:
A student prepares identical phospholipid vesicles in 300 mOsmol kg−1 sucrose, then dilutes them at t = 0 into the media below. Vesicle volume is inferred from light scatter (larger vesicles scatter less in this geometry). Temperature 25 °C. n = 6 aliquots; scatter reported as mean ± s.d. arbitrary units (higher = smaller vesicles).

Medium after dilution | 10 s | 60 s | 300 s
A: 300 mOsmol sucrose (control) | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 0.99 ± 0.03 | 1.01 ± 0.02
B: 150 mOsmol sucrose | 0.71 ± 0.04 | 0.52 ± 0.05 | 0.48 ± 0.06
C: 150 mOsmol sucrose + 0.1 mM HgCl2 (water-channel blocker in this model) | 0.92 ± 0.03 | 0.80 ± 0.04 | 0.61 ± 0.05
D: 150 mOsmol sucrose + aquaporin proteoliposomes fused at 5 mol% | 0.40 ± 0.06 | 0.33 ± 0.05 | 0.34 ± 0.04

A second table lists initial rates estimated from 0–10 s, treating scatter drop as swelling:

Condition | Δscatter / 10 s
A | ~0
B | −0.029
C | −0.008
D | −0.060

The student claims: “Swelling requires a hypotonic bath, is slowed when water pores are blocked, and is accelerated when extra water pores are added, so the membrane’s phospholipid bilayer is not the main path in B–D.”

items.stem: Which of the following best states the author's central claim about translation?

choices.text: Fluent, natural-sounding translations are the only honest ones, because delay is proof that a translator has failed.

Translation is a set of decisions about which foreign silences remain audible; selling fluency as fidelity recruits the text into local habits rather than receiving it, so a trace of difficulty can be a form of hospitality.
Wooden calques and untranslated exhibits are the only ethically acceptable methods, because any English rendering is a betrayal.
Publishers should be abolished, since markets can never influence which books readers finish.

items.explanation: The passage rejects the pipe metaphor and treats translation as decisions about audible silences. Fluency sold as fidelity enrolls a text in local etiquette and hides hospitality; delay can honestly report a conceptual mismatch. The author equally refuses the opposite piety of difficulty-as-exhibit. Choice B keeps both refusals and the hospitality thesis. The other options inflate a rejected tactic, invert the smoothness critique, or turn a market remark into an abolition program the text never offers.

distractorRationales.A: The author treats the belief that a text which does not delay us has been understood as the more serious failure, not as a standard of honesty.
distractorRationales.C: The third paragraph explicitly denies a case for wooden calques and the museum of untranslated words, calling those tactics their own piety.
distractorRationales.D: Publishers are said to be right about the market and wrong about meaning; the passage does not propose abolishing publishing.

passage.title: The courtesy of untranslatability
passage.body:
Historians of language like to treat translation as a pipe: meaning enters one end, equivalent wording exits the other, and any turbulence is a defect in the plumber. The figure is flattering to publishers, who can then sell fluency as fidelity, and it is flattering to readers, who can then consume a foreign argument as if it had always been written in their kitchen. The figure is also false. A translation is not a transfer of a stable cargo. It is a series of decisions about which silences will remain audible and which will be paved over so that a page turns without snagging.

Consider the ordinary boast that a novel has been rendered into "perfectly natural" English. Natural for whom? The boast treats the target language as a climate rather than as a historically specific set of habits, class markers, and tolerated opacities. When a rural insult is recast as a metropolitan joke, or a liturgical cadence is recast as a magazine paragraph, the text has not been rescued from awkwardness. It has been enrolled in a local etiquette. The reader who thanks the translator for making the book "not feel translated" is thanking the translator for hiding the fact that hospitality occurred. Hospitality, if it is more than a smile, leaves a trace of the guest.

This is not an argument for wooden calques or for the museum of untranslated words left standing like exhibits. Those tactics can become their own piety, a performance of difficulty that congratulates the reader for enduring it. The more serious failure is the opposite one: the belief that a text which does not delay us has therefore been understood. Delay is sometimes the only honest report of a conceptual mismatch. A legal term that organizes a whole civic world cannot be swapped for a near-synonym without smuggling in the civic world of the synonym. To refuse the delay is to pretend that the two worlds already agreed.

Publishers will object that readers abandon books that snag. They are not wrong about the market. They are wrong to treat the market as a theory of meaning. A culture that will only receive what has already been made to sound like itself is not receiving; it is recruiting. The translated page then becomes a mirror with a foreign name on the title page, and the prestige of the foreign name is used to ratify what the reader already believed. That is why "accessible" can function as a political adjective. It names not a reading level but a refusal of conceptual immigration.

None of this requires contempt for the reader. It requires a different courtesy: the courtesy of letting a sentence remain slightly foreign so that the reader can notice the foreignness as information rather than as a stain. The translator's invisibility, long praised as professionalism, is in this light a kind of disappearance of evidence. We might instead want translators to be visibly responsible for their choices, not as celebrities, but as people who can be asked why a silence was kept or filled.

The practical consequence is modest and severe. Reviewers should stop treating smoothness as a synonym for accuracy. Teachers should stop treating a bilingual dictionary as a moral instrument. And readers who want to be hosts rather than consumers should learn to tolerate, even to prize, the small resistances that prove a text has not been entirely naturalized. What cannot be made to sound like us is often the part that most needed to travel.

items.stem:
1.00 g of compound C (M = 180 g mol−1) is burned in a bomb calorimeter whose water equivalent is 2.00 kg of water. Use c = 4.18 J g−1 °C−1. The temperature rises 3.50 °C. q_cal = m c ΔT; for combustion ΔU ≈ −q_cal / moles.
What is ΔU per mole of C?

choices.text: +5.27 × 10^3 kJ mol−1 (wrong sign)
−29.3 kJ mol−1 (reporting the heat per gram as if it were per mole)
−5.27 kJ mol−1 (off by 10^3)

items.explanation: The calorimeter absorbs q = 2000 g × 4.18 J g−1 °C−1 × 3.50 °C = 2.926 × 10^4 J = 29.26 kJ for 1.00 g. One mole is 180 g, so 29.26 kJ g−1 × 180 g mol−1 = 5.27 × 10^3 kJ mol−1. Combustion heats the calorimeter, so the chemical system released that energy and ΔU is negative: −5.27 × 10^3 kJ mol−1. Treating 29.26 kJ as already molar, or dropping the factor of 1000 between J and kJ incorrectly, produces the smaller distractors; a positive sign ignores that the water warmed.

distractorRationales.A: The calorimeter temperature rose, so the reaction released heat; ΔU is negative.
distractorRationales.B: 29.26 kJ is the heat for 1.00 g; multiplying by 180 g mol−1 is required for a molar value.
distractorRationales.C: 29 260 J per gram times 180 is 5.27 × 10^6 J mol−1 = 5.27 × 10^3 kJ mol−1, not 5.27 kJ mol−1.

items.stem: A ground squirrel is more likely to give a predator alarm when nearby listeners are close female kin than when they are unrelated. Hamilton’s rule is offered as the explanation. Which inequality, and which concept, is being invoked?

choices.text: Trivers’s reciprocal altruism, which requires the named sisters to repay the alarm next week as a contract
Wynne-Edwards group selection as the MCAT-preferred substitute for relatedness
Harlow’s contact comfort, because cloth mothers alarm-call
rB > C: inclusive fitness/kin selection can favor a costly alarm when relatedness times benefit to recipients exceeds the cost to the caller

items.explanation: Hamilton’s inclusive-fitness rule says a social behavior is favored when rB > C: relatedness times the benefit to recipients exceeds the actor’s cost. Alarm calling that tracks kinship is a classic illustration. Reciprocal altruism (Trivers) can explain aid among nonkin given later repayment, which the stem does not require. Naive group-selection accounts are not the standard MCAT mechanism here. Harlow showed infants prefer cloth comfort to a wire feeder; that is attachment, not kin-selected alarms.

distractorRationales.A: The stem varies relatedness, not a repayment contract.
distractorRationales.B: MCAT-level evolutionary social behavior uses inclusive fitness, not Wynne-Edwards as the preferred engine.
distractorRationales.C: Harlow’s surrogate mothers are a different literature.

items.stem: 25.0 mL of 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa = 4.74) is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. At the equivalence point, which statement about the solution is correct?

choices.text: The pH is 7.00 because moles of acid equal moles of base.
The pH is greater than 7 because the solution is aqueous sodium acetate, and acetate hydrolyzes to produce OH−.
The pH equals 4.74 because that is the pKa of acetic acid.
The pH is less than 7 because leftover acetic acid still dominates.

items.explanation: Equivalence for this 1:1 titration occurs at 25.0 mL of NaOH, when essentially all CH3CO2H has been converted to CH3CO2−. The flask then contains a solution of the conjugate base of a weak acid. Acetate reacts with water (CH3CO2− + H2O ⇌ CH3CO2H + OH−), so the equivalence-point pH is basic (typically ~8.7 for these concentrations), not 7. pH 7 is the equivalence pH only for a strong acid–strong base titration. pH = pKa occurs at the half-equivalence point, not at equivalence. No significant free acetic acid remains at equivalence.

distractorRationales.A: Equal moles mean neutralization of HA to A−, not a neutral pH, when A− is a weak base.
distractorRationales.C: pH = pKa at half-equivalence, where [HA] = [A−], not at equivalence.
distractorRationales.D: At equivalence the weak acid has been consumed; leftover HA is the situation before equivalence.

items.stem: A protein elutes from a calibrated size-exclusion column in native buffer at an apparent mass of 160 kDa. Reducing SDS-PAGE of the same sample shows a single band at 40 kDa. The protein contains no cysteine. Which description of quaternary structure is most consistent with the data?

choices.text: Four identical polypeptide chains associate noncovalently as a homotetramer
A single 160 kDa polypeptide is cleaved by SDS into 40 kDa fragments
Four 40 kDa chains are joined by isopeptide bonds that SDS cannot break
The native species is a heterodimer of 40 kDa and 120 kDa subunits

items.explanation: Size-exclusion chromatography in native buffer reports the hydrodynamic size of the oligomer, here 160 kDa. SDS unfolds chains and, with reductant, separates polypeptides that are not covalently linked; a single 40 kDa band implies one subunit type whose mass is one-fourth of 160 kDa. Absence of cysteine rules out interchain disulfides, so the tetramer must be held by noncovalent interfaces. SDS does not hydrolyze peptide bonds, covalent isopeptide tetramers would still look large on SDS-PAGE, and a 40 plus 120 kDa heterodimer would give two SDS bands.

distractorRationales.B: SDS is a denaturant, not a protease; it does not cut a 160 kDa chain into 40 kDa pieces.
distractorRationales.C: Isopeptide cross-links would survive SDS and the gel would not collapse to 40 kDa.
distractorRationales.D: A 40/120 heterodimer would produce two bands on SDS-PAGE, not one.

items.stem: Stokes’ drag is F = 6π η r v. Force has dimensions M L T−2, r is L, v is L T−1. What are the dimensions of viscosity η, and which of the following is dimensionless? (Reynolds number Re = ρ v L / η, with ρ = M L−3.)

choices.text: η is dimensionless; Re has dimensions of η
η has dimensions M L−1 T−1; Re has dimensions of density
η has dimensions M L−1 T−1; Re is dimensionless
η has dimensions M L T−1; Re has dimensions of velocity

items.explanation: From F = η r v, ignoring the 6π, η = F / (r v) so [η] = (M L T−2) / (L · L T−1) = M L−1 T−1. Then Re = ρ v L / η has [ρ v L] = (M L−3)(L T−1)(L) = M L−1 T−1, which cancels [η], leaving a pure number. That is why Re can be used to compare flows of different size and speed. η is not dimensionless (oil and air have different SI values with units Pa s). Re is not a velocity or a density; those dimensions already cancelled. The 6π factor is a pure number and does not affect dimensions.

distractorRationales.A: η has SI unit Pa s = kg m−1 s−1, so it is dimensional; Re is the dimensionless combination.
distractorRationales.B: The η dimensions are right, but Re is constructed precisely so density cancels.
distractorRationales.D: The extra L in the numerator of that option would be [F]/[v] without dividing by r.

items.stem: A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal table. A horizontal 10 N force is applied, and kinetic friction on the block is 4 N while it slides. The acceleration of the block is:
items.explanation: Newton's second law uses the net force, not the applied force alone. Horizontal forces are 10 N forward and 4 N of kinetic friction backward, so F_net = 6 N. Then a = F_net / m = 6 N / 2 kg = 3 m/s^2 in the direction of the 10 N pull. Vertical forces cancel (normal force balances weight), so they do not contribute to the horizontal acceleration. Ignoring friction or adding the friction force both produce a wrong net force.

distractorRationales.B: This is 10 N / 2 kg, which treats the table as frictionless. The 4 N kinetic friction must be subtracted before dividing by mass.
distractorRationales.C: This is (10 + 4)/2, adding friction to the pull as if both forces pointed the same way. Kinetic friction opposes sliding, so it reduces F_net.
distractorRationales.D: This is 4 N / 2 kg, using only the friction force. Friction is not the net force while a larger applied force acts forward.

items.stem: If the pipetted HA volume were 25.00 mL but the true concentration were 0.080 mol L−1, the equivalence volume would be

choices.text: 25.00 mL still, because the burette does not care.
20.00 mL of 0.100 mol L−1 NaOH.

items.explanation: Moles HA = 0.02500 L × 0.080 mol L−1 = 0.00200 mol. At 0.100 mol L−1 NaOH, V = 0.00200/0.100 = 0.0200 L = 20.00 mL. Units must stay in litres or cancel as millimoles: 25.00 mL × 0.080 mmol mL−1 = 2.00 mmol; 2.00/0.100 = 20.0 mL. 25 mL assumes the labelled 0.100. 12.5 is half of the labelled equivalence, not this hypothetically weaker stock.

distractorRationales.A: Equivalence tracks moles, not the intended 25 mL ritual.
distractorRationales.C: Half of 25 mL is the original half-equivalence, not the new end point.
distractorRationales.D: Would correspond to an even more dilute or mis-pipetted sample.

passage.title: Unknown weak acid titration
passage.body:
25.00 mL of monoprotic unknown HA (0.100 mol L−1 stated by the stockroom) is titrated with 0.100 mol L−1 NaOH at 25 °C. pH is measured with a probe calibrated at 4.00 and 10.00.

V(NaOH) / mL | pH
0.00 | 2.88
5.00 | 3.46
12.50 | 4.20
20.00 | 4.94
24.00 | 5.56
25.00 | 8.72
26.00 | 11.24
30.00 | 12.15

A classmate says the equivalence volume must be 12.50 mL because that is “half way on the page.” Another wants Ka from the initial pH alone, treating HA as if it were a strong acid.

items.stem:
Optical density (OD600) of a bacterial batch culture:

Time (h) | OD600
0.0 | 0.10
1.0 | 0.20
2.0 | 0.40
3.0 | 0.80
4.0 | 1.50
5.0 | 1.60
6.0 | 1.55

Which description of growth phases is justified?

choices.text: Death phase begins at 1 h because the first doubling has already occurred
Exponential growth continues through 6 h because OD remains above 0.10
Exponential doubling time is 1.0 h from 0–3 h; the culture is entering stationary phase by 4–6 h
The culture is in lag phase for the entire 6 h because OD never exceeds 2

items.explanation: From 0.10 to 0.80 in 3 h the OD doubles every hour (0.10→0.20→0.40→0.80), the definition of exponential growth with a 1 h doubling time. Between 3 and 4 h the increase is less than a doubling (0.80→1.50), and by 5–6 h OD plateaus near 1.6, i.e. stationary phase. Lag would be a delay before doubling starts, but doubling is immediate here. Death phase would be a sustained OD fall, not a 1.60 to 1.55 wobble after a plateau. Remaining above the inoculum OD does not mean exponential growth continues.

distractorRationales.A: Completing a doubling is exponential growth, not death.
distractorRationales.B: After 3 h the successive ratios are 1.50/0.80 and 1.60/1.50, not a constant factor of 2, so exponential growth has ended.
distractorRationales.D: Lag is a period without net increase; this culture doubles immediately, so it is not in lag.

items.stem:
Physical data for three chlorides:

Compound | melting point (°C) | electrical conductivity of liquid | ΔEN (Pauling)
NaCl | 801 | high | 2.1
MgCl2 | 714 | high | 1.8
SiCl4 | −70 | none | 1.2

Which bonding assignment matches the table?

choices.text: NaCl and MgCl2 are ionic lattices that melt to mobile ions; SiCl4 is a covalent molecular liquid with no free ions
SiCl4 is ionic because chlorine is present, which is why it melts at −70 °C
NaCl is molecular, because 801 °C is too low for a lattice
All three are giant covalent networks, so all should conduct when molten

items.explanation: High melting points plus molten conductivity are the ionic-lattice signature: Na+Cl− and Mg2+Cl− melt into mobile ions. SiCl4 melts at −70 °C and does not conduct, so it is a discrete SiCl4 molecule held by weak intermolecular forces, consistent with a smaller electronegativity gap. Chlorine content does not make a compound ionic. 801 °C is a typical ionic melting point, not a molecular one. A giant covalent chloride would not melt at −70 °C, and molten NaCl/MgCl2 conductivity would then be unexplained if there were no ions.

distractorRationales.B: An ionic lattice does not melt at −70 °C, and molten SiCl4 does not conduct.
distractorRationales.C: 801 °C and high molten conductivity are ionic, not molecular, markers.
distractorRationales.D: SiCl4’s −70 °C melting point and zero conductivity rule out a giant network, and networks do not produce ionic conductivity on melting.

items.stem: A hoist lifts a 50 kg crate at constant speed through 4.0 m in 8.0 s. g = 10 m s−2. Work against gravity is mgh. Average power is W/t. What are W and P? If the motor is only 50% efficient, what electrical power input is required?

choices.text: W = 16 000 J; P = 2000 W (using mgh t)
W = 2000 J; P = 250 W; input 500 W
W = 2000 J; P = 250 W; input 250 W, ignoring efficiency
W = 400 J; P = 50 W (using 50 kg as if it were newtons)

items.explanation: Weight = 500 N, so W = 500 × 4.0 = 2000 J. Average output power = 2000/8.0 = 250 W. At 50% efficiency the electrical input must be 250 / 0.50 = 500 W. Efficiency less than one always means a larger input than the useful mechanical output. Treating 50 kg as 50 N undercounts work by g. Multiplying by t instead of dividing inflates power. Constant speed means the motor force equals weight, so W = mgh is the useful work.

distractorRationales.A: Power is work/time, not work × time; 2000 J in 8 s is 250 W.
distractorRationales.C: 50% efficiency doubles the required input relative to the 250 W mechanical output.
distractorRationales.D: Force is 50 × 10 = 500 N, not 50 N; work is 2000 J.

items.stem: Expert typists and novices type a standard paragraph either alone or with three classmates watching. Experts become faster and more accurate with the audience; novices become slower and make more errors. Which account best fits both results?

choices.text: Social loafing: an audience always reduces effort, so both groups should slow
Deindividuation: the audience makes experts anonymous and therefore more skilled
Social facilitation (Zajonc): presence of others raises arousal and the dominant response—correct for experts, errors for novices
Bystander effect: each spectator assumes another spectator will type

items.explanation: Social facilitation is the effect of an audience or co-actors on individual performance. Zajonc’s drive account says mere presence increases arousal, which potentiates the dominant response. For a well-learned skill the dominant response is the correct one, so experts improve; for a poorly learned skill the dominant response is error, so novices worsen. Loafing predicts less effort when output is pooled, which is not this design. Deindividuation is reduced self-awareness in anonymous crowds, not a skill-enhancing audience. Bystander logic applies to helping in emergencies, not to typing.

distractorRationales.A: Experts improved, which loafing cannot explain, and typing was an individual task with identifiable output.
distractorRationales.B: Named classmates watching is the opposite of anonymity, and deindividuation does not turn novices’ errors into expertise.
distractorRationales.D: Spectators were not potential helpers in an emergency; they were an audience for a performance task.

items.stem: After a steelman of “speed is care,” which closing move actually answers it rather than merely mentioning it?

choices.text: “Of course some delays harm, but that fact supports targeted speed for clinical windows, not a general rule that whoever can buy a shorter clock is therefore caring.”
“As mentioned, there is another view. In conclusion, waiting is deep.”
“I respect all opinions equally, so both speed and waiting are correct.”
“See comment 2.”

items.explanation: Answering a counterargument means altering or delimiting your thesis in light of it, or showing why the strongest objection still fails. A grants medical windows and then blocks the slide from those windows to a market in shorter clocks. That is a reply. B names the other view and then vapours. C collapses into a draw that the task did not ask for. A bare “see comment 2” is a pointer, not a thought. The craft is steelman-and-answer, not a polite wave. Under time, one precise delimitation is enough. A is the delimitation.

distractorRationales.B: Mention plus a vague profundity about waiting does not meet the harm-from-delay objection.
distractorRationales.C: Equal respect for all opinions abandons evaluation, which is the Task A job.
distractorRationales.D: Pointing at a comment is not an answer; the essay still has to do the distinguishing work.

items.stem: Rats drink novel saccharin and, hours later, receive lithium that produces nausea; they later avoid saccharin. The same rats do not readily associate a click with nausea, nor saccharin with immediate footshock. Garcia and Koelling’s preparedness result most directly challenges which assumption of early Pavlovian/Skinnerian theory?

choices.text: The existence of operant schedules, because variable-ratio is still most extinction-resistant
That taste can ever be a CS, because only auditory CSs work
Bandura’s claim that rats cannot learn without a live model
Equipotentiality: any CS can be equally associated with any US given temporal contiguity

items.explanation: Garcia showed one-trial, long-delay taste–illness learning and selectivity: tastes pair with nausea more readily than clicks do, and audiovisual cues pair more readily with shock. That violates the equipotentiality assumption that the CS–US slot is content-free and that close contiguity is always required. Operant schedule rankings are a different chapter of associative learning. Tastes clearly can be CSs. Bandura’s observational learning is not the target of the bait-shyness experiments.

distractorRationales.A: VR extinction resistance is true but is not what Garcia’s selective associations challenge.
distractorRationales.B: The point is that taste is an especially good CS for illness, not that taste cannot be a CS.
distractorRationales.C: Garcia’s rats learned without observation of a model; Bandura is not the foil here.

items.stem: Adolescents privately choose a longer study plan when deciding alone. After three classmates mock studying as “try-hard,” many switch to a shorter plan in a public roundtable, but an anonymous questionnaire still shows preference for the long plan. Which process is illustrated?

choices.text: Informational social influence, because they now believe the classmates have better academic data
Social loafing on homework effort in a group project
Normative peer pressure: public compliance without private acceptance
Deindividuation, because the classroom lights were off

items.explanation: Peer pressure often operates through normative influence: people go along to gain approval or avoid ridicule even when they do not change their private belief. The split between public shortening and anonymous endorsement of the long plan is compliance without internalization. Informational influence would update the private questionnaire as well, because the person would think the others were right. Loafing is about effort on a pooled task, not about which plan is announced. Deindividuation was not manipulated with anonymity or darkness in the stem.

distractorRationales.A: Unchanged private scores mean they did not adopt the classmates’ view as information about what works.
distractorRationales.B: No collective product is being under-produced; the measure is a publicly stated plan.
distractorRationales.D: Lights-off anonymity is not described; students were identifiable in a roundtable.

items.stem: An autosomal recessive disease occurs in 1/10,000 newborns in a large, randomly mating population that meets Hardy–Weinberg assumptions. What is the expected frequency of heterozygous carriers?

choices.text: 1/10,000, equal to the incidence of affected homozygotes.
Approximately 1/50, because q^2 = 10^−4 so q = 0.01 and 2pq ≈ 2(1)(0.01) = 0.02.
1/100, equal to the allele frequency q rather than the heterozygote frequency 2pq.
1/200, because Hardy–Weinberg counting includes only half of the heterozygotes.

items.explanation: Under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium the frequency of affected homozygotes is q^2. If q^2 = 1/10,000, then q = 0.01. For a rare allele p ≈ 1, so the heterozygote (carrier) frequency 2pq ≈ 2 × 0.01 = 0.02, or 1 in 50. The incidence of affected births is q^2, not the carrier rate. The allele frequency q is 0.01 (1/100), which is not 2pq. There is no Hardy–Weinberg convention of counting only half of heterozygotes; 2pq already is the full heterozygote frequency.

distractorRationales.A: 1/10,000 is q^2, the affected homozygote frequency, not the much larger pool of heterozygous carriers.
distractorRationales.C: q = 0.01 is the recessive allele frequency; carriers are 2pq ≈ 0.02.
distractorRationales.D: 2pq already counts all heterozygotes; there is no extra factor of 1/2 in the standard carrier calculation.

items.stem: A radiology group installs a new computer-aided detection overlay. The same attendings read the same chest films. Hit rate for subtle nodules rises, but so does the false-alarm rate; a signal-detection analysis finds d′ unchanged. Which change in the decision process best accounts for the pattern?

choices.text: Sensory discriminability improved, because more true nodules are now named
Readers adopted a more liberal criterion, accepting more yes responses at a fixed d′
The payoff matrix became more conservative, raising the criterion and cutting false alarms
Weber fractions for luminance shrank, so smaller density differences became detectable

items.explanation: Signal-detection theory separates sensitivity (d′, distance between noise and signal-plus-noise distributions) from criterion (β or C). A liberal shift increases both hits and false alarms while leaving d′ unchanged, which is the overlay pattern. Improved discriminability would raise d′ and typically improve hits without a matched false-alarm rise. A conservative criterion does the opposite of what was observed. Weber’s law is a ratio of intensity increments, not a yes/no decision policy on films.

distractorRationales.A: More hits with matching false alarms and flat d′ is a criterion shift, not a true sensitivity gain.
distractorRationales.C: A conservative criterion would lower, not raise, both hits and false alarms.
distractorRationales.D: Weber’s law does not describe yes/no nodule calls or ROC parameters on radiographs.

items.stem: A thin converging lens has focal length 10 cm. A real object stands 30 cm from the lens. Using the real-is-positive convention, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Linear magnification m = −v/u. Where is the image, and what is m?

choices.text: Real image 7.5 cm from the lens, m = −0.25
Real image 15 cm from the lens, inverted, half size (m = −0.50)
Virtual image 15 cm behind the object, m = +2.0
Real image 30 cm from the lens, m = −1.0

items.explanation: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 3/30 − 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15, so v = 15 cm, real, on the far side. m = −15/30 = −0.50: inverted and half as tall. A virtual image would require a negative v, which occurs for u < f, not for u = 3f. Equal object and image distances would need u = 2f = 20 cm, the 2f–2f case, not 30 cm. 7.5 cm would be f/something other than the lens equation. The object is outside f, so the image of a converging lens is real and inverted.

distractorRationales.A: 7.5 cm is not 1/(1/10 − 1/30); that difference of reciprocals is 1/15.
distractorRationales.C: u = 30 cm > f, so the image is real and inverted, not virtual and upright.
distractorRationales.D: u = v = 30 cm would require f = 15 cm (1/30+1/30=1/15), not f = 10 cm.

items.stem:
A stock solution is 2.00 M HCl. Dilution uses C1V1 = C2V2.
Step 1: 10.0 mL stock is made up to 100.0 mL (flask A).
Step 2: 10.0 mL of A is made up to 100.0 mL (flask B).
Step 3: 10.0 mL of B is made up to 100.0 mL (flask C).
What is [HCl] in flask C?
items.explanation: Each step multiplies concentration by 10.0/100.0 = 0.100, a tenfold dilution. Three successive tenfold dilutions multiply by 10−3, so 2.00 × 10−3 = 0.00200 M. After one step the solution would be 0.200 M and after two steps 0.0200 M; stopping the count early produces those distractors. Four tenfold steps would give 0.000200 M. The volumes are consistent with C1V1 = C2V2 at each stage: 2.00 × 10.0 = C × 100, and repeating.

distractorRationales.B: 0.0200 M is the concentration after two dilutions, flask B, not flask C.
distractorRationales.C: 0.200 M is flask A, after a single 10 → 100 mL dilution.
distractorRationales.D: 0.000200 M would be a fourth tenfold dilution that was not performed.

items.stem: A uniform 4.0 m beam weighs 80 N. It rests on supports at both ends (A left, B right). A 40 N crate sits 1.0 m from A. Vertical equilibrium: RA + RB = 120 N. Torque about A: clockwise 80 N at 2.0 m plus 40 N at 1.0 m equals RB × 4.0 m. What are RA and RB?

choices.text: RA = 80 N; RB = 40 N, each support taking the nearer load only
RA = 60 N; RB = 60 N, splitting the 120 N equally
RA = 70 N; RB = 50 N
RA = 50 N; RB = 70 N

items.explanation: Moments about A: 80 × 2.0 + 40 × 1.0 = 160 + 40 = 200 N m = RB × 4.0, so RB = 50 N. Then RA = 120 − 50 = 70 N. The left support carries more because the crate is closer to A. Swapping 70 and 50 puts the larger reaction at the far end. Assigning each support only the object next to it ignores that the beam’s own 80 N is shared. Equal 60 N reactions would be correct only if the extra 40 N sat at the midpoint.

distractorRationales.A: The beam’s weight acts at the centre and is supported by both ends, not solely by A.
distractorRationales.B: Equal reactions would require the 40 N load at mid-span, not 1.0 m from A.
distractorRationales.D: The crate is nearer A, so A must carry the larger share; moments about A already fix RB = 50 N.

items.stem: Which paraphrase best captures the author's view of notation without turning it into a call to abolish scores?

choices.text: Notation is a historically specific technology that captures some relations and leaks others; scores remain tools, not the work's ontology.
All written music is a fraud, so conservatories should teach only unrecorded improvisation.
The metronome proved that village dances were secretly in three all along.
Recordings have finally made the score unnecessary because microphones are neutral.

items.explanation: The passage attacks score-as-work while saying the upshot is not to burn scores: maps are superb, the crime is calling the map the territory. Notation captures and leaks. That is A. B inflates critique into abolition the last paragraph denies. C inverts the village-dance remark. D ignores the politics of which night and which microphone. A good paraphrase keeps the tool/ontology split rather than picking a pole the author refused.

distractorRationales.B: The author explicitly says the practical upshot is not to burn scores.
distractorRationales.C: “In three” is a notational decision a dance may never have made; the metronome is a later fantasy of a ruler.
distractorRationales.D: Recordings are a new paper with their own aiming and hierarchy, not a neutral replacement.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

items.stem: Equal amounts of NADH and of succinate (feeding electrons via Complex II) are oxidized by intact mitochondria. Why does NADH oxidation support more ATP synthesis per pair of electrons?

choices.text: NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I) pumps protons, whereas Complex II does not, so NADH-derived electrons drive a larger proton-motive force per 2e−.
Electrons from succinate enter at Complex IV, skipping Complex III and cytochrome c, so fewer protons are pumped.
NADH reduces oxygen directly in the matrix, producing an extra substrate-level GTP.
Succinate dehydrogenase consumes ATP to transfer electrons to ubiquinone.

items.explanation: Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, which translocates protons, then proceed through ubiquinone, Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV, which also pump protons. Electrons from succinate/FADH2 enter at Complex II, which does not pump protons, and join the chain at ubiquinone; they therefore miss the Complex I contribution to Δp. The smaller proton yield per 2e− means a lower P/O ratio for succinate than for NADH. Succinate does not skip Complex III, NADH does not reduce O2 directly, and Complex II does not hydrolyze ATP to reduce Q. Those facts explain why NADH oxidation supports more ATP per electron pair.

distractorRationales.B: Succinate electrons enter at Complex II/ubiquinone, not at Complex IV, and they still pass through Complex III and cytochrome c. Skipping pumps is not how succinate feeds the chain.
distractorRationales.C: NADH is oxidized by Complex I, not by a direct matrix reaction with O2, and that path does not make substrate-level GTP.
distractorRationales.D: Complex II transfers electrons from succinate to Q without ATP hydrolysis; it is not an ATP-consuming pump.

items.stem: An inhibitor binds the FAD-dependent enzyme that oxidizes a four-carbon citric-acid-cycle intermediate to a trans-unsaturated four-carbon product. The same polypeptide is an integral component of the inner mitochondrial membrane electron-transport chain. Which enzyme is it, and which reduced cofactor does it produce?

choices.text: Malate dehydrogenase; NADH
Succinate dehydrogenase; enzyme-bound FADH2 that reduces ubiquinone
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; NADPH
Fumarase; NADH
