+ 4 cm | one ninhydrin-positive spot
0 cm (origin) | one spot
− 4 cm | none

Which assignment is consistent?

choices.text: Both amino acids are at the origin because they are zwitterions in the solid state
Lysine is at −4 cm because pI 9.7 is larger, so it must be negative
Glycine migrates to the cathode at its isoelectric pH
The origin is glycine (net zero at pH = pI); the cathodic spot is lysine (net positive at pH 6.0 < 9.7)

items.explanation: At pH 6.0 glycine is at its pI, so its net charge is zero and it stays at the origin. Lysine’s pI is 9.7, so at pH 6 both its carboxylates and its extra side-chain ammonium are such that the net charge is positive; it moves toward the cathode (+4 cm). There is no anodic spot, matching the absence of a net-negative species. Solid-state zwitterions still acquire a net charge in a pH 6 buffer if pI ≠ 6. A higher pI means more basic, hence cationic at pH 6, not anionic. Migration of glycine at its pI would contradict the definition of pI.

distractorRationales.A: The strip shows a second spot at +4 cm, so they do not both remain at the origin.
distractorRationales.B: pI > pH produces a cation, which moves to the cathode, the +4 cm position, not the anode.
distractorRationales.C: At pH = pI the net charge is zero; glycine is the origin spot.

items.stem: Extrapolating the 10 min half-life to t = 60 min predicts net rate nearest

choices.text: 0, because all nuclei vanish at 6 half-lives.

items.explanation: 60 min is 6 half-lives from t = 0: 800 / 2^6 = 800/64 = 12.5 min−1. That is already comparable to the subtracted background of 12, so the extrapolation is numerically 12.5 but experimentally fragile—an extra honesty the overlay interpolation/extrapolation topic includes as limits of the data. Not 800, not one half-life, and not a hard zero at six half-lives (1/64 remains).

distractorRationales.A: That is t = 0.
distractorRationales.C: That is t = 10 min.
distractorRationales.D: Six half-lives leave 1/64 of the activity, not a magical zero.

passage.title: Counting a short-lived sample
passage.body:
A detector records decays from a small source. Background, measured overnight with the source removed, is 12 counts per minute. The table is net rate after subtracting that background (already done by the software). Clock time starts when the sample is placed.

t / min | net counts per minute
0 | 800
5 | 566
10 | 400
15 | 283
20 | 200
25 | 141
40 | 50

The software also reports a 2-minute count at t = 10 min as 800 counts (raw, including background). A student wants the half-life from any two points and also wants activity in Bq.

items.stem: Measured pKa values: acetic acid 4.76, chloroacetic acid 2.87, dichloroacetic acid 1.35. Which explanation accounts for the trend?

choices.text: Chlorine donates electron density by resonance into the carboxylate, making the acid weaker as more Cl is added
Each chlorine withdraws electron density inductively through the σ framework, stabilizing the conjugate base and lowering pKa
Chlorinated acids are strong mineral acids like HCl, so pKa collapses to that of hydrochloric acid
Chlorine increases the hydrophobicity of the acid, which always increases pKa in water

items.explanation: Carboxylic-acid strength in this series is controlled by inductive stabilization of the conjugate base. Electronegative chlorines pull electron density through the C–C σ bonds toward themselves, dispersing the negative charge on the carboxylate and favoring dissociation. More chlorines, or chlorines closer to the carboxyl, give a larger effect, matching the stepwise drop in pKa. Resonance donation from Cl into the carboxylate would raise pKa, which is the opposite of the data. These are still weak organic acids, not fully dissociated mineral acids, and hydrophobicity is not the parameter that tracks this halogen trend.

distractorRationales.A: Inductive withdrawal, not resonance donation, is the dominant substituent effect of alkyl chlorides on aliphatic acids. The data show stronger, not weaker, acids.
distractorRationales.C: Even dichloroacetic acid is not HCl. It remains an equilibrium weak acid, albeit a relatively strong one among carboxylic acids.
distractorRationales.D: Adding chlorines lowers pKa here. A generic ‘hydrophobic acids are weaker’ rule does not explain the observed trend.

items.stem:
An object starts from rest with constant acceleration a. Then s = (1/2) a t^2. Four timings are:

t (s) | s (m)
1.0 | 2.0
2.0 | 8.0
3.0 | 18
4.0 | 32

Which graph is linear, and what acceleration does its slope give?

choices.text: s versus t is linear with slope 8.0 m s−1, so a = 8.0 m s−2.
s versus t is linear with slope 2.0 m s−1, so a = 4.0 m s−2.
s versus t^2 is linear with slope 8.0 m s−2, so a = 8.0 m s−2.
s versus t^2 is linear with slope 2.0 m s−2, so a = 4.0 m s−2 because slope = a/2.

items.explanation: Check s / t^2: 2.0/1 = 2.0, 8.0/4 = 2.0, 18/9 = 2.0, 32/16 = 2.0 m s−2 at every row. Therefore s = 2.0 t^2, which is a straight line of slope 2.0 m s−2 when s is plotted against t^2. Comparing with s = (1/2) a t^2 gives a/2 = 2.0, so a = 4.0 m s−2. A plot of s versus t is a parabola (2, 8, 18, 32 m at equal time steps), not a straight line. Taking the last-over-first slope (32 − 2)/(4 − 1) ≈ 10 m s−1 is not a. Using slope = a instead of a/2 on the t^2 graph would report 2.0 m s−2, which is not among the options that pair the correct graph with a = 4.0 m s−2 except D.

distractorRationales.A: s versus t is not linear: the successive s values 2, 8, 18, 32 are not in arithmetic sequence. Constant a produces a parabola on an s–t graph.
distractorRationales.B: s versus t is parabolic, not linear. A slope of 2.0 m s−1 also does not match the tabulated Δs/Δt values, which increase with t.
distractorRationales.C: s versus t^2 is linear, but its slope is 2.0 m s−2, not 8.0. Even if the slope were 8, that would be a/2, implying a = 16 m s−2, not 8.

items.stem:
A heating curve for 18 g (1.00 mol) of H2O at 1 atm uses Lf = 6.0 kJ mol−1 and Lv = 41 kJ mol−1, and c = 75 J mol−1 K−1 for liquid water. The curve’s plateaux are:

Segment | T (°C) | heat absorbed (kJ) | process
AB | 0 | 6.0 | ice → water
BC | 0 → 100 | 7.5 | warming liquid
CD | 100 | 41 | water → steam

Which statement is required by the data?

choices.text: Latent-heat plateaux occur at the melting and boiling points; warming the liquid 100 °C costs 1.00 × 75 × 100 J = 7.5 kJ, matching BC
The longest energy segment is melting, because AB is drawn first
Temperature rises during AB and CD, because heat is being absorbed
BC should cost 41 kJ, the same as vaporisation

items.explanation: At 1 atm, ice melts at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C; during those phase changes T is constant while the latent heats 6.0 and 41 kJ are absorbed. Between them, q = n c ΔT = 1.00 × 75 J K−1 × 100 K = 7500 J = 7.5 kJ, which is row BC. Vaporisation dwarfs fusion (41 versus 6.0 kJ), so CD, not AB, is the costly plateau. Heat absorbed at a phase change does not raise T; that is why they are plateaux. Equating the liquid-warming leg to Lv confuses sensible heat with latent heat.

distractorRationales.B: AB is 6.0 kJ; CD is 41 kJ, so boiling, not melting, is the largest energy step.
distractorRationales.C: The table lists constant T for AB and CD; absorbed heat there breaks intermolecular forces, not the thermometer reading.
distractorRationales.D: 41 kJ is Lv for CD; BC is the 7.5 kJ sensible-heat calculation.

items.stem: A 10.0 L flask at 300 K holds 0.20 mol O2 and 0.80 mol N2. Dalton’s law: each gas’s partial pressure is its mole fraction times Ptotal, and Ptotal = ntotal RT/V with R = 0.080 L atm mol−1 K−1. Graham’s law: rate of effusion ∝ 1/√Mr. What is p(O2), and how many times faster does O2 (Mr 32) effuse than SO2 (Mr 64) through the same pinhole?

choices.text: p(O2) = 2.4 atm; O2 effuses 2 times faster
p(O2) = 0.48 atm; O2 effuses 2 times faster (64/32 without the square root)
p(O2) = 0.080 atm; rates are equal because both are gases
p(O2) = 0.48 atm; O2 effuses √2 ≈ 1.4 times faster than SO2

items.explanation: ntotal = 1.00 mol, so Ptotal = 1.00 × 0.080 × 300 / 10.0 = 2.4 atm. Mole fraction of O2 is 0.20, so p(O2) = 0.48 atm. Graham’s ratio is √(64/32) = √2 ≈ 1.41, not 2. Using Ptotal as if it were p(O2) gives 2.4 atm. Dropping the square root doubles the effusion ratio. p(O2) is not R, and molar mass clearly separates the effusion rates.

distractorRationales.A: 2.4 atm is the total pressure, not the oxygen partial pressure; the effusion factor 2 omitted the square root and used the wrong pairing anyway if applied to O2/SO2 without √.
distractorRationales.B: The 0.48 atm figure is right, but effusion rates go as the square root of the inverse mass ratio, √2 not 2.
distractorRationales.C: 0.080 is R, not a pressure here; different Mr values mean different effusion rates.

items.stem: With thirty minutes for Task A, which structure best uses the opening, middle, and close?

choices.text: Opening: “According to the dictionary, justice means…” Middle: three unrelated news headlines. Close: restatement of the dictionary line.

Opening: a contestable thesis about whose clock counts. Middle: one developed example plus a steelmanned objection. Close: a sharpened version of the thesis after the objection, not a copy of sentence one.
Opening: a joke about the invigilator. Middle: the joke again. Close: “In conclusion, as I said.”
Opening skipped. Middle: a single paragraph that tries to do everything. Close: omitted because time ran out after the throat-clearing.

items.explanation: Structure under time is not a five-paragraph template; it is a job for each part. The opening should stake. The middle should earn, including by meeting an objection. The close should be cheaper than a new idea but more than echo—typically a delimited thesis. Dictionary openings waste the most valuable sentences. Jokes about invigilators do not stake a civic claim. Skipping the opening and then drowning is how many scripts die. B is the portable skeleton that still looks like thinking. It can be written in thirty minutes if the example stays single and specified.

distractorRationales.A: Dictionary openings and headline scatter are two classic ways not to argue.
distractorRationales.C: Invigilator jokes do not open a socio-cultural argument, and a copied close adds nothing.
distractorRationales.D: Throat-clearing that consumes the clock is a structure failure, not a personality trait markers must forgive.

items.stem: The two newspaper headings most nearly illustrate

choices.text: identical reporting of a transport miracle.
rival social framings of the same image: order restored versus children exposing a dead service.
that overseas papers cannot see children.
that strikers printed both papers.

items.explanation: Same photograph, two headings: normality versus mockery of a dead line. That is sociological commentary on how a crowd of children is enlisted to different public stories. A denies the split. C is false. D is unsupported. The headings are doing social meaning-making, which is why they are quoted at all.

distractorRationales.A: The headings disagree.
distractorRationales.C: The overseas heading is about children.
distractorRationales.D: Ownership of the papers is not given.

passage.title: Note on a cancelled tram
passage.body:
In the third week of the lockout the company ran a single tram, brightly lit, along the route at dusk, with no passengers permitted. Officials called it a demonstration of service. Strikers called it a lantern on a coffin. Children ran beside it anyway, as they had when the cars were working, and were photographed. The photograph was printed in the morning paper under the heading NORMALITY RETURNS, and in an overseas paper under the heading CHILDREN MOCK THE DEAD LINE.

A clerk in the tram office, years later, wrote that he had been told to leave the lights on even if the generator complained, because darkness would look like surrender. He added, without apparent bitterness, that surrender had already occurred in the timetable. What remained was a moving argument about who owned the look of a street at evening.

Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

items.stem: The claim that an interview “can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette” plays which role in the argument?

choices.text: It is offered as evidence that official gazettes are generally more accurate than spoken testimony and should therefore remain the backbone of public history.
It blocks the inference that switching from paper to speech is by itself a democratic solution, by asserting that control can migrate into the making of the interview.
It is a concession that colonial records should be discarded because their tightness makes them unusable as historical sources.
It defines democracy as a property of recording technology, so that any taped interview counts as a democratic act.

items.explanation: The oral-history paragraph grants that interviews can admit people the file forgot, then immediately warns that the corrective is not automatic. The gazette comparison is the argumentative block: if prompting, recording, and cutting can be as tightly managed as an official publication, then orality as such does not deliver democracy. What the author wants instead is visibility of the historian in the manufacture of the record. The sentence is not a defense of gazettes, a call to throw them out, or a technological definition of democracy. Its logical job is to undercut an inference the preceding sentences might otherwise have licensed.

distractorRationales.A: The author never ranks gazette accuracy above speech; the comparison is about manageability of production, not about which genre is truer.
distractorRationales.C: The passage refuses abandonment of documents and does not argue that colonial tightness makes written sources unusable.
distractorRationales.D: Responsible oral history is distinguished by visible steering and refusal, not by the mere fact that a machine was running.

passage.title: The archive and the street
passage.body:
Historians often speak as if the past were a reluctant witness who can be coaxed into testimony if only the right box is opened. The letter, the minute-book, the trial transcript, and the parish register are treated not as remnants but as the event itself, patiently waiting to be interviewed. The metaphor is professionally convenient. It locates virtue in attentiveness and implies that an archive, handled without aggression, will speak of its own accord. Archives do not speak. They are offices that decide, usually long before a scholar arrives, which traces of life will be kept, numbered, and thereby made eligible for later recovery. To mistake a folder for a microphone is to forget that someone built the studio, invited some guests, and switched the machine off when the conversation became inconvenient.

This is not a case for abandoning documents. It is a case against a piety now common in public history: the belief that proximity to a primary source is itself a moral credential. Museum captions announce that an object was found in an attic or rescued from a demolition site, as if its later career in a glass case were a continuation of its first life rather than a conversion into evidence. Conversion is what historians do. Trouble begins when conversion is narrated as rescue, because that narration conceals the historian's power and, more consequentially, conceals the people who never generated a paper trail to be rescued.

Oral historians have pressed this objection for decades, sometimes with more hope than caution. They have offered the recorded interview as a democratic patch, a way of admitting those whom the file forgot. The patch is real; it is not automatic. An interview is also a document, made under conditions of prompting, recording, transcription, and later cutting. It can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette. What distinguishes a responsible oral history is not orality as such, but the historian remaining visible in the manufacture of the record—visible enough that a later reader can see where a question steered, where a narrator pushed back, and where a silence was not a hole but a refusal.

The sharper problem is civic rather than technical. If the only past that can be cited is the past that was filed, public memory will go on over-representing those who employed clerks. Cities make the point more bluntly than seminars do. A demolished neighborhood deposits fewer cartons than a merchant's townhouse; a street seller deposits fewer than a chartered company. When a preservation trust then campaigns to save the townhouse because it is richly documented, the trust is not merely selecting architecture. It is ratifying a distribution of paperwork as a distribution of historical weight. The house is asked to stand for an age, and the undocumented street is invited, if at all, to supply atmosphere.

Honesty does not require the fantasy that every life can be reconstructed with equal density. Some absences are final. The decent procedure is to treat those absences as facts about power rather than as temporary vacancies that a more heroic search will fill. A history that admits what cannot be known is more public-minded than a history that performs completeness by adding still more pages to an already thick dossier. The archive will remain necessary. It need not remain innocent.

items.stem: The plaque “THEY WERE NOT LATE. THEY WERE PREVENTED.” is best read, in context, as

choices.text: a transport apology for a delayed tram.
a refusal of a lateness story in favour of a story of being stopped, which the corridor then makes physical.
proof the sculptor wanted more names.
the veteran’s slogan.

items.explanation: The whole piece is about blocked passage and the sculptor’s anti-healing door. The plaque’s contrast late/prevented reassigns blame from the dead to an agent of stopping. The critic later says prevention becomes a body insisting on width. A imports the other extract’s tram. C contradicts no names. D is a different speaker. Main claim of the plaque inside this extract is that re-description, not a timetable.

distractorRationales.A: Trams belong to another passage; this is a memorial corridor.
distractorRationales.C: The work has no names; the sculptor is not asking for a directory here.
distractorRationales.D: The veteran speaks about hating and remaining; he does not author the plaque.

passage.title: On the new memorial
passage.body:
The memorial is a corridor of rusted uprights, each the height of a person, irregularly spaced so that you must turn sideways to pass. At noon they look like a failed fence. At dusk they look like a crowd that has agreed not to face you. There are no names. A small plaque at the exit says only: THEY WERE NOT LATE. THEY WERE PREVENTED.

Tourists complain that they do not know whom to pity. School groups count the uprights and get different numbers, because some are so close they read as one. A veteran interviewed on the steps said he hated it, then stood there until the lights came on, then said he hated that he did not hate it enough.

The sculptor, in a panel discussion, refused the word healing. “If it heals,” she said, “it has failed at being a door you cannot swagger through.” Critics split between those who call this moral bullying in Cor-Ten steel and those who call the tourists’ complaint the point.

I went through twice. The second time a child asked why the fence was broken. His father said it was not a fence. The child, satisfied with a new category, ran. I was not satisfied. Prevention is a bureaucratic word. In the corridor it becomes a body insisting on its width.

items.stem: Which pair of claims does the passage hold together without treating them as a contradiction?

choices.text: Scores should be burned, and recordings are the true work.
The worry about impressionistic study without a text is real in a university, and some traditions still rightly treat the night’s playing as the work.
Jazz time is a failed metronome grid, and village dances were always in three.
Microphones are neutral, and fans who own every take therefore know what the music is for.

items.explanation: Paragraph three grants the university’s need for a shared object and immediately limits the grant: the worry is less real where the night is the work. That is a qualification, not a collapse. The last paragraph repeats the pattern with maps. A, C, and D assemble positions the author rejects. Internal consistency here is the author’s habit of granting a real institutional problem without letting it dictate ontology.

distractorRationales.A: Both burning scores and treating recordings as the true work are refused.
distractorRationales.C: Jazz time is a negotiation, not a failed grid; dances may never have been “in three.”
distractorRationales.D: Recordings smuggle politics; owning takes can multiply facts while missing purpose.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

items.stem:
Formation of nickel complexes in water (Ni2+ is d8):

Species | added ligand | colour | proposed formula | coordination number
aqua ion | H2O | green | [Ni(H2O)6]2+ | 6
+ excess NH3 | NH3 | blue-violet | [Ni(NH3)6]2+ | 6
+ excess CN− | CN− | yellow | [Ni(CN)4]2− | 4

Charge on the cyano complex: Ni2+ plus 4 CN−. Which statement is consistent?

choices.text: The aqua ion is [Ni(H2O)4]2+ because the cyano complex is four-coordinate
Adding NH3 oxidises Ni2+ to Ni3+, which is why the colour changes
Water and ammonia give octahedral Ni(II); cyanide, a strong-field ligand, gives a four-coordinate [Ni(CN)4]2− of charge 2−
[Ni(CN)4]2− must contain Ni(IV) because the charge is 2−

items.explanation: The aqua and ammine rows are both coordination number 6, the usual octahedral Ni(II) complexes, with ligand substitution (not a change of oxidation state) explaining the green to blue-violet shift. Four cyanide ligands on Ni2+ give overall charge 2 + 4(−1) = −2, matching [Ni(CN)4]2−, a well-known square-planar strong-field complex of d8 Ni(II). Charge 2− does not require Ni(IV) (that would be Ni4+ + 4 CN− = 0). The aqua ion is listed as six-coordinate. Colour change on adding NH3 is ligand-field substitution of H2O, not oxidation to Ni3+.

distractorRationales.A: The table assigns the aqua ion coordination number 6, [Ni(H2O)6]2+.
distractorRationales.B: The ammine formula still contains Ni2+; NH3 is not an oxidant here.
distractorRationales.D: Ni2+ + 4 CN− = −2 overall with nickel still in the +2 state.

items.stem: A draft reads: “They never understood me. They were wrong. I was right. The end.” What is the principal reflective-voice failure, and which revision begins to repair it?

choices.text: Failure: too much world, not enough self. Repair: delete every concrete table and name only “society.”
Failure: the “I” prosecutes without examining itself. Repair: “I called it misunderstanding because that word hurt less than admitting I had used silence as a weapon too.”
Failure: presence of any family. Repair: write about interest rates.
Failure: brevity. Repair: triple the length with adjectives of rage.

items.explanation: The draft’s “I” is a verdict machine. Reflection would turn the lens around: how the writer named the hurt, what the naming protected, whether silence went both ways. The repair sentence does that without cancelling the hurt. Making the piece less particular or fleeing into rates would be a task error. Lengthening rage is still prosecution. Voice here is not decoration; it is the difference between a diary dump and a piece of thought. B names the failure and a first repair that a marker could actually reward.

distractorRationales.A: The draft is already short on world; more fog is not the cure.
distractorRationales.C: Family is legitimate Task B material; the failure is unexamined verdict, not the topic.
distractorRationales.D: More rage without self-scrutiny would intensify the same failure.

items.stem: A 10 kg crate on a rough horizontal floor is pulled by a 20 N horizontal force. Kinetic friction is 5.0 N. Newton’s second law is ΣF = ma. Starting from rest, what is the acceleration, and how far has the crate moved after 4.0 s?

choices.text: a = 2.5 m s−2; s = 20 m (adding friction to the pull)
a = 2.0 m s−2; s = 16 m (friction omitted)

items.explanation: Net force = 20 − 5.0 = 15 N, so a = 15/10 = 1.5 m s−2. From rest, s = (1/2) a t² = 0.50 × 1.5 × 16 = 12 m. Omitting friction gives a = 2.0 m s−2 and 16 m. Using only the 5 N friction as the net force gives 0.50 m s−2. Adding friction to the pull as if both acted forward gives 25 N and 2.5 m s−2. The free-body diagram has the pull forward and friction backward.

distractorRationales.A: 0.50 m s−2 would be 5.0 N / 10 kg, using friction alone and ignoring the 20 N pull.
distractorRationales.B: Friction does not add to the pull; it subtracts from it on a horizontal floor.
distractorRationales.D: Friction 5.0 N opposes the 20 N pull, so the net force is 15 N, not 20 N.

items.stem: A mutant Escherichia coli cannot synthesize meso-diaminopimelic acid, an amino acid of the peptidoglycan peptide stem. In hypotonic medium the cells swell and lyse unless 0.5 M sucrose is added as an osmotic stabilizer. Integrity of which structure has been lost?

choices.text: The 70S ribosome, which normally resists turgor by covalently cross-linking phospholipids
The peptidoglycan cell wall, whose peptide cross-links bear turgor pressure
The nuclear envelope, which is the load-bearing wall of Gram-negative bacteria
Flagellar hooks, which osmotically clamp the periplasm

items.explanation: Peptidoglycan is a mesh of glycan chains cross-linked through short peptides; meso-DAP is a stem residue used in those cross-links in E. coli. Without it the wall cannot be completed, so it cannot oppose the osmotic driving force for water influx, and the inner membrane ruptures in hypotonic medium. Sucrose outside the cell raises external osmolarity and reduces net water entry, rescuing the spheroplasts. Ribosomes do not bear turgor, bacteria have no nuclear envelope, and flagella are motility organelles rather than the hydrostatic exoskeleton.

distractorRationales.A: Ribosomes synthesize protein; they are not a pressure-bearing sac and do not cross-link membrane lipids.
distractorRationales.C: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear envelope; the wall, not a nucleus, is the turgor-resistant layer.
distractorRationales.D: Flagella propel the cell; they do not substitute for a missing peptidoglycan sacculus.

items.stem: A eukaryotic mRNA recovered from the cytosol is unusually unstable and poorly translated. The 5′ end is a free triphosphate rather than 7-methylguanosine attached by a 5′–5′ triphosphate bridge. Which nuclear processing step failed?

choices.text: Cleavage and polyadenylation at the 3′ end
Assembly of U2 snRNP on the first intron branch point
Aminoacylation of initiator tRNA Met
Capping of the pre-mRNA 5′ end

items.explanation: The eukaryotic 5′ cap is 7-methylguanosine joined to the first transcribed nucleotide by a 5′–5′ triphosphate linkage, added shortly after initiation by RNA polymerase II. The cap is bound by eIF4E, supporting scanning-dependent translation, and it protects mRNA from 5′ exonucleases. A cytosolic RNA that still ends in a 5′ triphosphate has not been capped, which explains both poor translation and rapid decay. Poly(A) status is a 3′-end event, U2 assembly is a splicing event, and tRNA charging is a translation-factor issue that would not change the chemical structure of the mRNA 5′ end.

distractorRationales.A: Defective polyadenylation would alter the 3′ tail, not replace a 5′ cap with a free 5′ triphosphate. The chemistry described is specifically the uncapped 5′ end.
distractorRationales.B: U2 snRNP functions in splicing; failure to splice would retain intron sequences but would not leave a 5′ triphosphate in place of the cap.
distractorRationales.C: Initiator tRNA charging affects translation globally but does not remodel the 5′ end of an already synthesized mRNA.

items.stem: A patient takes high-dose exogenous glucocorticoid for ten days. Endogenous hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal function is expected to show:

choices.text: increased CRH and ACTH with hypertrophy of the adrenal cortex
no change, because exogenous steroid cannot reach hypothalamic neurons
suppressed ACTH (and CRH) with possible atrophy of the cortisol-producing adrenal cortex
conversion of glucocorticoid receptors into Gs-coupled peptide receptors

items.explanation: Cortisol and related glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering CRH and ACTH. Without ACTH trophic drive, the zona fasciculata can atrophy during prolonged exogenous therapy—the reason withdrawal must be tapered. Exogenous steroid is exactly what the feedback sensors see. Receptors do not change protein class from nuclear transcription factors into GPCRs.

distractorRationales.A: This is the response to cortisol deficiency (loss of feedback), not to glucocorticoid excess.
distractorRationales.B: Lipophilic steroids readily reach hypothalamic and pituitary cells; that access is why feedback works.
distractorRationales.D: Receptor family identity does not switch from nuclear receptor to GPCR because ligand concentration is high.

items.stem: A Task A thesis states that “whoever owns the clock owns the apology.” Which use of an example is weakest, and why?

choices.text: Weakest: a fully specified case of an airline keeping passengers on the tarmac without a true estimated time, then offering a voucher in lieu of an explanation of the delay’s cause.
Weakest: “Companies these days are bad.” It names no clock-owner, no delayed public, and no apology-substitute, so the thesis’s parts have nothing to inhabit.
Weakest: a hospital’s public dashboard that shows average wait while omitting the longest decile, if the essay explains how the omitted tail is the apology being owned.
Weakest: a comparison between a minister’s press conference time and a benefits helpline’s hold music, if both clocks are identified.

items.explanation: The thesis has moving parts: ownership of time, and an apology that can be captured or replaced. A, C, and D, though imperfect, still give those parts somewhere to live. “Companies these days are bad” is a mood, not a case; it cannot earn a claim about clocks or apologies. Task A examples fail most often by staying at that altitude. The question is not which story is nicest but which one leaves the thesis unemployed. B is the unemployed example. Specificity is a thinking tool, not an ornament.

distractorRationales.A: The tarmac case supplies a clock, a public, and a voucher as a substitute apology; it is usable, not weakest.
distractorRationales.C: A dashboard that hides the worst waits is a precise illustration of owning how delay is narrated.
distractorRationales.D: Two named clocks in different registers can earn a comparison about whose time is treated as expensive.

items.stem: Bilateral lesions of the suprachiasmatic nuclei in a hamster abolish circadian rhythmicity of wheel-running; activity fragments into short bouts across the 24-hour day even under a light–dark cycle. Retinas and pineal glands remain intact. This pattern most directly supports which claim about circadian architecture?

choices.text: The pineal is the master pacemaker, so the finding is unexpected
Primary visual cortex is required to tell time of day from light
REM-on pontine cells are the clock, because dreams keep a 90-minute period even after SCN damage
The SCN is the master circadian oscillator; the pineal’s melatonin signal is downstream of it

items.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the mammalian master clock. Its destruction eliminates coherent circadian organization even when eyes can still sense light and the pineal can still make melatonin. Light reaches the SCN via the retinohypothalamic tract, not via V1. The pineal is a slave endocrine output, not the pacemaker. The 90-minute NREM–REM cycle is an ultradian oscillator in the brainstem/forebrain, distinct from the SCN’s near-24-hour clock.

distractorRationales.A: Pineal melatonin is timed by the SCN; it is not the master oscillator.
distractorRationales.B: Circadian photoreception uses specialized retinal ganglion cells to the SCN, bypassing striate cortex.
distractorRationales.C: REM cycling is ultradian and does not substitute for the SCN as a 24-hour pacemaker.

items.stem: Relative to the historians who argue about whether the tram lengthened or shortened the dispute, the clerk’s sentence is presented as

choices.text: useless because he lacked bitterness.
more useful because it identifies what the night’s conflict was actually about: the look of the street, not a simple duration effect.
proof the board was frightened.
proof the men were humiliated.

items.explanation: The commentator says historians still disagree on lengthen versus shorten, then prefers the clerk: the fight had become illumination. That evaluates two duration-arguments as less adequate than a claim about stakes. Lack of bitterness is how the clerk sounds, not why he is useful. C and D pick the camps. Comparing arguments means seeing the essay change the question rather than picking a winner among the original pair.

distractorRationales.A: Without bitterness is tone; usefulness is the illumination claim.
distractorRationales.C: That is one historian camp, left unsettled.
distractorRationales.D: The other camp, also unsettled.

passage.title: Note on a cancelled tram
passage.body:
In the third week of the lockout the company ran a single tram, brightly lit, along the route at dusk, with no passengers permitted. Officials called it a demonstration of service. Strikers called it a lantern on a coffin. Children ran beside it anyway, as they had when the cars were working, and were photographed. The photograph was printed in the morning paper under the heading NORMALITY RETURNS, and in an overseas paper under the heading CHILDREN MOCK THE DEAD LINE.

A clerk in the tram office, years later, wrote that he had been told to leave the lights on even if the generator complained, because darkness would look like surrender. He added, without apparent bitterness, that surrender had already occurred in the timetable. What remained was a moving argument about who owned the look of a street at evening.

Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

items.stem: The caption “Attention is not the same as attendance” uses gallery language to

choices.text: separate showing up from actually looking, a media-literate distinction the table's photo counts dramatize
prove that hour 11 did not happen
advertise a new census form
scold visitors for using language

items.explanation: Attendance is visitor counts; attention is indexed, roughly, by photographing the stairs. Hour 12 has attendees and a talk but zero stair photos. That is a media/language point about what counts as looking. It does not erase hour 11 or sell census stationery.

distractorRationales.B: Hour 11 is the peak row.
distractorRationales.C: The caption is curatorial, not a government form.
distractorRationales.D: Language is not the target; looking versus mere presence is.

passage.title: Two ways of hearing a census
passage.body:
Poem (untitled, 2019)

We counted rooms as if rooms were people.
The spare one kept its coat on.
In the column for language we wrote the kettle.
Nobody asked the stairs their age.

Commentary by L. Okonkwo, catalogue essay for an exhibition of household inventories:
The poem is easy to misread as anti-data. It is not. It notices that a census already poetizes: it decides what may stand for a life (rooms, language, age) and what must remain downstairs, unasked. The coat on the spare room is not a joke about furniture. It is a figure for surplus — the part of a household that official forms cannot rent. When the poem puts a kettle in the language column, it is not claiming kettles speak. It is showing how quickly a form will accept a proxy if the proxy is small and warm.

A table printed beside the poem in the gallery listed visitors by hour and by whether they photographed the stairs:
Hour 10: 14 visitors, 2 photographed stairs
Hour 11: 31 visitors, 18 photographed stairs
Hour 12: 9 visitors, 0 photographed stairs (docent talk in progress)
The curator captioned the table: Attention is not the same as attendance.

A radio host later called the exhibition “political because it made a kettle into a citizen.” Okonkwo's essay had already refused that flattening. The political cut, for her, is not enfranchising objects. It is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss.

items.stem: Electrolysis of aqueous AgNO3 deposits Ag(s) at the cathode: Ag+ + e− → Ag. Faraday’s constant is taken as 96 500 C mol−1, so 96 500 C deposits 1.00 mol of silver (Mr = 108). A current of 10.0 A runs for 193 s. How much silver is deposited?
items.explanation: Charge passed = 10.0 A × 193 s = 1930 C. Moles of electrons = 1930 / 96 500 = 0.0200 mol. For Ag+ / Ag the mole ratio is 1 e− per Ag, so 0.0200 mol Ag = 0.0200 × 108 g = 2.16 g. Half that mass (1.08 g) would be 0.0100 mol of electrons. 21.6 g is 0.200 mol, which would require 19 300 C (1930 s at 10.0 A). 0.216 g is a factor-of-ten slip on 2.16 g.

distractorRationales.A: 0.216 g is 2.16 g with the decimal shifted; 0.0200 mol of Ag is 2.16 g.
distractorRationales.C: 1.08 g is 0.0100 mol of Ag, half the 0.0200 mol of electrons passed.
distractorRationales.D: 21.6 g is 0.200 mol, ten times the charge actually passed in 193 s.

items.stem: A diet contains only amino acids that cannot yield net oxaloacetate or other gluconeogenic intermediates. Which pair consists of the two purely ketogenic amino acids?

choices.text: Alanine and glutamate, which are transaminated to pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate
Aspartate and asparagine, which feed into oxaloacetate
Valine and isoleucine, both of which are exclusively ketogenic branched-chain amino acids
Leucine and lysine, which are catabolized to acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate without net glucose production

items.explanation: A purely ketogenic amino acid cannot produce net pyruvate or citric-acid-cycle intermediates that can exit to gluconeogenesis; its carbons yield acetyl-CoA or ketone bodies. Leucine and lysine are the two standard amino acids in that class. Alanine and glutamate are glucogenic (pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate). Aspartate and asparagine yield oxaloacetate. Among branched-chain amino acids, valine is glucogenic and isoleucine is mixed (both glucogenic and ketogenic), so that pair is not exclusively ketogenic. A diet of only leucine and lysine therefore cannot support net glucose synthesis from amino-acid carbon, matching the stem.

distractorRationales.A: Alanine → pyruvate and glutamate → α-ketoglutarate are classic glucogenic conversions, so this pair can make net glucose.
distractorRationales.B: Aspartate and asparagine are glucogenic via oxaloacetate, not purely ketogenic.
distractorRationales.C: Valine is glucogenic and isoleucine is mixed; they are not the two purely ketogenic amino acids.

items.stem: Hot aqueous NaOH is used in an attempt to convert each of the following lipids into water-soluble carboxylate soaps. Which compound does not yield fatty-acid soaps under those saponification conditions?

choices.text: Glyceryl tristearate (a triacylglycerol)
1,2-Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine
Unesterified cholesterol
Cetyl palmitate (a wax ester)

items.explanation: Saponification is nucleophilic acyl substitution of an ester by hydroxide, releasing carboxylate salts (soaps). Triacylglycerols contain three fatty-acyl esters and produce three soaps plus glycerol. Glycerophospholipids similarly have two fatty-acyl esters that hydrolyze. Wax esters such as cetyl palmitate are also saponifiable. Free cholesterol is a sterol alcohol (a 3β-OH on a tetracyclic nucleus) and contains no fatty-acyl ester unless it has been separately esterified. Hydroxide therefore cannot liberate a fatty-acid soap from unesterified cholesterol.

distractorRationales.A: Triacylglycerols are the textbook saponifiable fats; hot NaOH yields three carboxylates and glycerol.
distractorRationales.B: The two fatty-acyl chains of phosphatidylcholine are esters and saponify; soaps still form even though the phosphodiester head group is a different linkage.
distractorRationales.D: Waxes are long-chain esters and undergo the same hydroxide-mediated ester hydrolysis as triglycerides.

items.stem: Standard reduction potentials: Cu2+/Cu = +0.34 V; Zn2+/Zn = −0.76 V. A Daniell cell runs Zn | Zn2+ (1.0 M) || Cu2+ (1.0 M) | Cu with E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V and n = 2. The Nernst equation at 25 °C is E = E° − (0.060/n) log10 Q, with Q = [Zn2+]/[Cu2+]. If [Zn2+] = 1.0 M and [Cu2+] = 0.010 M, what is E?
items.explanation: Q = 1.0 / 0.010 = 100, log10 Q = 2.00. The correction is (0.060/2) × 2.00 = 0.060 V. E = 1.10 − 0.060 = 1.04 V. The cell is slightly less than E° because the product ion is at 1 M while the reactant Cu2+ is depleted. Omitting the log term leaves 1.10 V. Adding instead of subtracting the 0.060 V gives 1.16 V. Using 0.060 × 2 without dividing by n would subtract 0.12 V and give 0.98 V.

distractorRationales.B: 1.10 V is E° at Q = 1; here Q = 100.
distractorRationales.C: 1.16 V would be E° plus the 0.060 V term, the wrong sign in Nernst’s − (RT/nF) ln Q.
distractorRationales.D: 0.98 V subtracts 0.12 V, as if n were omitted when applying 0.060 log Q.

items.stem: The later commentator is used, historically, to show

choices.text: how a small civic act is rewritten after the fact in the language of a school
that Kant visited the lost-property desk
that archives always preserve the clerk's own words
that magistrates in that city were trained as philosophers

items.explanation: The commentator writes after the clerk is dead and assigns a Kantian costume. That is a historical-commentary move: posterity interprets. The passage never places Kant at the desk, never says the clerk's words were archived intact, and never trains magistrates as philosophers.

distractorRationales.B: Kant is a label in a later essay, not a visitor.
distractorRationales.C: The clerk's own account is habit, which the commentator overwrites.
distractorRationales.D: No claim is made about magistrates' training.

passage.title: On keeping a promise to a stranger
passage.body:
When the magistrate asked why he had returned the purse, the clerk did not say honesty. He said habit. He had been taught, in a household that measured virtue by small repetitions, that a found object remains someone else's until the world has been given a fair chance to reclaim it. The purse contained little money and a letter, unsealed, beginning: I will not be there when you arrive. He did not finish it. To finish it, he thought, would convert a duty into a story, and stories have a way of making the finder important.

Philosophers like to treat this as a puzzle about property and knowledge. If he does not know the owner, is the duty weaker? If the letter would have saved a marriage, does withholding it become a harm? The clerk would have found the questions indecent. He was not refusing knowledge so much as refusing a role. The city had clerks for lost property; it did not have clerks for other people's farewells.

A later commentator, writing after the clerk was dead, praised him as a Kantian saint: he acted from a maxim he could will as universal. The praise is too clean. The clerk's maxim was local and slightly ashamed. He did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not universality, kept his eyes off the page. That is not a lesser ethics. It is an ethics that knows how quickly curiosity dresses itself as concern.

The owner collected the purse the next morning and did not thank him. In the commentary this becomes a test of whether virtue needs recognition. The clerk, if asked, would have said only that the counter was busy.

items.stem: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha so that the G protein cannot hydrolyze GTP. In an intestinal epithelial cell this modification is expected to:

choices.text: Persistently activate adenylyl cyclase, elevating cAMP and protein kinase A activity
Decrease cAMP because Gs-alpha is destroyed
Convert the receptor into a receptor tyrosine kinase as the toxin’s enzymatic product
Directly ligate voltage-gated calcium channels closed, lowering cAMP as a secondary effect

items.explanation: Gs-alpha stimulates adenylyl cyclase only while GTP is bound. GTP hydrolysis, often with help from the G protein's intrinsic GTPase, turns the subunit off. Cholera toxin covalently ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha and blocks that hydrolysis, locking the ON state. cAMP therefore remains high, PKA stays active, and in gut epithelium CFTR-mediated chloride secretion produces watery diarrhea. The alpha subunit is not degraded, RTK conversion does not occur, and the primary lesion is constitutive cyclase activity rather than a direct Ca2+-channel ligation that would lower cAMP.

distractorRationales.B: The toxin freezes Gs-alpha in the GTP-bound active form; it does not destroy it or lower cAMP.
distractorRationales.C: ADP-ribosylation of a G protein does not create a tyrosine kinase receptor.
distractorRationales.D: Cholera’s canonical cascade is Gs-cAMP-PKA, not direct voltage-gated Ca2+ blockade as the cAMP-lowering step.

items.stem: A homodimeric extracellular protein is held together solely by one interchain disulfide and has no other covalent links between subunits. Aliquots are run on SDS-PAGE with or without β-mercaptoethanol. Which banding pattern is expected?

choices.text: A monomer band of identical apparent mass in both the reducing and nonreducing lanes
A dimer band in both lanes, because SDS alone cannot disrupt a protein–protein interface
A dimer band only in the reducing lane and a monomer band only in the nonreducing lane
A band at the dimer mass without reductant and a band at approximately half that mass with reductant

items.explanation: SDS denatures noncovalent subunit interfaces, so a dimer that is held together only by a disulfide still migrates as a covalent dimer on nonreducing SDS-PAGE. β-Mercaptoethanol reduces the cystine to two free thiols, releasing the polypeptides, which then migrate at the monomer mass—about half the dimer mass for a homodimer. The reducing lane therefore cannot show the dimer if the disulfide was the only cross-link, and the nonreducing lane cannot show free monomer as the major species. This comparison is the standard test for interchain disulfides.

distractorRationales.A: Without reductant the interchain disulfide remains, so the nonreducing lane should not collapse to monomer.
distractorRationales.B: SDS disrupts noncovalent interfaces; a disulfide-linked dimer is the exception that survives without reductant, not with it.
distractorRationales.C: This pattern reverses the chemistry: reductant breaks the disulfide, so the dimer should disappear in the reducing lane.

items.stem:
Water potential ψ = ψs + ψp (MPa) along a transpiring shoot at midday:

Compartment | ψs | ψp | ψ
Soil solution | −0.20 | 0.00 | −0.20
Root cortex | −0.60 | +0.20 | −0.40
Xylem sap | −0.10 | −1.10 | −1.20
Leaf cell | −1.50 | +0.20 | −1.30

Water moves toward more negative ψ. Which path is possible?

choices.text: Soil → root → xylem → leaf, because −0.20 > −0.40 > −1.20 > −1.30 (less negative to more negative)
Leaf → xylem → root → soil, following the pressure potential ψp alone
Xylem cannot contain liquid water because ψp is negative
The root is a barrier to uptake because its ψs is more negative than the soil’s

items.explanation: The summed ψ values become steadily more negative from soil (−0.20) to root (−0.40) to xylem (−1.20) to leaf (−1.30), the required downhill gradient for transpiration. Negative xylem ψp is tension in a continuous water column, not an empty pipe; liquid xylem sap is the standard cohesion–tension state. Root ψs is more negative than soil, which is how the root lowers its ψ below the soil and takes up water; that is a driving force, not a barrier. Ranking by ψp alone would send water the wrong way because it ignores solute potential.

distractorRationales.B: Using only ψp would drive water out of the pressurised root toward the soil (0.00) and miss the actual ψ gradient.
distractorRationales.C: Negative hydrostatic pressure in xylem is tension in liquid water, the cohesion–tension mechanism.
distractorRationales.D: A more negative root ψs contributes to a more negative root ψ than soil, which is required for uptake.

items.stem: Preschoolers watch an adult batter a Bobo doll. One film ends with the adult receiving praise and snacks; another ends with a scolding. Children are then left with the doll and are not themselves rewarded or punished. Imitation of the aggressive acts is highest after the rewarded model. This most directly supports:

choices.text: Classical conditioning of fear to the doll
Central-route persuasion by a two-sided statistical message
Cognitive dissonance from being forbidden to play with the doll
Social-cognitive observational learning: vicarious reinforcement changes imitation without direct operant shaping of the child

items.explanation: Bandura’s social cognitive theory holds that people can acquire and regulate behavior by observing models, and that seeing a model rewarded (vicarious reinforcement) increases later imitation even when the observer is not directly reinforced. The Bobo design is the classic demonstration. Classical conditioning would pair the doll with an aversive unconditioned stimulus to produce fear, which is not the outcome. ELM concerns message scrutiny, not filmed aggression. Dissonance from forbidden toys is a different paradigm (insufficient justification / reactance-adjacent), and the stem does not forbid play.

distractorRationales.A: The children attack the doll rather than avoiding it, which is the opposite of conditioned fear.
distractorRationales.B: No argument quality or statistical message is involved; the children watch a behavioral model.
distractorRationales.C: Play was not forbidden, and dissonance is not required to explain imitation of a rewarded model.

items.stem: A 10 V battery with negligible internal resistance is connected to two 2 Ω resistors. The current drawn from the battery is largest when the resistors are arranged so that:

choices.text: they are in series, because then Req = 4 Ω and I = 2.5 A
they are in series, because then voltages add and I = 10 A
they are in parallel, because then Req = 1 Ω and I = 10 A
they are in parallel, because then Req = 4 Ω and I = 2.5 A

items.explanation: Battery current is I = V / Req. Two equal 2 Ω resistors in series have Req = 4 Ω, so I = 10/4 = 2.5 A. In parallel, 1/Req = 1/2 + 1/2, so Req = 1 Ω and I = 10/1 = 10 A. The parallel hookup therefore draws the larger current because it presents the smaller equivalent resistance. Series resistors add; they do not produce I = V/R of a single 1 Ω or a free 10 A from 'adding voltages.' Parallel resistors combine as a reciprocal sum, which for two equal resistors is half of one resistor, not the series sum.

distractorRationales.A: The series numbers are computed correctly (Req = 4 Ω, I = 2.5 A), but that current is smaller than the parallel current, not larger.
distractorRationales.B: Series voltages across the two resistors add to 10 V, but that does not make I = 10 A. Current is V/Req = 10/4 = 2.5 A.
distractorRationales.D: Parallel combination of two 2 Ω resistors is 1 Ω, not 4 Ω. Four ohms is the series sum, which would give the smaller current.

items.stem: In aqueous solution, Li+ has a larger hydrated radius and a more negative hydration enthalpy than Cs+, even though the bare Li+ ion is smaller. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: Li+ has higher charge density, so it orients and holds more water molecules more tightly via ion–dipole forces.
Li+ is less polarizing, so water binds more loosely and the hydrated radius expands.
Cs+ hydrolyzes water to H3O+ while Li+ does not, shrinking the cesium hydration shell.
Hydration enthalpy tracks only mass, so the heavier Cs+ must have the more negative hydration enthalpy.

items.explanation: Ion–dipole attraction scales with charge density (charge/volume). Li+ is much smaller than Cs+ at the same +1 charge, so the electric field at its surface is stronger. Water dipoles pack more tightly and in greater number around Li+, producing a larger hydrodynamic (hydrated) radius despite the smaller ionic radius, and a more exothermic hydration enthalpy. Cs+ is weakly hydrated. Hydrolysis to H3O+ is characteristic of small, highly charged metal ions such as Al3+, not of Cs+. Mass alone does not set hydration enthalpy.

distractorRationales.B: Li+ is more polarizing, not less; tighter—not looser—water binding is the point.
distractorRationales.C: Neither alkali cation is a strong hydrolyzing acid in water; that description fits Al3+ or Fe3+ aquo ions.
distractorRationales.D: Heavier Cs+ is less strongly hydrated. Hydration enthalpy correlates with charge density, not with mass in this pair.

items.stem: A clinician taps the patellar tendon, stretching the quadriceps. The shortest-latency pathway that extends the knee is:

choices.text: Golgi tendon organ to cerebellum to contralateral cortex to spinal motor neuron
cutaneous nociceptor to brainstem to gamma motor neuron only
Ia afferent from the muscle spindle to the spinal cord to an alpha motor neuron innervating the same muscle
visual startle via cranial nerve II to extraocular muscles only

items.explanation: The tendon tap stretches muscle spindles, firing Ia afferents that monosynaptically excite homonymous alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord—the phasic stretch reflex. That loop does not require cortex or cerebellum for the shortest latency, is not a nociceptive withdrawal via gamma neurons alone, and is unrelated to CN II. Golgi tendon organs are in series with extrafusal fibers and are not the primary receptors for this brief stretch-of-spindle test.

distractorRationales.A: Long-loop transcortical or cerebellar paths exist for some stretch responses but are not the shortest-latency knee jerk, which is spinal and Ia-driven.
distractorRationales.B: This is not a pain-withdrawal reflex, and gamma motor neurons alone do not extend the knee by contracting extrafusal fibers.
distractorRationales.D: Vision and extraocular muscles are irrelevant to a patellar tendon tap with the eyes uninvolved in the circuit.

items.stem: Which statement correctly classifies the nitrogenous bases of nucleic acids as aromatic heterocycles?

choices.text: Adenine and guanine are monocyclic pyrimidines; cytosine, thymine, and uracil are bicyclic purines
All five bases are porphyrins, the same macrocycle found in heme
Adenine is an indole, matching the side chain of tryptophan
Adenine and guanine are bicyclic purines (fused pyrimidine + imidazole); cytosine, thymine, and uracil are monocyclic pyrimidines

items.explanation: Purine is a 6–5 fused heterocycle (pyrimidine fused to imidazole). Adenine (6-aminopurine) and guanine (2-amino-6-oxopurine) are purines and attach to C1′ of the sugar at N9. Cytosine, uracil, and thymine (5-methyluracil) are single six-membered pyrimidine rings and attach at N1. The mnemonic that pyrimidines are the smaller bases matches the monocyclic structures. Porphyrin is a different tetrapyrrole macrocycle used in heme and chlorophyll. Indole is the fused benzene–pyrrole of tryptophan, not of adenine.

distractorRationales.A: This inverts the classification. Purines (A, G) are bicyclic; pyrimidines (C, T, U) are monocyclic.
distractorRationales.B: Porphyrins are 18π tetrapyrrole macrocycles. Nucleic-acid bases are purines and pyrimidines, not porphyrins.
distractorRationales.C: Indole is Trp’s side chain. Adenine is a purine; the two bicyclic systems are not the same heterocycle.

items.stem: After a left inferior-frontal infarct, a patient speaks in effortful telegraphic phrases, omits function words, and repeats poorly, but she follows two-step commands and points accurately to named objects. This profile is most consistent with which classical aphasia?

choices.text: Wernicke’s (receptive) aphasia from superior temporal damage
Conduction aphasia from isolated arcuate-fasciculus damage with fluent speech and intact comprehension
Global aphasia with essentially no comprehension and no speech
Broca’s (expressive) aphasia from inferior frontal damage

items.explanation: Broca’s aphasia (usually posterior inferior frontal gyrus, Broca’s area) is nonfluent, agrammatic, with relatively spared comprehension and poor repetition. Wernicke’s aphasia is fluent, paraphasic, and comprehension-poor. Conduction aphasia is fluent with good comprehension and disproportionately poor repetition. Global aphasia devastates both fluency and comprehension. The stem matches the Broca pattern and the named frontal lesion.

distractorRationales.A: Wernicke’s aphasia would impair comprehension of commands and yield fluent but empty speech.
distractorRationales.B: Conduction aphasia is fluent; the stem is effortful and telegraphic.
distractorRationales.C: Spared two-step commands rule out global aphasia.

items.stem:
DNA per nucleus is plotted for a cell that starts at 6.0 pg (diploid G1, 2C). The trace is: 0–8 h, DNA rises 6.0 → 12.0 pg; 8–10 h, DNA stays 12.0 pg; at 10 h the nucleus divides into two nuclei of 6.0 pg; at 11 h those two divide again into four nuclei of 3.0 pg. There is no second S-phase plateau at 12 pg after the first division.
Which process is shown?

choices.text: Mitosis, which would also finish at 3.0 pg after a single division.
Endoreduplication without nuclear division, which would leave one 12 pg nucleus.
Two S phases then one mitosis, which would require a second rise 6 → 12 pg after 10 h.
Meiosis: one S phase then two divisions, producing 3.0 pg (1C) nuclei.

items.explanation: Meiosis replicates DNA once (6 → 12 pg) and then divides twice without another S phase, so the products are 1C (3.0 pg) if G1 diploid was 6.0 pg. Mitosis would stop after the first division, leaving two 6.0 pg G1 nuclei. Endoreduplication would not split the nucleus. A second S phase would be visible as another 6 → 12 pg rise after 10 h, which the trace lacks. The four 3 pg nuclei at 11 h are therefore meiotic products.

distractorRationales.A: Mitosis yields two 6 pg nuclei, not four 3 pg nuclei.
distractorRationales.B: The plot shows divisions at 10 h and 11 h, not a single undivided 12 pg nucleus.
distractorRationales.C: After 10 h DNA falls rather than rising through a second S phase.

items.stem: A virus-infected epithelial cell presents a viral peptide on MHC class I. The lymphocyte that recognizes this complex and kills the infected cell is a:

choices.text: CD8 cytotoxic T cell, whose TCR surveys peptide-MHC I
CD4 helper T cell restricted to MHC class II on that epithelium as the sole killing receptor
Naive B cell secreting IgM without MHC restriction
Neutrophil expressing a T-cell receptor that binds MHC I

items.explanation: Almost all nucleated cells express MHC I and display cytosolic (often viral) peptides. CD8 binds the MHC I alpha-3 domain, and the CD8 T-cell receptor recognizes the peptide-MHC I complex, triggering perforin/granzyme or FasL killing. CD4 T cells recognize peptide-MHC II on professional antigen-presenting cells and are helper rather than the classic killers of infected epithelium. B cells bind native antigen with immunoglobulin and do not use MHC to see intracellular viral peptides on the epithelial surface. Neutrophils are innate phagocytes without TCRs.

distractorRationales.B: CD4 is MHC II-restricted and does not mediate the standard MHC I-restricted cytotoxic hit on infected epithelia.
distractorRationales.C: B-cell receptors see extracellular native epitopes, not MHC I-displayed peptides, as the killing mechanism here.
distractorRationales.D: Neutrophils lack TCRs and MHC-restricted clonal antigen receptors.

items.stem: A toddler who has heard only “went” and “went” nonetheless says “I goed to clinic.” Nativist accounts following Chomsky treat such overregularization as evidence for which claim?

choices.text: Skinnerian verbal behavior: every utterance is a reinforced copy of a parental exemplar
Sapir–Whorf linguistic determinism: English past-tense morphology forces the child to invent travel
Children extract abstract grammatical rules (here, add -ed) that they apply beyond the input, consistent with a language-acquisition device and poverty of the stimulus
Wernicke’s area has myelinated, so comprehension errors must produce “goed”

items.explanation: Overregularization shows children are not limited to echoing reinforced strings; they generalize a rule to irregulars they have not heard inflected that way. Chomsky argued that the input is too poor and error-riddled to explain such abstract competence without innate grammatical constraints (the LAD / universal grammar). Skinner’s account struggles with forms that were never reinforced. Whorf concerns thought following language categories, not past-tense invention. Wernicke’s area is an adult lesion story, not toddler morphology.

distractorRationales.A: “Goed” is precisely a form that was not copied from adult input or obviously reinforced.
distractorRationales.B: Whorf does not explain overregularization of inflectional rules.
distractorRationales.D: Toddler overregularization is a developmental grammar phenomenon, not Wernicke aphasia.

items.stem: A dermatology clinic serves patients with highly visible port-wine stains. Several describe “passing” in dim light and dreading disclosure in a gown. Goffman’s analysis of stigma would classify the mark as which kind of spoiled identity, and which emotion-laden process is central?

choices.text: Ethnocentrism toward one’s own ethnic in-group, which is identical to stigma
Stereotype threat on a GRE, which is the only named stigma process
Institutional discrimination by ZIP code, which Goffman defined as a personal blemish
A discredited stigma when visible, managed by information control when it can be hidden; shame and audience management are central, not a Sherif tournament

items.explanation: Goffman distinguished discredited stigmas (already visible) from discreditable ones (concealable, managed by passing and information control). A port-wine stain can shift between those as lighting and clothing change. The self is “spoiled” in the eyes of a virtual audience, producing shame and careful impression work. Ethnocentrism is in-group/out-group cultural ranking. Stereotype threat is a performance decrement in a evaluated domain. Institutional discrimination is structural, not Goffman’s interactional stigma vocabulary.

distractorRationales.A: Ethnocentrism is not Goffman’s definition of a spoiled personal identity.
distractorRationales.B: Steele’s stereotype threat is a different, test-performance literature.
distractorRationales.C: Goffman analyzed face-to-face stigma, not ZIP-code allocation rules.

items.stem: Four otherwise identical E. coli cultures are grown with: (1) glucose only, (2) glucose plus lactose, (3) lactose only, or (4) no utilizable carbon source. lacZYA mRNA is quantified during exponential growth (or, for culture 4, during carbon starvation). Which culture has the highest lac transcription, and why?

choices.text: Culture 1, because glucose is the inducer that binds LacI and catabolite repression activates the operon.
Culture 2, because both sugars must occupy the operator simultaneously before RNA polymerase can bind.
Culture 3, because allolactose inactivates the lac repressor while high cAMP allows the cAMP–CAP complex to recruit RNA polymerase at the lac promoter.
Culture 4, because ppGpp alone fully induces every catabolic operon in the absence of any sugar.

items.explanation: The lac repressor binds the operator and blocks polymerase unless allolactose (from lactose) occupies LacI and lowers operator affinity. Independently, glucose starvation raises cAMP so that cAMP–CAP binds upstream of the lac promoter and strongly activates transcription. Maximal expression therefore requires lactose present (repressor off) and glucose absent (CAP on), which is culture 3. Glucose alone leaves the repressor bound. Glucose plus lactose yields only CAP-independent, lower transcription. Starvation without lactose leaves LacI on the operator; stringent-response ppGpp does not replace allolactose and CAP at lac.

distractorRationales.A: Glucose is the preferred carbon source that lowers cAMP and causes catabolite repression; it is not the lac inducer, and LacI remains bound without lactose.
distractorRationales.B: Neither sugar binds the operator DNA. Glucose plus lactose is the induced but CAP-off condition, not the expression maximum.
distractorRationales.D: Without lactose the repressor still occupies the operator; carbon starvation does not constitutively fire lacZYA via ppGpp alone.

items.stem: Which statement correctly classifies calcium and iron by block and family?

choices.text: Both are s-block main-group metals.
Calcium is an alkaline-earth (s-block) metal; iron is a d-block transition metal.
Both are d-block transition metals.
Calcium is a halogen; iron is an alkali metal.

items.explanation: Calcium is [Ar] 4s^2, a group 2 alkaline-earth metal in the s-block. Iron is [Ar] 4s^2 3d^6, a d-block transition metal with a partially filled d subshell and the variable oxidation states that classification implies. Calling both s-block ignores iron's 3d electrons; calling both transition metals ignores that Ca has no d electrons in its ground-state valence set. Calcium is not a halogen (halogens are p-block, group 17), and iron is not an alkali metal (alkali metals are group 1, ns^1).

distractorRationales.A: Calcium is s-block, but iron's distinguishing electrons occupy 3d. Iron is not a main-group s-block metal.
distractorRationales.C: Iron is a transition metal; calcium is not. Group 2 elements are main-group alkaline earths, not d-block.
distractorRationales.D: Calcium is group 2, not a halogen. Iron is group 8/d-block, not group 1. Both family assignments are swapped into the wrong columns.

items.stem: A flexible container holds a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant pressure. The absolute temperature is raised from 300 K to 360 K. The gas volume is:

choices.text: multiplied by 300/360
unchanged, because pressure is fixed
multiplied by 360/27, using the Celsius temperatures
multiplied by 360/300

items.explanation: Charles's law, or PV = nRT at constant n and P, requires V proportional to absolute temperature. The volume scale factor is therefore T2/T1 = 360/300 = 1.20. Celsius temperatures must not be inserted into V/T, and holding P fixed is what makes V change with T rather than what keeps V constant. Inverting the temperature ratio describes a constant-volume pressure drop, not this isobaric expansion.

distractorRationales.A: This is T1/T2, the factor for an isobaric cooling or for inverted Charles's law. Temperature rose, so volume rises.
distractorRationales.B: Constant pressure is the condition that lets volume change with temperature. It does not freeze the volume.
distractorRationales.C: The ideal-gas temperature in PV = nRT is Kelvin, not Celsius. Using 87 C and 27 C as if they were absolute temperatures is invalid.

items.stem: A critic notes that light scatter can also fall if vesicles lyse and fragments leave the beam. Which extra measurement would best protect the swelling interpretation?

choices.text: Repeating only condition A.
Assaying trapped marker retained inside vesicles at 300 s for B and D; retention would argue against lysis as the main scatter drop.
Turning the room lights off.
Adding more HgCl2 to A.

items.explanation: If scatter drop were lysis, trapped contents should be lost. Retention of a marker at late time distinguishes intact swollen vesicles from fragments. A cannot speak to B/D. Darkness does not address lysis. Poisoning the isotonic control does not create a lysis control. Experimental design items should add a measurement that would go differently under the rival hypothesis.

distractorRationales.A: A already does not drop; it does not test lysis in hypotonic arms.
distractorRationales.C: Ambient light is not the rival mechanism named.
distractorRationales.D: HgCl2 in A changes two things and still does not measure intactness.

passage.title: Vesicle swelling under osmotic load
passage.body:
A student prepares identical phospholipid vesicles in 300 mOsmol kg−1 sucrose, then dilutes them at t = 0 into the media below. Vesicle volume is inferred from light scatter (larger vesicles scatter less in this geometry). Temperature 25 °C. n = 6 aliquots; scatter reported as mean ± s.d. arbitrary units (higher = smaller vesicles).

Medium after dilution | 10 s | 60 s | 300 s
A: 300 mOsmol sucrose (control) | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 0.99 ± 0.03 | 1.01 ± 0.02
B: 150 mOsmol sucrose | 0.71 ± 0.04 | 0.52 ± 0.05 | 0.48 ± 0.06
C: 150 mOsmol sucrose + 0.1 mM HgCl2 (water-channel blocker in this model) | 0.92 ± 0.03 | 0.80 ± 0.04 | 0.61 ± 0.05
D: 150 mOsmol sucrose + aquaporin proteoliposomes fused at 5 mol% | 0.40 ± 0.06 | 0.33 ± 0.05 | 0.34 ± 0.04

A second table lists initial rates estimated from 0–10 s, treating scatter drop as swelling:

Condition | Δscatter / 10 s
A | ~0
B | −0.029
C | −0.008
D | −0.060

The student claims: “Swelling requires a hypotonic bath, is slowed when water pores are blocked, and is accelerated when extra water pores are added, so the membrane’s phospholipid bilayer is not the main path in B–D.”

items.stem: An infant-cognition lab (looking-time methods in the Fantz/Baillargeon tradition) presents the same face for eight trials; looking declines. A new face restores looking. After the new face, the original face is shown again and looking briefly rises relative to the last familiar-face trial. Which pair of non-associative processes is illustrated?

choices.text: Habituation to the repeated face and dishabituation (recovery) when the stimulus changes
Classical conditioning to the face, then operant kicking for the new face
Sensory receptor fatigue only, which cannot recover to a new face that uses the same retina
Vicarious reinforcement in Bandura’s sense, because the infant watched the experimenter look

items.explanation: Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated, unchanging stimulus that is not explained by receptor fatigue or motor exhaustion. Dishabituation is recovery when a new stimulus appears (or, in some designs, when a novel interpolating event restores responding to the original). Infant looking-time exploits that pair to ask what babies discriminate. No CS–US pairing or response–reinforcer contingency is described. Bandura’s vicarious reinforcement is observational learning of a model’s consequences, not waning looking.

distractorRationales.B: No US or reinforcer is paired with looking; this is non-associative.
distractorRationales.C: Recovery to a new face, and often to the original after a novel event, is used to argue against pure receptor fatigue.
distractorRationales.D: The infant is not learning from a model’s rewarded action.

items.stem: A protein of isoelectric point 5.4 is focused to equilibrium in an immobilized pH gradient from 3 (anode) to 10 (cathode). Separately, the same protein is dissolved in pH 7.4 buffer. Which description is correct?

choices.text: It focuses at the anode (pH 3) because acidic proteins always migrate to positive electrodes in IEF
It focuses at the cathode (pH 10) because its pI is less than 7
It focuses at pH 7.4, the pH of blood, regardless of the gradient
It focuses at the pH 5.4 zone of the gradient; in pH 7.4 buffer its net charge is negative

items.explanation: In isoelectric focusing a protein is cationic when the local pH is below its pI and anionic when the local pH is above its pI, so it migrates until pH = pI and the net charge is zero. This protein therefore stops at pH 5.4, not at either electrode and not at 7.4. At pH 7.4, which is two units above the pI, acidic side chains are deprotonated in excess of the remaining cationic groups, so the protein carries a net negative charge and would migrate toward the anode in a uniform-pH gel.

distractorRationales.A: IEF does not park every acidic protein on the anode. Migration stops where pH equals pI, here 5.4.
distractorRationales.B: A pI of 5.4 is acidic, so the protein is not driven to the basic (cathode) end. High-pI proteins focus near the cathode.
distractorRationales.C: The focusing pH is the protein’s pI, a property of its titratable groups, not the pH of a later buffer experiment.

items.stem: In a laboratory replication of the classic epinephrine waiting-room study, students receive either epinephrine or saline. Half of the epinephrine group is correctly warned about palpitations and tremor; half is told the shot is inert. Each student then waits with a confederate who acts either euphoric or angry. Which group should give emotion ratings that most closely match the confederate’s mood?

choices.text: Informed epinephrine participants, because an accurate drug label maximizes emotional matching
Uninformed epinephrine participants, because unexplained arousal is attributed using the waiting-room cue
Saline participants, because only placebo arousal can be misattributed to a social cue
All epinephrine participants equally, because catecholamine level fixes the quality of emotion

items.explanation: Schachter–Singer two-factor theory says an emotion is unexplained physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from context. Uninformed epinephrine subjects have a real sympathetic surge they cannot credit to the injection, so they interpret it as euphoria or anger depending on the confederate. Informed subjects already have a sufficient explanation (the drug) and therefore have less need to use the social cue. Saline subjects lack the extra arousal. Catecholamines can intensify arousal, but they do not by themselves select the quality of the feeling.

distractorRationales.A: A correct explanation of palpitations reduces, rather than increases, the need to borrow an emotion label from the confederate.
distractorRationales.C: Saline produces little extra arousal to misattribute, so matching should be weaker, not stronger, than in the uninformed drug group.
distractorRationales.D: Two-factor theory denies that a catecholamine level by itself determines whether one feels anger versus euphoria; the cognitive label does that work.

items.stem: Which ion is amphiprotic in water, able both to donate a proton to water and to accept a proton from water?

choices.text: Cl−
HCO3−
Na+
ClO4−

items.explanation: Bicarbonate can act as an acid (HCO3− + H2O ⇌ CO3^2− + H3O+) or as a base (HCO3− + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 + OH−). That dual behavior is amphiprotic and is why NaHCO3 solutions are mildly basic (the Kb path is stronger than the Ka path for this ion). Cl− and ClO4− are conjugate bases of strong acids and have negligible basicity and no proton to donate. Na+ is neither a proton donor nor a meaningful proton acceptor in water; it is a spectator cation.

distractorRationales.A: Chloride has no proton to donate and is such a weak base that it does not accept protons from water to a measurable extent.
distractorRationales.C: Sodium ion is a closed-shell spectator; it is not amphiprotic.
distractorRationales.D: Perchlorate is the conjugate base of superacidic HClO4 and neither donates nor accepts protons in water.

items.stem: F+ Escherichia coli that are streptomycin-sensitive and lac+ are mixed with F- cells that are streptomycin-resistant and lac-. DNase is present in the medium throughout the 30-minute mating. Streptomycin-resistant lac+ colonies appear at high frequency. The DNA transfer mechanism is:

choices.text: Transformation with naked chromosomal DNA, which DNase would degrade in the medium
Conjugation through a pilus, which is DNase-resistant because DNA moves cell to cell inside a protected channel
Generalized transduction, which requires a lytic phage lysate that was not provided
Uptake of secreted lac mRNA and reverse transcription in the recipient

items.explanation: F plasmid conjugation transfers DNA through a conjugative pilus/pore. Because the nucleic acid never becomes free in the medium, extracellular DNase does not block the cross. Transformation is defined by uptake of naked DNA and is DNase-sensitive, so it is ruled out by the experimental design. Transduction requires phage particles to package and deliver DNA, which the stem does not supply.
