Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

items.stem:
A position–time graph for a walker is piecewise linear:

Interval | s(t)
0 to 3.0 s | s increases linearly from 0 to 12 m
3.0 to 7.0 s | s is constant at 12 m
7.0 to 10.0 s | s decreases linearly from 12 m to 0

Average velocity is displacement / time. Average speed is path length / time. For the whole 0–10.0 s motion, what is the average velocity?

choices.text: 0 m s−1

items.explanation: The walker starts at s = 0 and finishes at s = 0, so the displacement for 0–10.0 s is 0 m and the average velocity is 0. The path length is 12 m out plus 12 m back = 24 m, so the average speed is 24/10.0 = 2.4 m s−1. Those two averages are not interchangeable. 1.2 m s−1 would be 12 m / 10.0 s, using only the outbound distance as if it were displacement. 4.0 m s−1 is the slope of the first segment (12/3.0) and is an instantaneous velocity, not the 10 s average. Returning to the origin is the reason the signed average is zero even though the walker was moving for most of the time.

distractorRationales.B: 1.2 m s−1 uses a 12 m figure divided by 10 s. Displacement for the full trip is 0, not 12 m.
distractorRationales.C: 2.4 m s−1 is the average speed (24 m of path in 10 s), not the average velocity.
distractorRationales.D: 4.0 m s−1 is the velocity only on 0–3 s. Later the velocity is 0 and then −4.0 m s−1, so it is not the overall average.

items.stem: The first ionization energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. The best explanation is that:

choices.text: oxygen has a greater nuclear charge, which always lowers ionization energy across a period
nitrogen has a half-filled 2p^3 subshell; oxygen's extra 2p electron shares an orbital (2p^4) and is easier to remove
oxygen atoms are larger than nitrogen atoms, so the valence electron is farther from the nucleus
nitrogen lacks a filled 2s subshell, whereas oxygen has 2s^2 and is therefore harder to ionize

items.explanation: Across a period, first ionization energy generally rises with Zeff, so one would expect O > N, but the measured order is N > O. Nitrogen's 2p^3 configuration places one electron in each 2p orbital (Hund's rule), a half-filled subshell. Oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair in an already occupied orbital; electron–electron repulsion in that pair lowers the energy needed to remove it. Both N and O have filled 2s^2, and oxygen is smaller than nitrogen, so neither size nor a missing 2s shell explains the dip. Greater nuclear charge usually raises, rather than lowers, IE.

distractorRationales.A: Greater nuclear charge across a period generally increases ionization energy. That main trend is what the N > O exception interrupts, so this reason points the wrong way.
distractorRationales.C: Atomic radius decreases from N to O. Oxygen is not larger, and a size increase is not the origin of the IE dip.
distractorRationales.D: Both atoms have 2s^2. The relevant difference is 2p^3 versus 2p^4 pairing, not the 2s subshell.

items.stem:
A hexapeptide Asp–Lys–Ala–Glu–His–Gly is titrated in water. The relevant pKa values are:

Group | pKa
N-terminal α-COOH (Asp) | 2.0
Asp side chain | 4.0
Glu side chain | 4.5
His side chain | 6.0
N-terminal α-NH3+ | 9.0
Lys side chain | 10.5
C-terminal α-COOH (Gly) | 2.2

At pH 7.0 a group is taken as deprotonated if pH is more than 1 unit above its pKa and protonated if pH is more than 1 unit below its pKa. His (pKa 6.0) is treated as predominantly uncharged. What net charge does this rule set assign to the peptide?
items.explanation: At pH 7 the two carboxyl termini and both Asp and Glu side chains lie well above their pKa values, so each is COO− (−1 each, four carboxylates). The N-terminus (pKa 9.0) and Lys (pKa 10.5) remain NH3+ (+1 each). Histidine at pKa 6.0 is predominantly the neutral imidazole at pH 7, contributing 0. The algebraic sum is −4 + 2 = −1. Treating His as fully +1 would incorrectly give 0, and omitting one carboxylate would give 0 or −2.

distractorRationales.A: A net of 0 would require counting His as +1, but the stem’s ≥1-unit rule leaves His uncharged at pH 7.
distractorRationales.C: −2 would mean an extra anion, for example counting His as −1 or forgetting the two cationic amino groups.
distractorRationales.D: +1 would require most carboxylates still to be protonated, which is incompatible with pH 7 versus pKa values near 2–4.5.

items.stem: A purified pentapeptide of known sequence Asn-Ala-Phe-Gln-Lys is subjected to standard acid hydrolysis (6 M HCl, 110 °C, 24 h) and the hydrolysate is analyzed by amino-acid analysis. Compared with the intact peptide’s covalent sequence, which change in the composition table is expected from the chemistry of side-chain amides?

choices.text: Asparagine and glutamine peaks remain, and two extra free ammonia peaks appear from peptide-bond cleavage only
Asparagine and glutamine are recovered as aspartate and glutamate because their side-chain amides are hydrolyzed
Lysine is converted to norleucine, so the basic residue disappears from the chromatogram
Phenylalanine is fully destroyed, while Asn and Gln are recovered unchanged

items.explanation: Strong acid hydrolysis cleaves peptide bonds and also hydrolyzes the carboxamide side chains of asparagine and glutamine, converting them to aspartic acid and glutamic acid and releasing ammonia. Amino-acid analysis of a complete acid hydrolysate therefore cannot distinguish Asn from Asp or Gln from Glu; both amides appear in the Asx and Glx pools. Lysine is stable under these conditions, and phenylalanine is not destroyed (tryptophan is the aromatic residue that is lost). The composition table will show Asp and Glu rather than authentic Asn and Gln.

distractorRationales.A: Peptide-bond hydrolysis does not spare the side-chain amides; Asn and Gln do not survive standard acid hydrolysis.
distractorRationales.C: Lysine is not converted to norleucine during HCl hydrolysis; norleucine is sometimes used as an internal standard.
distractorRationales.D: Tryptophan, not phenylalanine, is destroyed by acid hydrolysis; the amides are not recovered intact.

items.stem: How does the recording paragraph function relative to the opening claim that paper sits still while performance disappears?

choices.text: It abandons the opening claim, because a recording proves performance never disappeared.
It extends the claim: a fixed take is a new stillness that solves disappearance only by freezing a particular night, seat, and social aim.
It is an unrelated complaint about fan culture and merchandise.
It argues that scores and recordings are identical technologies with identical politics.

items.explanation: The opening contrast is stillness versus disappearance. Recordings seem to solve disappearance and then recreate stillness as a loopable take with its own aiming. That is integration: same problem, new paper. A treats the seeming solution as a refutation. C ignores the microphone-and-hierarchy analysis. D over-identifies two tools the author compares without equating; scores capture pitch and duration, recordings freeze a night. The paragraph exists to stop the reader from thinking technology ended the ontology problem.

distractorRationales.A: The author says recordings seemed to solve disappearance, then shows the smuggled politics of a fixed take.
distractorRationales.C: Fans appear as an epistemic example, not a merchandise aside.
distractorRationales.D: Recordings are “a new paper,” analogous but not identical; the politics of the microphone are specified.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

items.stem: During the first weeks after implantation, syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, an LH analog. A neutralizing antibody to hCG given at week 5 would most likely:

choices.text: Raise corpus luteum progesterone output by blocking an inhibitory hormone
Block FSH receptors on Sertoli cells as its only relevant target in a pregnant woman
Prevent sperm capacitation in the epididymis after week 20, with no first-trimester effect
Cause luteal regression, a fall in progesterone, and loss of endometrial support for the pregnancy

items.explanation: The corpus luteum of pregnancy is rescued by trophoblastic hCG acting on luteal LH receptors, maintaining progesterone until the placenta assumes steroidogenesis (~8-10 weeks). Neutralizing hCG removes that luteotropic signal, progesterone collapses, and the progesterone-dependent endometrium cannot sustain the conceptus. hCG is not an inhibitor of progesterone at this stage. FSH/Sertoli biology is male and irrelevant to week-5 gestation, and epididymal capacitation is not the antibody's first-trimester target. This is why early pregnancy tests detect hCG and why luteal failure aborts early pregnancy.

distractorRationales.A: hCG is luteotropic; blocking it lowers, not raises, progesterone.
distractorRationales.B: The relevant hCG receptor here is luteal LH-R in the ovary, not male Sertoli FSH-R.
distractorRationales.C: Week 5 is first trimester; the mechanism is ovarian, not delayed epididymal.

items.stem: A construction-site reconstruction of the Gage injury is presented in clinic teaching: a tamping iron traverses ventromedial prefrontal cortex; language, gait, and basic sensation recover, but planning, social tact, and impulse control do not. Which conclusion about localization is most justified?

choices.text: The cerebellum is the seat of personality, because Gage’s gait was briefly unsteady
Ventromedial prefrontal cortex contributes to social-executive control rather than to primary motor or classical language maps
Broca’s area was destroyed, because personality change is the definition of Broca’s aphasia
The mesolimbic dopamine path was cut, so extraversion must fall by Eysenck’s ARAS theory

items.explanation: The historical Gage case, and modern vmPFC lesion series, link orbitofrontal/ventromedial prefrontal cortex to social judgment, planning, and inhibition, dissociable from primary motor and perisylvian language cortices. Cerebellar personality theories are not what the iron’s path demonstrates. Broca’s aphasia is a language-output syndrome, which recovered here. Eysenck’s extraversion–ARAS theory is a trait-arousal account, not a description of a vmPFC tamping-iron trajectory.

distractorRationales.A: A brief gait issue does not relocate personality to cerebellum in this lesion.
distractorRationales.C: Broca’s aphasia is nonfluent speech, not a personality-change definition.
distractorRationales.D: Eysenck’s ARAS extraversion model is not the localization lesson of the Gage trajectory.

items.stem: In poem 1, “as if the river were a problem in change” uses “change” to refer primarily to

choices.text: political revolution on the far bank.
small coins and the idea that a crossing is a calculable exchange.
the weather changing midstream.
the ferryman changing jobs.

items.explanation: The next lines take coins that had known other pockets; change is monetary and, by the simile, a reduction of the river to a transaction. Referents: ticket, coins, exchange. Revolution, weather, and employment are not cued. Follow-structure items should let the following sentence decide the pun’s weight; here coins cash the metaphor, while “problem in change” also names the speaker’s wish that leaving be arithmetical.

distractorRationales.A: No political programme is attached to the far bank in poem 1.
distractorRationales.C: Water’s questions are against the hull, not a forecast.
distractorRationales.D: The ferryman’s occupation is stable in the poem.

passage.title: Two short poems: Ferry
passage.body:
Poem 1 — “Ticket”
I bought a ticket to the other bank
as if the river were a problem in change.
The ferryman took coins that had known other pockets.
He did not ask what I was leaving.
The water did, in small repeated questions
against the hull.

Poem 2 — “Return”
On the way back the same boat
was a different animal.
I recognised the coins by their edges
and not the faces.
Someone on the far jetty waved
at a person I had not yet become
and I, traitor, waved.

items.stem: A 30-nm particle is purified from a lysate. It contains a 6 kb RNA genome encapsidated by protein, has no ribosomes and no plasma membrane of its own, and yields progeny only when incubated with live host cells. Classifying the particle as a cell would most directly contradict cell theory because:

choices.text: All cells must use DNA, never RNA, as genetic material

A cell is the autonomous unit of metabolism and reproduction, bounded by a membrane and capable of protein synthesis with its own ribosomes; this particle is an obligate intracellular replicator lacking that machinery
Cell theory requires every living particle to be visible by standard light microscopy
RNA genomes are forbidden in any biological entity, including viruses

items.explanation: Classical cell theory holds that the cell is the basic unit of life: a membrane-bounded compartment that carries out metabolism and arises from preexisting cells. Viruses and virus-like particles encapsidate nucleic acid but lack ribosomes, independent energy metabolism, and a self-contained plasma membrane; they replicate only by hijacking a host cell. RNA as a genome is fully compatible with being a virus and does not by itself decide cellular status. Size below the light-microscope limit also does not define a cell. The contradiction is the absence of autonomous cellular organization, not the chemical identity of the genome.

distractorRationales.A: Many viruses use RNA genomes; cell theory is about cellular organization, not a ban on RNA.
distractorRationales.C: Some authentic bacteria are near the diffraction limit; visibility is not a tenet of cell theory.
distractorRationales.D: RNA viruses are biological entities; they are simply not cells.

items.stem:
A 40 kDa GFP fusion is imaged 30 min after microinjection into the cytosol. Mean fluorescence intensities (arbitrary units) are:
GFP only: nucleus 22, cytosol 78 (ratio 0.28).
GFP with a nuclear localisation sequence (NLS): nucleus 81, cytosol 19 (ratio 4.3).
GFP–NLS after ATP depletion: nucleus 25, cytosol 75 (ratio 0.33).
GFP–NLS plus a nuclear-pore blocker: nucleus 18, cytosol 82 (ratio 0.22).
Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: GFP without an NLS is actively concentrated in the nucleus (ratio 0.28).
ATP depletion stimulates NLS-dependent import, because the ratio rises from 0.28 to 0.33.
NLS-dependent nuclear accumulation requires ATP and intact nuclear pores.
Blocking nuclear pores increases nuclear GFP–NLS (18 versus 81 in the untreated NLS sample).

items.explanation: Active nuclear import concentrates an NLS cargo: the nuclear/cytosolic ratio jumps from 0.28 (GFP alone) to 4.3 (GFP–NLS). Depleting ATP drops that ratio to 0.33, and blocking pores drops it to 0.22, both indistinguishable from passive distribution of GFP. Therefore concentration of the NLS protein needs both energy (Ran–importin cycle) and open nuclear pores. A ratio below 1 is not accumulation, and 18 nuclear units with the pore blocker is less than 81, not more.

distractorRationales.A: A nuclear/cytosol ratio of 0.28 means GFP is still mostly cytosolic; that is not active concentration.
distractorRationales.B: ATP depletion collapses the NLS ratio from 4.3 to 0.33; comparing 0.33 with GFP-only 0.28 is the wrong baseline.
distractorRationales.D: Nuclear intensity falls from 81 to 18 with the pore blocker, so pores are required rather than inhibitory.

items.stem: After a watershed infarct, a patient names colors and shapes of objects on a table and can match them by appearance, but cannot follow which cup the examiner slides left versus right and misreaches in depth. Ungerleider and Mishkin’s two-stream account most directly implicates which pathway?

choices.text: The ventral “what” stream through inferotemporal cortex, because naming is lost
The parvocellular geniculate layers alone, because they carry only motion
The optic chiasm, because only crossed fibers encode motion
The dorsal “where/how” stream through posterior parietal cortex, because spatial tracking and reaching fail while object identity is relatively spared

items.explanation: Ungerleider and Mishkin dissociated a ventral occipitotemporal “what” pathway (object identity, color, form; parvo-biased) from a dorsal occipitoparietal “where/how” pathway (location, motion, visually guided reaching; magno-biased). Spared naming with failed tracking and depth-reaching is a dorsal-stream pattern. Parvocellular layers carry color and acuity, not motion as their specialty. Chiasmal lesions would produce field cuts, not this identity-versus-space split.

distractorRationales.A: Ventral damage would impair identity and naming more than spatial tracking; the stem shows the reverse.
distractorRationales.B: Parvo layers are associated with color and form, not as the motion channel; magno/dorsal is the motion/space route.
distractorRationales.C: Chiasm lesions affect nasal-fiber crossing and fields, not a selective dorsal-stream visuospatial deficit.

items.stem: At 25 °C, Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10^−14. In an aqueous solution with [H3O+] = 2.0 × 10^−3 M, what is [OH−]?
items.explanation: Autoionization of water always supplies the product [H3O+][OH−] = Kw at a given temperature. With [H3O+] fixed at 2.0 × 10^−3 M by added acid, [OH−] = Kw/[H3O+] = 1.0 × 10^−14 / 2.0 × 10^−3 = 5.0 × 10^−12 M. Hydronium and hydroxide are not equal except in pure water. Kw is the product, not the hydroxide concentration. Multiplying Kw by [H3O+] instead of dividing is a common inversion error that yields a nonsensical 10^−17 M.

distractorRationales.A: Equal [H3O+] and [OH−] holds only for pure water (or strictly neutral solutions), not for a solution already 2 × 10^−3 M in hydronium.
distractorRationales.C: 1.0 × 10^−14 M is Kw, a product of two concentrations, not [OH−] itself.
distractorRationales.D: 2.0 × 10^−17 M is Kw × [H3O+], the inverse of the correct operation.

items.stem: Undergraduates undergo either a severe and embarrassing initiation or a mild one in order to join a discussion group that then proves dull. Later, severe-initiation members rate the group as more interesting than mild-initiation members do. Which process best explains the difference?

choices.text: Door-in-the-face compliance, because a large request was followed by a smaller one
Effort justification: suffering to join is inconsistent with believing the group is dull, so dissonance is reduced by raising liking for the group
Social loafing, because ratings were collected in a crowded room
Peripheral-route persuasion, because initiation is processed as a celebrity endorsement

items.explanation: Aronson and Mills’s initiation study is a standard effort-justification application of cognitive dissonance. If I went through something severe to get here, but the group is dull, those cognitions clash. Changing the memory of the ordeal is hard; changing the attitude toward the group is easier, so liking rises. Door-in-the-face is a sequential-request compliance tactic, not an initiation. Loafing is about effort on a collective performance. Initiation is not a peripheral celebrity cue in ELM terms.

distractorRationales.A: No large-then-small request sequence is described; members did not concede to a smaller favor after refusing a larger one.
distractorRationales.C: The dependent measure is liking, not reduced individual effort on a pooled task.
distractorRationales.D: A painful initiation is not a source-attractiveness cue; the mechanism is post-effort attitude shift.

items.stem: As literary narrative, the extract is primarily about

choices.text: a man who physically steals a supervisor's coat from a peg
using someone else's sentences for warmth and credit, and the small cowardice of almost admitting it
a scientific proof that authenticity is a mineral
bathroom plumbing in a university

items.explanation: The coat is a metaphor for borrowed sentences; the plot is the seminar paragraph, the friend's misrecognition, the mirror, and the two emails. That is a literary narrative of intellectual borrowing, not a theft of cloth, not a mineralogy paper, not plumbing. A main-claim reading has to keep both the warmth of the borrow and the nod-as-if-the-sleeves-were-yours, which only B does, including the outbox delay as character.

distractorRationales.A: The coat is figurative; no peg or garment theft occurs.
distractorRationales.C: Ethics talks as if authenticity were a mineral is a view the narrator complicates, not a proof.
distractorRationales.D: The bathroom is a setting for the mirror, not the subject.

passage.title: The borrowed coat
passage.body:
He wore other people's sentences the way some men wear coats: against weather, and with the labels left in. At the seminar he began, "One might argue," and then produced, almost unaltered, a paragraph his supervisor had emailed at midnight to save him. The room nodded. He felt the coat settle on his shoulders, warm and slightly too large in the sleeves.

Afterward a friend said, "That was the first time you sounded like yourself." He laughed too quickly. In the bathroom mirror the coat was still on. He tried to take it off by telling the truth to the glass: I do not know whether I think this. The glass, being a glass, offered his mouth moving.

Ethics talks as if authenticity were a mineral you either contain or fake. The evening suggested something cheaper and more ordinary. A borrowed argument can keep you from freezing. It can also teach your arms the wrong length. The crime, if there is one, is not the borrowing. It is the nod you collect as if the sleeves had always been yours.

He sent the supervisor a note: Thank you. I sounded like myself. He deleted it. He sent: Thank you. I used your paragraph. He left that one in the outbox until morning, which is a kind of cowardice that still knows the difference.

items.stem: A tennis ball of mass 0.060 kg hits a wall at 20 m s−1 and rebounds at 20 m s−1 in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.010 s. Impulse = Δp = F_avg Δt, taking incoming momentum as positive. What is the magnitude of the average force on the ball?
items.explanation: Incoming p = 0.060 × 20 = 1.2 kg m s−1. Outgoing p = −1.2 kg m s−1. Change in momentum = −1.2 − 1.2 = −2.4 kg m s−1, so |Δp| = 2.4 kg m s−1. F_avg = 2.4 / 0.010 = 240 N. Using |Δp| = 1.2 (as if the ball stopped) halves the force to 120 N. Forgetting to divide by 0.010 s leaves 1.2 N, the momentum change of a stop, not a force. 0.012 N treats Δt as 100 s or multiplies instead of dividing incorrectly. Reversal doubles the impulse relative to a dead stop.

distractorRationales.A: 120 N would be correct if the ball stopped and did not rebound, so |Δp| = 1.2 rather than 2.4.
distractorRationales.B: 1.2 N is |Δp| for a stop, with the 0.010 s omitted, and has the wrong unit role.
distractorRationales.C: 0.012 N is 0.060 × 0.20 or a similar product that is not Δp/Δt.

items.stem:
Lattice enthalpy magnitudes (kJ mol−1, all exothermic as negative) estimated from Born–Haber cycles:

Salt | |ΔH_latt|
NaF | 910
MgO | 3900
LiF | 1030
NaI | 700

Cation/anion radii increase Na+ < Mg2+ and F− < I−; charges are 1 or 2. Lattice energy scales roughly with |q+ q−| / r. Which comparison is required by that scaling and the table?

choices.text: All four lattice enthalpies must be equal because each formula unit contains two ions
MgO >> NaF mainly because of the 2×2 charge product, and NaI is weaker than NaF because I− is larger than F−
NaI should exceed MgO because iodine is heavier
LiF is weaker than NaF because Li+ is smaller than Na+

items.explanation: MgO’s |q+q−| = 4 versus 1 for NaF, and the ions are still small, so |ΔH_latt| jumps from 910 to 3900 kJ mol−1. NaI at 700 is below NaF at 910 because the larger iodide increases r in the denominator. LiF at 1030 is stronger than NaF, as expected for a smaller cation, not weaker. Mass of iodine is irrelevant to the Coulomb scaling. Counting ‘two ions’ would make every 1:1 salt identical, contradicting the 700–3900 spread.

distractorRationales.A: The four values 910, 3900, 1030 and 700 are not equal.
distractorRationales.C: NaI is the weakest lattice in the table (700), not stronger than MgO (3900).
distractorRationales.D: LiF is 1030, larger than NaF 910, matching the smaller Li+ radius.

items.stem:
A diethyl-ether solution contains naphthalene and benzoic acid. The solution is shaken with 1.0 M NaOH(aq); the layers are separated. The aqueous layer is then acidified with HCl and extracted with fresh ether.

Fraction | expected major organic
Original ether after NaOH wash | naphthalene
Alkaline aqueous layer | sodium benzoate
Ether extract after acidification | benzoic acid

Which separation principle is illustrated?

choices.text: HCl oxidises naphthalene, which is why it stays in ether
Deprotonation converts benzoic acid into a water-soluble salt, leaving naphthalene in ether; acidification regenerates the ether-soluble acid
Naphthalene is extracted into NaOH because it is more acidic than benzoic acid
Both organics remain in the original ether because ether is always the upper layer

items.explanation: Benzoic acid (pKa ~4.2) is deprotonated by NaOH to benzoate, an ionic species that partitions into water. Naphthalene has no acidic proton and remains in ether. Acidifying benzoate regenerates PhCO2H, which returns to ether. Naphthalene is not an acid relative to benzoic acid and does not dissolve in NaOH. If both stayed in the original ether, the scheme would not list sodium benzoate in the aqueous layer. HCl is used as an acid to protonate benzoate, not as an oxidant for naphthalene.

distractorRationales.A: No redox is invoked; HCl protonates PhCO2− back to PhCO2H.
distractorRationales.C: Naphthalene is the component that remains in ether after the NaOH wash, so it was not extracted.
distractorRationales.D: The table assigns benzoate to the alkaline aqueous layer, so a transfer occurred.

items.stem: A plus-end-directed kinesin mutant has kcat for ATP hydrolysis reduced 40-fold with little change in Km(ATP) or microtubule-binding affinity. In a gliding assay on polarity-marked microtubules (bright plus ends), wild-type motors drive cargo toward the bright end at 800 nm/s. The mutant cargo is most likely to:

choices.text: Reverse direction and move toward the minus end, because lowering kcat inverts motor polarity
Bind microtubules but translocate much more slowly toward the plus end, because stepping is tightly coupled to the ATPase cycle
Switch tracks onto F-actin, because kinesin becomes a myosin when ATP turnover is slow
Catastrophically depolymerize microtubules from the plus end, which is the normal function of conventional kinesin-1

items.explanation: Conventional kinesin is a plus-end-directed microtubule motor. Each eight-nanometer step is coupled to one ATP hydrolytic cycle, so a large drop in kcat slows the stepping rate without reversing the structural bias that selects the plus end. Km is unchanged, so the motor still saturates at physiologic ATP; the defect is catalytic throughput, not substrate binding. Kinesin does not become an actin motor when slow, and kinesin-1 is a transport motor rather than a microtubule depolymerase (that activity belongs to other kinesin families such as kinesin-13).

distractorRationales.A: Polarity is set by the motor domain's asymmetric interaction with the microtubule lattice, not by the numerical value of kcat.
distractorRationales.C: Kinesin and myosin are distinct ATPases with different track specificities; slowing ATP turnover does not convert one into the other.
distractorRationales.D: Kinesin-1 walks processively toward the plus end; plus-end catastrophe is not its physiologic role.

items.stem:
An enzyme obeys Michaelis–Menten kinetics with Km = 2.0 mM and Vmax = 80 µmol min−1. Initial rates measured without inhibitor are:

[S] (mM) | v (µmol min−1)
2.0 | 40
6.0 | 60
8.0 | 64

A competitive inhibitor raises the apparent Km to 6.0 mM without changing Vmax. What is v at [S] = 6.0 mM in the presence of that inhibitor?

choices.text: 40 µmol min−1
60 µmol min−1
20 µmol min−1
30 µmol min−1

items.explanation: With the inhibitor, v = Vmax [S] / (Km,app + [S]) = 80 × 6 / (6 + 6) = 480 / 12 = 40 µmol min−1. That is half of Vmax because [S] now equals the new Km. The uninhibited rate at 6 mM is 60, which is the no-inhibitor row in the table, not the inhibited value. Using the original Km of 2 mM with the inhibited formula would incorrectly give 60 again.

distractorRationales.B: 60 µmol min−1 is the uninhibited rate at 6 mM, when Km is still 2 mM, not the inhibited rate.
distractorRationales.C: 20 µmol min−1 would be v = Vmax [S] / (Km,app + 3[S]) or a similar extra factor; the competitive rate law does not introduce that.
distractorRationales.D: 30 µmol min−1 is Vmax × 6 / (6 + 10) or half of the uninhibited 60; neither matches Km,app = 6 mM.

items.stem: A point mutation doubles an enzyme’s Km for substrate without changing kcat or the enzyme concentration. Assays are run at a substrate concentration equal to the wild-type Km. Relative to wild type, the mutant’s initial velocity is:

choices.text: Unchanged, because velocity depends only on kcat
Equal to the new Vmax, because [S] still saturates the mutant
Lower: wild type runs at Vmax/2 while the mutant runs at Vmax/3
Higher, because a larger Km means a larger first-order rate constant

items.explanation: The Michaelis–Menten equation is v = Vmax [S] / (Km + [S]). For wild type, [S] = Km so v = Vmax/2. The mutant has Km′ = 2 Km and the same Vmax (kcat and [E]t unchanged). Substituting [S] = Km gives v = Vmax · Km / (2 Km + Km) = Vmax/3. Thus the observed rate falls. Velocity at subsaturating [S] depends on both kcat and Km, so an unchanged kcat is not enough. [S] equal to the old Km is only half of the new Km, far from saturation. Increasing Km reflects weaker apparent substrate interaction, which slows—not accelerates—the rate at fixed [S].

distractorRationales.A: At [S] near Km, v is sensitive to Km as well as kcat; only Vmax is set by kcat[E]t at saturating [S].
distractorRationales.B: Saturation requires [S] ≫ Km. Here [S] is only half of the mutant Km, so v is well below Vmax.
distractorRationales.D: A larger Km is poorer apparent affinity; the first-order constant Vmax/Km decreases when Km doubles at constant Vmax.

items.stem:
Amino-acid differences in a 100-residue protein among four species:

Pair | differences
A–B | 2
A–C | 8
B–C | 8
A–D | 20
B–D | 20
C–D | 20

A molecular clock is assumed, so distance is proportional to time since divergence. Which unrooted tree topology and relative branching order are supported?

choices.text: A star phylogeny with all four lineages splitting at once, because every pair differs
A and B are sister taxa; C joins that pair next; D is the deepest split
A and D are sister taxa because 20 is the largest number
C and D are sister taxa; A and B attach as a distant outgroup pair with 2 differences to D

items.explanation: The smallest distance (A–B = 2) identifies the most recent split. C is equally 8 steps from A and from B, so C joins after A and B have already diverged, at a depth of 4 substitutions per lineage (8/2). D is 20 from every other taxon, a deeper stem of 10 substitutions per lineage, and the equal A/B/C-to-D distances indicate a clock-like outgroup split, not a C–D clade. A star would not produce a 2-versus-8-versus-20 hierarchy. Large distances mark old splits, not sister pairs.

distractorRationales.A: A simultaneous four-way split cannot explain the nested 2, 8 and 20 classes.
distractorRationales.C: The largest distance marks the oldest divergence, so A and D are the least closely related pair, not sisters.
distractorRationales.D: C and D differ by 20, the maximum, so they are not sisters; A–B = 2 is not a distance to D.

items.stem:
Sound intensity level in decibels is L = 10 log10(I / I0) with I0 = 1.0 × 10^−12 W m−2. Two measurements at the same frequency are:

Location | Intensity I (W m−2)
P | 1.0 × 10^−6
Q | 1.0 × 10^−4

The difference is ΔL = LQ − LP = 10 log10(IQ / IP). What is ΔL?

choices.text: 2 dB
20 dB
100 dB
200 dB

items.explanation: The intensity ratio is (1.0 × 10^−4) / (1.0 × 10^−6) = 100. Then ΔL = 10 log10(100) = 10 × 2 = 20 dB. Equivalently, LP = 10 log10(10^6) = 60 dB and LQ = 10 log10(10^8) = 80 dB, so the difference is 20 dB. Using log10(100) = 2 without the factor of 10 gives 2 dB. Using the ratio 100 itself as a decibel figure gives 100 dB. Using 10 × 100 or confusing log10 with ln can produce 200 dB. The factor of 10 in the definition is required because the bel is 10 times smaller than the decibel scale used here.

distractorRationales.A: 2 dB is log10(IQ/IP) without multiplying by 10. The definition of L already includes that factor of 10.
distractorRationales.C: 100 dB is the intensity ratio quoted as if it were already in decibels. Decibels are 10 times the log of the ratio, not the ratio itself.
distractorRationales.D: 200 dB would correspond to an intensity ratio of 10^20, far larger than the tabulated factor of 100.

items.stem: A mitochondrion oxidises one acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle, producing 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP. The electron-transport accounting used in this laboratory is: 10 H+ translocated per NADH, 6 H+ per FADH2, and 4 H+ re-entering per ATP formed (3 through ATP synthase plus 1 for phosphate import). GTP is counted as equivalent to 1 ATP. How many ATP equivalents are obtained from that one acetyl-CoA?
items.explanation: Each NADH yields 10/4 = 2.5 ATP, so three NADH give 7.5. FADH2 yields 6/4 = 1.5 ATP. Adding the substrate-level GTP gives 7.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 10 ATP equivalents. The older integer tally of 12 counted 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2 (9 + 2 + 1). Fifteen would treat all four reducing equivalents as NADH at the old 3 ATP factor. Four would count only the substrate-level phosphorylation plus a single reduced cofactor.

distractorRationales.A: Fifteen would be 3 NADH plus 1 FADH2 all billed at 3 ATP each, plus GTP, which overcounts FADH2 and uses the old NADH factor.
distractorRationales.B: Four ATP would ignore most of the proton-motive force from the three NADH and the FADH2.
distractorRationales.D: Twelve is the classical integer yield (3×3 NADH + 2 FADH2 + 1 GTP), not the 10/4 and 6/4 proton arithmetic given here.

items.stem: Hydrogen and oxygen react according to 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. A vessel is charged with 2 mol H2 and 2 mol O2, and the reaction goes to completion. Afterward the vessel contains:

choices.text: 2 mol H2O and 1 mol O2 remaining
4 mol H2O and no leftover gas
2 mol H2O and 1 mol H2 remaining
1 mol H2O and 1 mol O2 remaining

items.explanation: The stoichiometric ratio is 2 mol H2 per 1 mol O2. Starting with 2 mol H2 therefore requires only 1 mol O2 and produces 2 mol H2O; hydrogen is limiting. One mole of the original 2 mol O2 is left unreacted. Treating the recipe as 1:1 because the vessel was filled with equal moles of each gas overconsumes oxygen and invents 4 mol of water, which would have needed 4 mol H2. Swapping the limiting reagent leaves leftover hydrogen instead of leftover oxygen. The coefficients, not the equal starting moles, decide the leftover.

distractorRationales.B: Producing 4 mol H2O would require 4 mol H2 and 2 mol O2. Only 2 mol H2 are present, so water cannot exceed 2 mol.
distractorRationales.C: This treats O2 as limiting. Two moles of O2 would need 4 mol H2; extra oxygen remains, not extra hydrogen.
distractorRationales.D: A 1:1:1 reading of the equation ignores the coefficient 2 on H2 and on H2O. Two moles of H2 yield two moles of water, not one.

items.stem:
Successive ionisation energies of element M (kJ mol−1) are:
IE1 577; IE2 1817; IE3 2745; IE4 11 577; IE5 14 842.
A large jump indicates that the next electron is taken from a noble-gas core. In which group does M belong?

choices.text: Group 1, because only IE1 is below 600 kJ mol−1
Group 13, because the jump occurs after three valence electrons (IE3 → IE4)
Group 2, because IE2 is already large (1817)
Group 18, because several ionisation energies are listed

items.explanation: IE1–IE3 lie in the thousands or below (577, 1817, 2745) while IE4 leaps to 11 577, more than four times IE3. Three relatively removable electrons then a core-like fourth means three valence electrons: group 13 (for example aluminium). Group 1 would jump after IE1 (IE2 huge). Group 2 would jump after IE2; here IE3 is still only 2745, not core-like. Noble gases do not show three modest IEs before a jump at IE4. The pattern uses only the given numbers.

distractorRationales.A: IE2 and IE3 are still sequential valence ionisations (1817, 2745); a group-1 jump would appear at IE2.
distractorRationales.C: IE2/IE1 ≈ 3 is ordinary; the diagnostic jump is IE4/IE3 ≈ 4.2.
distractorRationales.D: Listing five IEs does not place an element in group 18; noble-gas cores explain the jump, not the group of M.

items.stem: An IV bag of saline (density 1000 kg/m^3) is hung so the free fluid surface is 80 cm above a venous catheter. Taking g = 10 m/s^2, the gauge pressure at the catheter due to the saline column is:
items.explanation: Gauge hydrostatic pressure is rho g h. Convert 80 cm to 0.80 m, then 1000 times 10 times 0.80 equals 8000 Pa, or 8.0 x 10^3 Pa. Leaving h in centimeters without converting, omitting g, or treating the height as 8 m each shifts the answer by an order of magnitude. Atmospheric pressure is already excluded because the question asks for gauge pressure from the column alone.

distractorRationales.A: This is far too small and usually comes from dropping both density conversion and g, or from treating 80 cm as 0.080 m and then dropping another factor.
distractorRationales.B: This matches rho times h with h in meters but omitting g (1000 x 0.80 = 800), or using g = 1 in SI.
distractorRationales.D: This is the result of using h = 8.0 m instead of 0.80 m (1000 x 10 x 8 = 8 x 10^4 Pa).

items.stem: Acetone is deprotonated with one equivalent of LDA at −78 °C, benzaldehyde is added, and the reaction is quenched with mild aqueous acid without heating. What is the principal carbon–carbon bond-forming pathway and product class?

choices.text: Benzaldehyde’s enolate attacks acetone, giving a β-hydroxy aldehyde
Cannizzaro disproportionation of benzaldehyde, with acetone as an uninvolved spectator
The acetone enolate adds to benzaldehyde in a crossed aldol, giving a β-hydroxy ketone
No addition occurs, because LDA destroys both carbonyls by over-reduction

items.explanation: LDA is a strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base that irreversibly generates the kinetic enolate of acetone. Benzaldehyde has no enolizable α-hydrogen, so it cannot form an enolate and cannot undergo Cannizzaro chemistry under these aprotic, strongly basic but hydride-free conditions. The acetone enolate therefore adds to the aldehyde carbonyl in a crossed aldol addition. Mild, unheated workup protonates the alkoxide to a β-hydroxy ketone (4-hydroxy-4-phenylbutan-2-one) rather than forcing dehydration to the enone. LDA is a base, not a hydride reductant like LiAlH4.

distractorRationales.A: Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot form an enolate. Acetone is the only competent enolate precursor here.
distractorRationales.B: Cannizzaro requires a non-enolizable aldehyde plus hydroxide and no other electrophile; it is not the pathway when a preformed ketone enolate is added to benzaldehyde.
distractorRationales.D: LDA deprotonates; it does not reduce carbonyls the way aluminum hydrides do. The aldol addition proceeds.

items.stem: A diprotic acid H2A (pKa1 = 2.0, pKa2 = 7.0) is titrated with strong base. Which description of the titration curve is correct?

choices.text: A single steep equivalence jump at pH 7, because the average of the two pKa values is 4.5 and that is irrelevant.
No buffer regions, because diprotic acids are always strong in both protons.
Three equivalence points, one for each hydrogen in H2A plus the solvent.
Two buffer regions (near pH 2 and near pH 7) and two equivalence points: the first converts H2A to HA− and the second converts HA− to A2−.

items.explanation: A diprotic acid with well-separated pKa values (here five units apart) shows two distinct neutralization stages. Halfway to the first equivalence point, pH ≈ pKa1 and the buffer is H2A/HA−. At the first equivalence point the principal species is HA− (amphiprotic; pH ≈ ½(pKa1 + pKa2) ≈ 4.5). Halfway to the second equivalence, pH ≈ pKa2 with buffer HA−/A2−. The second equivalence point is a solution of A2− and is basic. There are two, not three, acidic protons to neutralize. Neither proton is strong given these pKa values.

distractorRationales.A: Two separated pKa values produce two jumps, not one. pH 7 is the second buffer region (pKa2), not a unique single equivalence.
distractorRationales.B: pKa 2 and 7 describe a weak first proton and a weaker second proton; both generate buffer plateaus.
distractorRationales.C: H2A has two titratable protons, hence two equivalence points (solvent water is not a third analyte proton here).

items.stem: Lactic acid has pKa = 3.86. In a solution buffered at pH 5.86, which statement about the lactic acid / lactate pair is correct?

choices.text: The acid form predominates by a factor of 100.
The two forms are present in equal concentration.
The lactate (conjugate base) form predominates by a factor of 100.
Virtually all of the material is fully protonated because pH is still less than 7.

items.explanation: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]), so log([A−]/[HA]) = 5.86 − 3.86 = 2, hence [A−]/[HA] = 10^2 = 100. Two pH units above pKa, the deprotonated form is 100-fold more abundant. Equal concentrations occur only at pH = pKa. Predominance of HA would require pH below pKa. Neutrality (pH 7) is irrelevant to the HA/A− ratio; that ratio is fixed by pH − pKa, not by whether the solution is “acidic” relative to 7. For physiological acids this is the same reasoning used for blood buffers.

distractorRationales.A: A 100-fold excess of HA would require pH = pKa − 2 (about 1.86), not pH 5.86.
distractorRationales.B: Equal concentrations require pH = pKa = 3.86.
distractorRationales.D: pH 5.86 is still below 7 but is two units above this pKa, so the base form dominates. Comparison to 7 is the wrong reference.

items.stem:
A first-order decomposition has k = 0.069 min−1. Because t1/2 = ln 2 / k and ln 2 ≈ 0.69, t1/2 = 10 min. Starting from 80 mg of reactant, remaining masses are:

Time (min) | mass (mg)
0 | 80
10 | 40
20 | 20
30 | 10

A catalyst is found to double k at the same temperature. What is the new t1/2, and how much remains at 10 min from the same 80 mg start?

choices.text: t1/2 = 20 min; 40 mg remains (catalyst slows the reaction)
t1/2 stays 10 min; 40 mg remains, because half-life is independent of k
t1/2 = 5.0 min; 10 mg remains (three half-lives in 10 min)
t1/2 = 5.0 min; 20 mg remains at 10 min (two half-lives)

items.explanation: Doubling k halves t1/2 to 5.0 min. Ten minutes is then two half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 mg. Catalysts increase k, they do not lengthen half-life. First-order t1/2 is independent of concentration but inversely dependent on k. Three half-lives would be 15 min at the new k, leaving 10 mg, not a 10 min point.

distractorRationales.A: A catalyst increases k, so t1/2 falls rather than rises to 20 min.
distractorRationales.B: t1/2 = 0.69/k, so it must change when k doubles.
distractorRationales.C: 10 min / 5 min = 2 half-lives, not 3; 10 mg would be the 15 min mark.

items.stem:
Human lymphocytes (2n = 46) are treated with colchicine, which prevents spindle assembly. Mitotic figures are scored:
Control: mitotic index 4%; 28% of mitoses in metaphase; mean chromosome number 46.
Colchicine 4 h: mitotic index 18%; 91% of mitoses in metaphase; mean chromosome number 46.
Colchicine 24 h, then drug wash and one subsequent cell cycle: mitotic index 5%; 30% of mitoses in metaphase; mean chromosome number 92.
Which interpretation fits?

choices.text: Prolonged spindle failure blocks anaphase; after wash, some cells enter the next cycle tetraploid (92 chromosomes).
Colchicine lowers the mitotic index from 4% to 18%, proving fewer cells enter mitosis.
Control cells already have 92 chromosomes, matching a normal human karyotype.
Four hours of colchicine is enough to double the chromosome number to 92 in the arrested metaphases.

items.explanation: Without a spindle, chromatids cannot separate, so cells pile up in metaphase: mitotic index rises 4% → 18% and metaphase among mitoses rises 28% → 91%, while the count remains 46. If the block lasts long enough that cells exit mitosis without cytokinesis and then replicate DNA again, the next mitosis shows 92 chromosomes. That appears only after the 24 h treatment plus wash, not at 4 h. An increase in mitotic index is arrest, not fewer mitoses. Diploid human cells have 46 chromosomes, shown in the control row.

distractorRationales.B: 18% is higher than 4%; colchicine increases the apparent mitotic index by metaphase arrest.
distractorRationales.C: The control mean is 46, the diploid human number, not 92.
distractorRationales.D: The 4 h row still lists 46 chromosomes; doubling appears only in the post-wash 92-chromosome row.

items.stem: Approximate pKa values: ethanol 16, phenol 10, ethanoic acid 4.8, HCl −7. Aqueous buffers are prepared at pH 7.0. A species is taken as deprotonated if pH > pKa + 1 and protonated if pH < pKa − 1. Which species is predominantly deprotonated at pH 7.0?

choices.text: None of them, because pH 7 is neutral
Ethanoate ion from ethanoic acid; phenol and ethanol remain protonated; HCl is fully deprotonated as Cl−
Ethanol, because pKa 16 is the largest
Phenol only, because 10 is closest to 7

items.explanation: Ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8) lies more than 1 unit below pH 7, so it exists as ethanoate. Phenol (pKa 10) lies more than 1 unit above pH 7, so it remains PhOH. Ethanol (pKa 16) is fully protonated. HCl (pKa −7) is a strong acid, fully Cl−. Largest pKa means weakest acid, least deprotonated, so ethanol is not deprotonated. Closeness of 10 to 7 without the ±1 rule still leaves phenol mostly protonated (ratio [A−]/[HA]=10^(7−10)=0.001). Neutrality of water does not set every solute’s protonation state; pKa versus pH does.

distractorRationales.A: pH 7 compared with pKa 4.8 already requires ethanoate as the major form.
distractorRationales.C: A pKa of 16 means ethanol holds its proton at pH 7 by an enormous factor.
distractorRationales.D: Phenol’s pKa 10 is still 3 units above pH 7, so it is not predominantly phenolate.

items.stem: D-Glucose and D-galactose are both aldohexoses. They differ in configuration at a single carbon, C4. Which term correctly names that relationship?

choices.text: Enantiomers
Anomers
Constitutional isomers
C4 epimers (diastereomers)

items.explanation: Epimers are diastereomers that differ in configuration at exactly one stereocenter. D-Glucose and D-galactose share the D configuration at C5 and differ only at C4, so they are C4 epimers. Enantiomers would invert every stereocenter (D-glucose versus L-glucose). Anomers are a special pair of epimers that differ only at the anomeric carbon (C1 of an aldose in cyclic form), as in α-D-glucose versus β-D-glucose. Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity, not merely in configuration; both sugars are 2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanals.

distractorRationales.A: Enantiomers are mirror images. Galactose is not the mirror image of glucose; L-glucose is.
distractorRationales.B: Anomers differ at C1 (the hemiacetal carbon), not at C4. α/β-D-glucose are anomers of each other.
distractorRationales.C: The two sugars have the same connectivity. The difference is stereochemical at C4.

items.stem: In a photoelectric cell, 400 nm light of intensity I0 ejects electrons with K_max = 1.1 eV at a rate of 2.0 × 10^12 s−1 (when every absorbed photon liberates one electron). The intensity is then doubled to 2 I0 without changing wavelength. What happens to K_max and to the electron rate?

choices.text: K_max doubles to 2.2 eV; the rate stays 2.0 × 10^12 s−1
K_max stays 1.1 eV; the rate is unchanged because one photon still has energy 3.1 eV
K_max and the rate both fall, because more photons crowd the surface
K_max stays 1.1 eV; the electron rate doubles to 4.0 × 10^12 s−1

items.explanation: K_max depends only on photon energy hc/λ minus φ, both unchanged when intensity changes at fixed λ, so K_max remains 1.1 eV. Doubling intensity doubles the photon arrival rate and therefore doubles the photoelectron rate to 4.0 × 10^12 s−1. Classical wave theory would have put the extra intensity into K_max; the photon picture does not. Keeping the rate fixed ignores that more photons arrive per second. Extra photons do not suppress emission; they increase the count of independent one-photon events.

distractorRationales.A: Intensity is photon number per second, not photon energy; K_max is fixed by λ.
distractorRationales.B: Each photon’s energy is unchanged, but there are twice as many of them, so the electron rate doubles.
distractorRationales.C: Rate rises, and K_max is unchanged; crowding is not a stopping mechanism here.

items.stem: A mixture of glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) and lysine (pI ≈ 9.7) is spotted at the origin of a paper electrophoresis strip equilibrated in a pH 7.0 buffer. After the field is applied, which migration pattern is expected?

choices.text: Both amino acids migrate toward the cathode
Both amino acids migrate toward the anode
Glycine migrates toward the cathode and lysine migrates toward the anode
Glycine migrates toward the anode and lysine migrates toward the cathode

items.explanation: The sign of an amino acid’s net charge is set by pH relative to pI: if pH is above pI the molecule is net negative and moves toward the anode; if pH is below pI it is net positive and moves toward the cathode. At pH 7.0, glycine (pI 6.0) is slightly anionic and therefore anodal, whereas lysine (pI 9.7) remains cationic because its side-chain ammonium is still protonated and it migrates to the cathode. The two residues therefore move in opposite directions, which is the basis of separating them electrophoretically at this pH.

distractorRationales.A: Glycine is above its pI at pH 7 and is not cationic, so it does not join lysine toward the cathode.
distractorRationales.B: Lysine is below its pI at pH 7 and remains positive, so it does not migrate toward the anode.
distractorRationales.C: This choice reverses both signs: glycine is the anion and lysine is the cation at pH 7.

items.stem:
Standard enthalpy changes (kJ mol−1) are:
(1) C + O2 → CO2    ΔH = −394
(2) H2 + 1/2 O2 → H2O(l)    ΔH = −286
(3) 2C + 3H2 + 1/2 O2 → C2H5OH(l)    ΔH = −278
Combustion: C2H5OH(l) + 3 O2 → 2 CO2 + 3 H2O(l).
Using Hess’s law, ΔH_comb = 2(ΔH1) + 3(ΔH2) − (ΔH3). What is ΔH_comb?

choices.text: −1646 kJ mol−1 (omitting −(ΔH3))
−1368 kJ mol−1
+1368 kJ mol−1
−278 kJ mol−1, the formation enthalpy of ethanol

items.explanation: Products: 2 CO2 contribute 2 × (−394) = −788 kJ and 3 H2O contribute 3 × (−286) = −858 kJ, sum −1646 kJ. Ethanol’s formation enthalpy is −278 kJ, and O2 is 0, so subtract −278: ΔH_comb = −1646 − (−278) = −1368 kJ mol−1. Combustion of an alcohol is exothermic, so the sign is negative. Leaving out the ethanol term stops at −1646. The formation value −278 kJ is for building ethanol from elements, not for burning it.

distractorRationales.A: That sum is only the product formation enthalpies; Hess’s law still subtracts the reactant ethanol ΔHf.
distractorRationales.C: The magnitude is right but combustion releases heat, so ΔH is negative.
distractorRationales.D: −278 kJ mol−1 is equation (3), formation, not combustion.

items.stem: A 0.20 M solution of the weak acid HA has Ka = 2.0 × 10^−6. Neglecting water autoionization and using the x ≪ [HA] approximation, what is the pH?
items.explanation: For a weak acid, [H+] ≈ √(Ka C) = √(2.0 × 10^−6 × 0.20) = √(4.0 × 10^−7) = 6.3 × 10^−4, so pH = 3.20. Equivalently, pH = ½ pKa − ½ log C with pKa = 5.70 and log(0.20) = −0.70, giving ½(5.70 + 0.70) = 3.20. The approximation x/C ≈ 0.003 is well under 5%. pH = 0.70 would treat HA as a strong acid (−log C). pH = 5.70 is the pKa, not the pH of the unbuffered weak acid. 6.80 is not the result of the square-root expression.

distractorRationales.B: 0.70 is −log(0.20), the pH if HA were a strong acid that fully dissociated.
distractorRationales.C: 5.70 is −log(Ka) = pKa, which is the pH of a 1:1 buffer of HA and A−, not of HA alone.
distractorRationales.D: 6.80 does not follow from √(Ka C) or from the half-pKa formula; it may come from incorrectly averaging pKa with 14 or with −log C.

items.stem:
Core temperature (°C) in a climate chamber. Effectors: shivering if core < set-point − 0.2 °C; sweating if core > set-point + 0.2 °C. Normal set-point 37.0 °C.

Time (min) | chamber air (°C) | core (°C) | observed effector
0–20 | 22 | 37.0 | none
20–40 | 42 | 37.4 | sweating
40–60 | 42 | 37.0 | sweating (less)
60–90 | 42, pyrogen injected | 37.0 → 39.0 | shivering then none

Which control scheme matches the record?

choices.text: The set-point is the chamber air temperature, which is why core follows 42 °C
Pyrogen destroys effectors, which is why shivering appears
Negative feedback around a 37.0 °C set-point, then a pyrogen-induced rise in set-point to 39.0 °C that transiently makes 37.0 °C feel ‘cold’
Positive feedback, because sweating at 37.4 °C further raises core temperature

items.explanation: In the heat, core edges up to 37.4 °C and sweating is recruited, then core returns to 37.0 °C despite air at 42 °C: negative feedback defending 37.0 °C. After pyrogen, the same 37.0 °C now lies below a new 39.0 °C set-point, so shivering raises core until 39.0 °C, a controlled fever, not effector failure. Sweating lowers, rather than raises, core temperature. Core never equals the 42 °C air, so air is a disturbance, not the set-point.

distractorRationales.A: Core stays near 37 then 39, not 42, so the regulated variable is core temperature, not air.
distractorRationales.B: Shivering is an intact heat-gain effector acting toward a higher set-point, not a destroyed effector.
distractorRationales.D: Sweating is a cooling effector; core falls from 37.4 back to 37.0, the opposite of positive feedback.

items.stem: A sarcomere shortens from 2.2 um to 1.9 um during an isometric-to-shortening transition in which thick and thin filament lengths are independently measured and found constant. Which statement is consistent with sliding-filament theory?

choices.text: A-band length shortens in proportion to the sarcomere because myosin filaments contract like springs
Z-lines move apart as thin filaments are pushed out of the lattice
Titin is hydrolyzed to power each power stroke, shortening the thick filament
A-band length stays constant while I-band and H-zone shorten as thin filaments slide over thick filaments

items.explanation: Sliding-filament theory states that force comes from myosin cross-bridges walking on actin, not from shortening of the filaments themselves. The A band is the thick-filament array and keeps its length; the I band (thin filaments not overlapping myosin) and H zone (thick filaments not overlapped by actin) shrink as overlap increases and Z-lines approach. Constant measured filament lengths in the stem rule out myosin-spring models and titin hydrolysis as the shortening engine. Titin is an elastic linker, not a fuel that is cleaved each stroke.

distractorRationales.A: A-band length is the thick filament length and remains constant during physiologic shortening.
distractorRationales.B: Z-lines move closer together in contraction, not apart.
distractorRationales.C: Titin is not consumed as a hydrolyzed fuel to shorten thick filaments.

items.stem: Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate (fumarate/succinate E°′ ≈ +0.03 V) using a covalently bound FAD rather than NAD+. NAD+/NADH has E°′ = −0.32 V. Which thermodynamic reason is most compelling?

choices.text: FADH2 always has a more negative E°′ than NADH, so FAD is required as a stronger reductant to reduce NAD+.
NAD+ is a poorer electron acceptor from succinate than enzyme-bound FAD, whose potential can be tuned near the succinate/fumarate couple; electrons then enter the chain via ubiquinone.
NAD+ cannot enter the mitochondrial matrix, whereas free FAD diffuses in as a substrate of Complex II.
Only flavoproteins can pump protons; NAD-linked dehydrogenases cannot, so succinate oxidation must use FAD to contribute to the proton-motive force.

items.explanation: A redox reaction is thermodynamically favorable when the acceptor’s E°′ is more positive than the donor’s. NAD+ at −0.32 V is a poor acceptor from the succinate/fumarate couple at about +0.03 V, so ΔE°′ for succinate → NAD+ is negative. Protein-bound FAD can have its potential raised near or above that of succinate, allowing oxidation; the resulting FADH2 then reduces ubiquinone. NAD+ is abundant in the matrix; impermeability is not the issue. Bound FAD is not a more negative couple than NADH in the sense that would make it a stronger reductant used to reduce NAD+, and proton pumping is a property of Complexes I, III, and IV, not a unique feature of all flavoproteins. Complex II itself does not pump protons.

distractorRationales.A: NADH is the stronger reductant (more negative E°′). Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD because NAD+ is too poor an acceptor, not to reduce NAD+.
distractorRationales.C: NAD+ is present in the matrix and is the acceptor for many matrix dehydrogenases; Complex II’s FAD is a prosthetic group, not a freely diffusing substrate that replaces impermeable NAD+.
distractorRationales.D: Complex I is NAD-linked and pumps protons; Complex II is FAD-linked and does not pump protons, so this rationale inverts the bioenergetics.

items.stem: After a 24-hour fast, blood insulin is low and glucagon is high. Which tissue-specific fuel pattern is most accurate?

choices.text: Liver glycogen is depleted and the liver performs gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis; skeletal muscle oxidizes fatty acids and ketone bodies but does not export glucose; adipose tissue hydrolyzes triacylglycerol, releasing fatty acids and glycerol.
Muscle glycogen is converted to free glucose by glucose-6-phosphatase and becomes the main source of blood glucose.
The brain switches entirely to fatty acid oxidation and ceases using glucose or ketone bodies.
Adipose tissue esterifies fatty acids under glucagon, storing additional triacylglycerol throughout the fast.

items.explanation: After a day without food, hepatic glycogen is largely exhausted. High glucagon and low insulin induce hepatic gluconeogenesis and, as β-oxidation raises acetyl-CoA, ketogenesis. Adipose hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids and glycerol. Skeletal muscle oxidizes fatty acids and ketones and can break down its own glycogen only for local use; without glucose-6-phosphatase it cannot supply blood glucose. The brain continues to consume glucose and increasingly uses ketone bodies; it does not run on fatty acids. Glucagon does not drive net fat esterification, which is an insulin/fed-state program.

distractorRationales.B: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glycogenolysis there feeds glycolysis, not blood glucose; hepatic gluconeogenesis maintains glycemia after liver glycogen is gone.
distractorRationales.C: The brain cannot oxidize fatty acids at a meaningful rate; it uses glucose and, during fasting, ketone bodies.
distractorRationales.D: Glucagon and low insulin promote lipolysis, not net triacylglycerol synthesis, in adipose tissue.

items.stem: The Calvin–Benson cycle as written for net hexose is 6 CO2 + 18 ATP + 12 NADPH → C6H12O6 + 18 ADP + 17 Pi + 12 NADP+. Isolated chloroplasts at saturating light and 25 °C fix CO2 at 6.0 µmol min−1. Light is then reduced so that the measured NADPH supply falls to 6.0 µmol min−1 while ATP remains in excess. Assuming the carbon reactions are otherwise unlimited, what is the new maximum rate of net glucose formation?

choices.text: 1.0 µmol min−1
6.0 µmol min−1
0.25 µmol min−1
0.50 µmol min−1

items.explanation: Originally 6.0 µmol CO2 min−1 corresponds to 1.0 µmol glucose min−1 because six CO2 make one hexose, requiring 12 µmol NADPH min−1. When NADPH supply is only 6.0 µmol min−1, the NADPH/glucose stoichiometry of 12 limits glucose to 6/12 = 0.50 µmol min−1. ATP is stated to be in excess, so it is not limiting. Equating glucose rate to the CO2 rate (6.0) ignores the 6 CO2 per sugar. Halving twice would give 0.25 without a stoichiometric reason.

distractorRationales.A: 1.0 µmol min−1 is the original saturating-light glucose rate, which needed 12 µmol NADPH min−1, not 6.
distractorRationales.B: 6.0 µmol min−1 is the CO2 fixation rate, not the hexose rate, and it is the old, not the NADPH-limited, value.
distractorRationales.C: 0.25 µmol min−1 would be appropriate if both ATP and NADPH had been halved and both were co-limiting in series; only NADPH was halved.

items.stem:
Standard entropy changes (J K−1 mol−1) estimated from gas counts (each mole of gas ≈ 200 J K−1 mol−1, liquids/solids neglected):

Reaction | gas moles reactants → products | predicted ΔS°
N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3 | 4 → 2 | −400
CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g) | 0 → 1 | +200
2 SO2 + O2 → 2 SO3 | 3 → 2 | −200
H2O(l) → H2O(g) | 0 → 1 | +200

For which reactions is a high temperature most likely to make ΔG more negative if ΔH° is positive for the decomposition and vapourisation rows and negative for the two combination rows?

choices.text: None, because ΔS° does not enter ΔG
The CaCO3 decomposition and the water vaporisation, because both have ΔS° > 0 so −TΔS becomes more negative as T rises
The ammonia and SO3 syntheses, because they have the largest |ΔS°|
All four, because ΔG always falls with temperature

items.explanation: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. When ΔS° is positive, −TΔS° is negative and grows with T, favouring the endothermic CaCO3 and H2O(l)→H2O(g) processes at high temperature. The two combination reactions have ΔS° < 0, so −TΔS° is positive and high T makes ΔG° less favourable (Haber and SO3 synthesis are therefore low-T, high-K thermodynamically). Large |ΔS| with the wrong sign opposes high-T spontaneity. ΔG does not automatically fall with T, and ΔS is exactly the T-dependent piece of ΔG.

distractorRationales.A: The −TΔS term is the explicit temperature dependence of ΔG.
distractorRationales.C: Those syntheses have negative ΔS, so high T works against them thermodynamically.
distractorRationales.D: For negative ΔS, ΔG becomes more positive as T rises.

items.stem:
A diploid G1 nucleus contains 6.0 pg of DNA. Flow cytometry of an unsynchronised culture gives these peaks:
6.0 pg: 62% of cells; 9.0 pg: 8%; 12.0 pg: 26%; 3.0 pg: 0%.
Which assignment of the peaks is correct?

choices.text: 6.0 pg is G1 (2C), 12.0 pg is G2/M (4C), and 9.0 pg is S-phase DNA between 2C and 4C.
12.0 pg is G1, because G1 cells have just divided and therefore have the most DNA.
3.0 pg must be the G1 peak; its 0% occupancy means the culture is entirely haploid.
6.0 pg is G2, because most cells in a culture are always in G2.

items.explanation: G1 diploid DNA is given as 6.0 pg (2C). After replication, G2/M nuclei hold 12.0 pg (4C). S-phase cells are between those values, here the 9.0 pg shoulder (8% of the population). Most growing cells sit in G1, matching the 62% peak at 6.0 pg. A 3.0 pg (1C) peak would be haploid G1 after meiosis, but it is absent, so this is a mitotic diploid cycle. G2 is the smaller 12 pg peak (26%), not the majority 6 pg peak, and G1 cannot be 12 pg.

distractorRationales.B: Division halves DNA; G1 is the 6.0 pg peak, not 12.0 pg.
distractorRationales.C: Zero cells at 3.0 pg means there is no haploid G1 population; G1 here is 6.0 pg.
distractorRationales.D: G2 is 12 pg and only 26% of cells; the majority 6 pg peak is G1.

items.stem: g = 10 m s−2 and ρ_water = 1000 kg m−3. Gauge pressure at depth h is ρ g h. A cubical block of volume 2.0 × 10−3 m³ is fully submerged. Buoyant force F_B = ρ V g. The block weighs 30 N in air. What is the gauge pressure at 2.0 m depth, and what is the apparent weight of the submerged block?

choices.text: 2.0 kPa; apparent weight 10 N
20 kPa; apparent weight −10 N (block shoots out of the water)
20 kPa; apparent weight 10 N
20 Pa; apparent weight 30 N (buoyancy omitted)

items.explanation: ρ g h = 1000 × 10 × 2.0 = 20 000 Pa = 20 kPa. F_B = 1000 × 2.0×10−3 × 10 = 20 N. Apparent weight = 30 − 20 = 10 N, still downward, so the block sinks if released (density above water). Using Pa instead of kPa drops three orders of magnitude. Omitting g or a factor of 10 in ρgh can give 2.0 kPa. A 20 N buoyancy smaller than the 30 N true weight cannot invert the net force. Archimedes’ principle is the 20 N upthrust from the displaced 2.0 litres.

distractorRationales.A: ρgh with g = 10 and ρ = 1000 already gives 20 kPa, not 2.0 kPa.
distractorRationales.B: Net force is 10 N down, not up; the block is denser than water.
distractorRationales.D: 20 000 Pa is 20 kPa, and the 20 N upthrust must be subtracted from 30 N.

items.stem: Apical uptake of glucose against its concentration gradient in small-intestine epithelium uses the Na+-glucose cotransporter SGLT. If basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase is inhibited, that apical concentrative uptake:

choices.text: increases, because more ATP is then available for SGLT to hydrolyze
decreases, because the Na+ gradient that drives cotransport collapses
is unchanged, because SGLT itself does not bind or hydrolyze ATP
reverses solely because new glucose channels appear in the apical membrane

items.explanation: SGLT is secondary active transport: it couples uphill glucose influx to downhill Na+ influx. The Na+ gradient is restored by basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase. Blocking the pump lets Na+ accumulate inside, the inward Na+ driving force falls, and concentrative glucose uptake falls even though SGLT is not an ATPase. The trap is to treat 'no ATP hydrolysis at SGLT' as 'insensitive to pump blockade.' Secondary active transport is energetically parasitic on the primary pump.

distractorRationales.A: SGLT does not hydrolyze ATP, so spare ATP is irrelevant, and the pump's inhibition removes the real driving gradient rather than helping uptake.
distractorRationales.C: It is true that SGLT does not hydrolyze ATP, but that does not make uptake independent of the Na+ gradient the pump maintains. This is the intended secondary-transport trap.
distractorRationales.D: Pump blockade does not magically insert apical glucose channels as the mechanism of reversal. The SGLT cycle simply loses its Na+ driving force.

items.stem: X-ray intensity follows I = I0 e−μx. The half-value layer satisfies μ x½ = ln 2 ≈ 0.69. A beam has μ = 0.10 cm−1 in soft tissue. What is x½, and what fraction of I0 remains after 6.9 cm?

choices.text: x½ ≈ 6.9 cm; after 6.9 cm, I / I0 = 1/2
x½ ≈ 6.9 cm; after 6.9 cm, I = 0 because one HVL absorbs everything
x½ ≈ 69 cm; after 6.9 cm, I / I0 = 0.90

items.explanation: x½ = ln 2 / μ = 0.69 / 0.10 = 6.9 cm. By definition, one half-value layer leaves half the intensity, so 6.9 cm yields I/I0 = 1/2. The linear attenuation coefficient 0.10 cm−1 is not itself the HVL. One HVL does not zero the beam; it halves it (two HVLs would leave 1/4, and so on). Inverting μ without ln 2, or dropping a factor of ten, produces 69 cm and a 10% attenuation guess (e−0.1 ≈ 0.90 would be 1.0 cm of this tissue, not 6.9 cm). Exponential attenuation is therefore a repeated-halving process at the HVL scale.

distractorRationales.B: 0.10 cm−1 is μ, not x½; x½ = 0.69/μ = 6.9 cm.
distractorRationales.C: Half-value means half remains, not zero; the exponential never drops to exactly zero at finite x.
distractorRationales.D: 69 cm would be 1/μ without the 0.10 placement; e−μx at 6.9 cm is e−0.69 = 1/2, not 0.90.

items.stem: The pH change from 24.00 to 26.00 mL is 5.68 units for 2.00 mL of titrant. This steepness is most useful as evidence that

choices.text: the probe is stuck, because pH cannot move more than 0.1 per mL.
the region includes the equivalence jump, so an indicator changing in the high-pH range could still catch the end point.
Ka is greater than 1.
the unknown is a strong acid from the start.

items.explanation: A large ΔpH across a small volume is the practical signature of equivalence on a table. Weak-acid vs strong-base end points sit alkaline, so a high-pH indicator can work. Probes routinely record jumps. Ka > 1 would be a strong acid, inconsistent with initial pH 2.88 and half-equivalence 4.20. Comparing table rows is the point of an experimental-results item.

distractorRationales.A: Jumps of several pH units in 1–2 mL are expected near equivalence.
distractorRationales.C: pKa ≈ 4.2 implies Ka ≈ 6 × 10−5, not >1.
distractorRationales.D: Initial pH and buffer region show a weak acid.

passage.title: Unknown weak acid titration
passage.body:
25.00 mL of monoprotic unknown HA (0.100 mol L−1 stated by the stockroom) is titrated with 0.100 mol L−1 NaOH at 25 °C. pH is measured with a probe calibrated at 4.00 and 10.00.

V(NaOH) / mL | pH
0.00 | 2.88
5.00 | 3.46
12.50 | 4.20
20.00 | 4.94
24.00 | 5.56
25.00 | 8.72
26.00 | 11.24
30.00 | 12.15

A classmate says the equivalence volume must be 12.50 mL because that is “half way on the page.” Another wants Ka from the initial pH alone, treating HA as if it were a strong acid.

items.stem: A cohesive hospital credentials committee, isolated from outside reviewers, hears the chair state a preferred outcome in the opening minute. Dissenters stay silent; the group later misses a cluster of complications that a devil’s advocate would have flagged. Janis’s groupthink analysis most directly emphasizes which process?

choices.text: A shift toward a more extreme average preference after open debate (group polarization)
Social loafing, because each member’s vote was unidentifiable on a secret ballot
Premature concurrence-seeking under high cohesion, directive leadership, and insulation, with self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity
Deindividuation in a crowd, which requires anonymity and arousal in a street mob

items.explanation: Janis defined groupthink as concurrence-seeking that suppresses realistic appraisal in cohesive, insulated groups with directive leaders. Symptoms include self-censorship, mindguards, and an illusion of unanimity—the silence after the chair’s cue. Group polarization is a different phenomenon: the group mean becomes more extreme after discussion. Social loafing is reduced effort on additive tasks. Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in aroused anonymous crowds, not a boardroom consensus failure.

distractorRationales.A: Polarization is an extremity shift after discussion, not the suppressed dissent Janis named.
distractorRationales.B: The stem does not describe unidentifiable additive effort; it describes concurrence-seeking.
distractorRationales.D: Deindividuation is a crowd-anonymity process, not credentials-committee insulation.

items.stem: Which sentence better satisfies “particular over generic” for a Task B on inherited rooms?

choices.text: Family is important in today’s society, and we should all value our loved ones.
The spare chair at the end of the table was still set as if my brother might arrive, and nobody mentioned that he had not done so for three winters.
In the modern world, individuals struggle with identity.
Belonging, as philosophers have always said, is a universal human need.

items.explanation: Particular means a scene a camera could find: a chair, a table, three winters, an unmentioned absence. That still carries theme—belonging, denial, inherited staging—without announcing it as a slogan. A, C, and D are interchangeable across a thousand prompts. Markers are not rewarding furniture for its own sake; they are rewarding thought that has somewhere to live. Generic language cannot host mixed feeling. Under time, one chair beats a paragraph of “today’s society.” B is the sentence that could only belong to this theme.

distractorRationales.A: “Family is important” could be pasted onto any paper; it does not yet see a room.
distractorRationales.C: “Modern world” plus “identity” is the stock fog Task B is designed to punish.
distractorRationales.D: Appealing to what philosophers have always said is a generic inflate, not a scene.

items.stem: The claim that dropping a person from a census “is often a theory of the state” most nearly implies that

choices.text: omission is usually a random clerical mishap that reveals nothing about ministries.
some absences from the count express judgments about whose lives are worth the cost of verification or are inconvenient to total.
every uncounted person has formally petitioned to be excluded on philosophical grounds.
states publish coverage estimates only when they intend to abolish categories.

items.explanation: The third paragraph says dropping looks like a mishap and then reclassifies it as a theory: some lives are too expensive, mobile, or inconvenient. The implication is that omission can embody a judgment, not that every omission is a petition or that surveys signal abolition. A restates the appearance the author is rejecting. C invents a formal opt-out. D confuses later remarks about coverage estimates with a motive to abolish boxes.

distractorRationales.A: The sentence contrasts the look of a mishap with a political theory of whose lives get verified.
distractorRationales.C: The passage never describes petitions for exclusion; the forced box or drop is an administrative squeeze.
distractorRationales.D: Coverage estimates are the statisticians' ethic of naming error, not a prelude to abolishing categories.

passage.title: The census of the uncounted
passage.body:
Political arithmetic began as a courtly hobby: a way of estimating how many subjects a prince could tax, feed, or send to war. Its early practitioners treated people as a kind of harvest. What could be enumerated could be extracted. What could not be enumerated was, for administrative purposes, a rumor.

The modern census inherited the appetite and dressed it as representation. To be counted is now advertised as a civic right, a way of appearing in the distribution of schools, clinics, and parliamentary seats. The advertisement is not false. Under-counted neighborhoods do lose clinics. The advertisement is incomplete. A census is also a machine for deciding which kinds of life will be treated as facts and which will remain anecdotes told to a volunteer with a clipboard.

Consider the category. Every census must invent boxes. The boxes are not discovered in nature; they are negotiated among ministries, churches, and, later, identity movements. A person who lives in two houses, or in none, or who works in a language the form does not print, must be forced into a box or dropped. Dropping looks like a clerical mishap. It is often a theory of the state: some lives are too expensive to verify, too mobile to locate, too politically inconvenient to add to a total that will be used against the ministry next year.

Statisticians reply that they already know this, that they publish coverage estimates and post-enumeration surveys, that the professional ethic is to name the error. Naming the error is not the same as refusing the uses of the total. A coverage estimate can become a footnote that licenses the headline number. The public hears fifty million; the appendix whispers that the fifty million is a compromise among several less flattering models. Compromise is not a crime. Treating the compromise as a photograph is.

There is a further twist. Groups that have been historically erased often demand better counting, and they are right to. Visibility in a dataset can be a precondition of funds. Yet the same groups may later discover that a sharper count is also a sharper target: for policing, for debt collection, for the allocation of blame when a service fails. The census does not choose the policy. It does make the policy cheaper to aim.

None of this is an argument for ignorance. A state that refuses to count will invent its numbers in the back room and call the invention common sense. The argument is for a less enchanted relationship to the table. Read the boxes as arguments. Read the missing as a constituency. And when a politician says the numbers speak for themselves, notice that speech is exactly what numbers cannot do until someone supplies a sentence.

items.stem: A temperature-sensitive separase mutant is shifted to the nonpermissive temperature after chromosomes have aligned at the metaphase plate. Sister chromatids remain paired at centromeres and anaphase does not begin, although cyclin-B levels can still fall. The step that fails is:

choices.text: Cleavage of cohesin (kleisin) subunits, which is required to dissolve sister-chromatid cohesion at anaphase
DNA replication licensing, which must be repeated at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition
Nuclear-envelope breakdown, which has not yet occurred at metaphase in animal cells
