An uncoupler therefore stops rotation even while ATP is still abundant, proving the motor is not an ATP-burning dynein. Eukaryotic cilia and flagella are different machines: axonemal dynein hydrolyzes ATP to slide microtubule doublets. FtsZ is a tubulin homolog used in cytokinesis, and bacteria do not rotate flagella by polymerizing actin at the pole.

distractorRationales.A: Axonemal beating is ATP-driven dynein sliding; the uncoupler result shows the bacterial motor is PMF-driven, not an ATP ATPase like dynein.
distractorRationales.B: FtsZ GTP hydrolysis assembles the division ring; it does not power flagellar rotation.
distractorRationales.C: Some pathogens use actin polymerization for intracellular motility, not for rotating a Gram-negative flagellum.

items.stem: Suppose a government publishes a real-time mobility dashboard, updated from phone pings, with no category boxes, and uses it to send clinics to whichever grid cell shows density. How would the author most likely respond?

choices.text: This dissolves the problem, because the absence of boxes means no political decisions remain.
The dashboard still decides which lives become facts; a ping is another invented trace, and aiming services (or blame) can become cheaper still.
The author would refuse to comment, having limited the critique to paper forms printed by churches.
Phone pings would be praised as the photograph the passage wants totals to become.

items.explanation: The thesis is that counting systems decide which lives are facts and make policy cheaper to aim, not that paper boxes are the only sin. A ping without boxes still selects a trace and a grid. The author already says the census does not choose the policy but makes aiming cheaper; a density dashboard is that logic intensified. A treats missing boxes as missing politics. C is false: ministries and identity movements already sit beside churches. D inverts the warning against treating totals as photographs.

distractorRationales.A: The author treats boxes as one invented instrument, not as the sole site of political decision.
distractorRationales.C: The passage's actors already include ministries and movements, not only churches.
distractorRationales.D: Photograph-like faith in a number is exactly what the author wants to disenchant.

passage.title: The census of the uncounted
passage.body:
Political arithmetic began as a courtly hobby: a way of estimating how many subjects a prince could tax, feed, or send to war. Its early practitioners treated people as a kind of harvest. What could be enumerated could be extracted. What could not be enumerated was, for administrative purposes, a rumor.

The modern census inherited the appetite and dressed it as representation. To be counted is now advertised as a civic right, a way of appearing in the distribution of schools, clinics, and parliamentary seats. The advertisement is not false. Under-counted neighborhoods do lose clinics. The advertisement is incomplete. A census is also a machine for deciding which kinds of life will be treated as facts and which will remain anecdotes told to a volunteer with a clipboard.

Consider the category. Every census must invent boxes. The boxes are not discovered in nature; they are negotiated among ministries, churches, and, later, identity movements. A person who lives in two houses, or in none, or who works in a language the form does not print, must be forced into a box or dropped. Dropping looks like a clerical mishap. It is often a theory of the state: some lives are too expensive to verify, too mobile to locate, too politically inconvenient to add to a total that will be used against the ministry next year.

Statisticians reply that they already know this, that they publish coverage estimates and post-enumeration surveys, that the professional ethic is to name the error. Naming the error is not the same as refusing the uses of the total. A coverage estimate can become a footnote that licenses the headline number. The public hears fifty million; the appendix whispers that the fifty million is a compromise among several less flattering models. Compromise is not a crime. Treating the compromise as a photograph is.

There is a further twist. Groups that have been historically erased often demand better counting, and they are right to. Visibility in a dataset can be a precondition of funds. Yet the same groups may later discover that a sharper count is also a sharper target: for policing, for debt collection, for the allocation of blame when a service fails. The census does not choose the policy. It does make the policy cheaper to aim.

None of this is an argument for ignorance. A state that refuses to count will invent its numbers in the back room and call the invention common sense. The argument is for a less enchanted relationship to the table. Read the boxes as arguments. Read the missing as a constituency. And when a politician says the numbers speak for themselves, notice that speech is exactly what numbers cannot do until someone supplies a sentence.

items.stem: If adjacent rents rise after a park is planted, the author implies that defenders should

choices.text: admit the park is therefore not justice yet, without handing the land to the highest bidder.
immediately convert the park to lots, since rents prove the ledger was right all along.
stop paying gardeners, because maintenance caused the rents.
deny that parks have ever been used to raise rents.

items.explanation: The further-honesty paragraph says parks raise adjacent rents and that naming those uses does not hand land to the bidder; justice would include people priced off surrounding blocks. The implication for defenders is to drop the pretense that green is already justice. B takes the fact as a deed transfer. C blames maintenance, which the author treats as how openness lasts. D contradicts the named use. Implications stay inside that honesty-without-surrender move.

distractorRationales.B: Naming rent effects is explicitly not a transfer to the highest bidder.
distractorRationales.C: Winter gardeners are part of the adult defense, not the cause to be punished.
distractorRationales.D: The passage states that parks have been used to raise adjacent rents.

passage.title: The ledger of the commons
passage.body:
When a city puts a park on a map, it appears to have given something away: land that could have been lots, hours that could have been tolls. Developers are not wrong that the gift has a price. They are wrong when they treat the price as a leak from an otherwise watertight private order. The private order is already subsidized by streets, courts, pipes, and the patience of people who do not sue every time a stranger walks past a porch. A park is not the exception to property. It is one of the ways a dense city remains inhabitable enough for property to be worth wanting.

Accountants prefer a ledger in which every square metre has a named owner and a yield. Parks embarrass the ledger because their yield is a crowd that does not pay at the gate, a cooling that does not send an invoice, a child who learns a city can include her without a purchase. The embarrassment produces two crude policies. One is to fence and ticket until the park behaves like a venue. The other is to neglect the park until the crowd looks like a problem that only private security can solve. Both policies claim to be realistic. Both are ways of refusing to count the effects that made the park rational in the first place.

Friends of the park sometimes answer with a poetry of the unowned. The poetry is moving and strategically weak. A commons that cannot speak in maintenance budgets will lose to a spreadsheet that can. The more adult defense is to insist that the ledger is incomplete, not that ledgers are evil. Planting, lighting, toilets, and a gardener who is paid in winter are not betrayals of openness. They are how openness lasts past a ribbon-cutting.

There is a further honesty. Parks are not innocent. They have been used to raise adjacent rents, to move unhoused people out of sight, to display a city’s kindness to visitors who will never need the toilets. Naming those uses does not hand the land to the highest bidder. It prevents the park’s defenders from pretending that green on a map is already justice. Justice would be a park whose ledger includes the people who were priced off the blocks around it.

If urban politics cannot hold that thought, it will keep oscillating between the venue and the ruin, and calling the oscillation pragmatism.

items.stem: A pathogenic mtDNA mutation is heteroplasmic. An affected mother has both affected and unaffected sons and daughters; an affected father has no affected children. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: Mitochondrial genomes in humans are transmitted through sperm mitochondria that dominate the zygote, so fathers should transmit the trait.
mtDNA is maternally inherited; random partitioning of heteroplasmic mitochondria during oogenesis can produce different mutant loads among offspring, and paternal mtDNA is typically not transmitted.
The pedigree is X-linked recessive, which also spares all children of affected fathers and affects sons and daughters of affected mothers equally.
Crossing over between mitochondrial chromosomes during paternal meiosis eliminates the mutation from sperm, which is why fathers do not transmit it.

items.explanation: Human mtDNA is transmitted through the oocyte; sperm mitochondria are generally eliminated and do not set the child’s mtDNA genotype, so fathers do not transmit the trait. Heteroplasmy is a mixture of mutant and wild-type genomes. During oogenesis, random partitioning of mitochondria (vegetative segregation) can produce eggs with different mutant loads and thus both affected and unaffected sons and daughters. X-linked recessive inheritance can spare children of affected fathers in some respects, but affected mothers typically produce affected sons and carrier daughters rather than both sexes affected by a cytoplasmic genome. Paternal meiotic crossing over is not how mtDNA transmission is blocked.

distractorRationales.A: Paternal mitochondria do not determine the zygote’s mtDNA in humans; the observed pattern is maternal transmission.
distractorRationales.C: X-linked recessive disease in children of a heterozygous mother predominantly affects sons, not sons and daughters similarly, and does not explain heteroplasmic mtDNA genetics.
distractorRationales.D: Absence of paternal transmission reflects destruction or exclusion of sperm mitochondria, not meiotic recombination that ‘cleanses’ mtDNA in sperm.

items.stem: Which situation is most analogous to “help me to help you” as naming the price of entry into a language that pretends it is only asking for facts?

choices.text: A bank officer who says “just tell your story” while a form will accept only certain sequences of income, address, and remorse.
A metronome asking a dancer to keep still.
A park gardener paid in winter.
A census box labelled “other.”

items.explanation: The official’s phrase pretends to request facts while requiring a performable, matching story. A loan officer’s invitation to narrate, constrained by a form’s sequences, maps that relation: help offered as service, entry priced as plausibility in the institution’s language. B and C and D are images from other passages without the audition structure. Analogies should preserve the helper’s courtesy plus the hidden script, not merely any bureaucracy.

distractorRationales.B: Stillness versus dance is a different essay’s ontology problem.
distractorRationales.C: Winter gardeners belong to the commons ledger argument.
distractorRationales.D: An “other” box is a category problem, not the audition-for-help grammar.

passage.title: Courtesy at the checkpoint
passage.body:
A border official is trained in courtesy as if courtesy were a disinfectant. Smile, use the family name, apologize for the wait. The training manuals are not cynical. They are trying to prevent the obvious cruelty of a raised voice. What they cannot prevent is the deeper grammar of the encounter: one person may leave, the other must persuade a stranger that her life is plausible.

Liberal theory likes to treat this grammar as an unfortunate delay on the way to a principle. In the principle, the stranger is already a rights-bearer; the checkpoint is a bureaucratic remainder. On the ground, the remainder is the event. Rights that must be performed as a story—complete, sequential, tearful at the approved moments—are rights as an audition. The official who says “help me to help you” is not necessarily a villain. He is naming the price of entry into a language that pretends it is only asking for facts.

Scholars of hospitality distinguish welcome from inspection. The distinction is cleaner on the page than in a queue. Inspection can dress as welcome, and welcome can become inspection the moment a detail fails to match a database. A cup of tea in an interview room is not the opposite of a file. It can be the file’s most efficient instrument, loosening speech until it can be contradicted.

None of this requires pretending that states have no legitimate interest in knowing who crosses. It requires noticing that “legitimate interest” is not a measuring cup. It expands. Yesterday’s emergency power is today’s ordinary form. Tomorrow’s form will be justified by the person who told her story too well, or too badly, last year. The archive of interviews becomes a training set for suspicion.

The courteous checkpoint is therefore not a milder politics. It is a politics that has learned to sound like a service. If we want a different politics, we will need a different distribution of who must be plausible to whom—not a warmer script for the same audition.

items.stem: Human blood is buffered near pH 7.4 largely by carbonic acid (effective pKa1 ≈ 6.1 for dissolved CO2/H2CO3) and bicarbonate. Which statement follows from Henderson–Hasselbalch for this pair at pH 7.4?

choices.text: [H2CO3] ≈ [HCO3−], because blood is near neutrality.
Blood pH 7.4 is too far from any carbonic pKa for bicarbonate to function as a buffer.
The relevant buffer pair at pH 7.4 is HCO3−/CO3^2− (pKa2 ≈ 10.3), because that pKa is closer to 7.4 than 6.1 is.
[HCO3−]/[H2CO3] ≈ 20, so the conjugate base is in large excess and the system sits on the basic side of pKa1.

items.explanation: For H2CO3/HCO3−, pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−]/[H2CO3]). At pH 7.4 the log term is 1.3, so the ratio is about 20:1 in favor of bicarbonate. A buffer still functions when the ratio is not 1:1; the open CO2/bicarbonate system is the physiological buffer near 7.4. The HCO3−/CO3^2− pair has pKa ≈ 10.3, three units away, so carbonate is negligible at 7.4. Neutrality does not force equal HA and A−, and being 1.3 units from pKa1 is still within a usable (if uneven) buffer window, especially with continuous CO2 control.

distractorRationales.A: Equal concentrations require pH = pKa ≈ 6.1, not pH 7.4.
distractorRationales.B: The 20:1 bicarbonate/carbonic acid ratio is the classic demonstration that this pair does buffer arterial blood.
distractorRationales.C: pKa2 ≈ 10.3 is much farther from 7.4 than pKa1 is; essentially no CO3^2− is present, so that pair is not the blood buffer.

items.stem: A replication fork advances at 1000 nucleotides s−1 on each template. Lagging-strand Okazaki fragments are 2000 nucleotides of DNA, each primed by a 10-nucleotide RNA primer. For a 100 000 nucleotide lagging-strand stretch, how many RNA primers are laid down, and how much time elapses between successive primers at one fork?

choices.text: 10 primers, 2.0 s apart
50 primers, 2.0 s apart
50 primers, 0.010 s apart
100 primers, 2.0 s apart

items.explanation: Each 2000-nucleotide DNA fragment needs one primer, so 100 000 / 2000 = 50 primers. The fork polymerises 1000 nucleotides per second, so the time to synthesise one 2000-nucleotide Okazaki piece—and therefore the interval between primers—is 2000 / 1000 = 2.0 s. The 10-nucleotide primer length does not change how many primers are needed; it would only affect the tiny RNA mass. Using the primer length as the fragment size would wrongly suggest 10 000 primers or a 0.010 s interval.

distractorRationales.A: 10 primers would cover only 20 000 nucleotides at 2000 nt each, not 100 000.
distractorRationales.C: 0.010 s is the time to make a 10-nucleotide primer at 1000 nt s−1, not the time between Okazaki starts.
distractorRationales.D: 100 primers would be appropriate for 1000-nucleotide fragments, not 2000.

items.stem:
First ionisation energies (kJ mol−1) for consecutive second-period elements are:
Li 520; Be 899; B 801; C 1086; N 1402; O 1314; F 1681.
Which comparison is explained by a paired 2p electron being easier to remove than an unpaired electron from a half-filled 2p subshell?

choices.text: Be (899) versus Li (520), a drop from Li to Be
F (1681) versus O (1314), a drop from O to F
C (1086) versus B (801), a drop from C to B that does not occur
O (1314) versus N (1402), the drop from N to O

items.explanation: Nitrogen is 2p3 (three unpaired electrons). Oxygen is 2p4, so one 2p orbital is paired. Electron–electron repulsion in that pair lowers IE1: 1314 kJ mol−1 for O versus 1402 for N, against the general left-to-right rise. Lithium to beryllium actually increases (520 → 899) because Be has a filled 2s subshell. Fluorine is higher than oxygen (1681 vs 1314), and carbon is higher than boron (1086 vs 801); those are not drops caused by pairing at oxygen.

distractorRationales.A: IE increases from Li to Be; there is no drop, and the 2s pair in Be is more stable, not easier to remove than Li.
distractorRationales.B: F is higher than O, so this is not a pairing-induced drop.
distractorRationales.C: C is higher than B; the B-to-C step is not a pairing drop at oxygen.

items.stem:
Skeletal-muscle fibres are treated with ouabain, which blocks Na+/K+ ATPase. Intracellular concentrations (mM) versus time:
0 min: [Na+] 12, [K+] 140.
20 min: [Na+] 28, [K+] 118.
60 min: [Na+] 61, [K+] 82.
Which mechanism explains the table?

choices.text: [Na+]in falls because the pump is the only pathway for sodium to enter.
[K+]in rises because potassium is trapped once the pump stops.
Sodium leaks in and potassium leaks out down their gradients, so [Na+]in rises and [K+]in falls.
Concentrations are unchanged at 60 min (still 12 and 140 mM).

items.explanation: The pump continuously extrudes Na+ and imports K+ to offset passive leaks. Blocking it with ouabain leaves those leaks unopposed: [Na+]in climbs from 12 to 61 mM while [K+]in falls from 140 to 82 mM. Sodium is more concentrated outside, so it cannot fall inside when its active export stops. Potassium is more concentrated inside, so it cannot rise when its active import stops. The 60 min row is clearly not the t = 0 pair.

distractorRationales.A: [Na+]in increases (12 → 61), so sodium is entering through leak channels, not leaving.
distractorRationales.B: [K+]in decreases (140 → 82); K+ leaves through K+ channels rather than being trapped.
distractorRationales.D: By 60 min the values are 61 and 82 mM, not the original 12 and 140 mM.

items.stem:
Combustion and unsaturation data:

Hydrocarbon | combustion: mol O2 per mol hydrocarbon | mol H2 absorbed over Pt | formula
P | 8.0 | 0 | C5H12
Q | 7.5 | 1.0 | C5H10
R | 7.0 | 2.0 | C5H8

Complete combustion of CnHm is CnHm + (n + m/4) O2 → n CO2 + (m/2) H2O. Which structural conclusion follows?

choices.text: R is more saturated than P because it absorbs more H2
Q must be an alkyne, because 7.5 is half-integral
P is an alkane; Q has one double bond or ring; R has two double-bond equivalents (diene, alkyne, or cycloalkene)
All three are alkanes, because each contains only C and H

items.explanation: For C5H12, n + m/4 = 5 + 3 = 8, matching P, and zero H2 uptake is a saturated alkane. C5H10 is one degree of unsaturation (double bond or ring): 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 mol O2 and 1 mol H2. C5H8 has two degrees of unsaturation, 7.0 mol O2 and 2 mol H2. Hydrocarbons include unsaturated series. Absorbing H2 diagnoses unsaturation, so R is less, not more, saturated than P. A half-integral O2 coefficient is normal for odd hydrogen counts, not an alkyne fingerprint (C5H8 would be the alkyne formula, which is R, not Q).

distractorRationales.A: H2 absorption measures unsaturation; R absorbing 2 mol is less saturated than P absorbing 0.
distractorRationales.B: Q is C5H10, one DUE, typically an alkene or cycloalkane; the alkyne formula C5H8 is R.
distractorRationales.D: Q and R absorb H2 and match C5H10 and C5H8, the unsaturated formulae.

items.stem:
A resonance tube of length 0.42 m is driven in air of speed 336 m s−1. A spectrum analyser shows intensity peaks only at the frequencies below (no peak is detected at 400 Hz or 800 Hz):

Observed peak (Hz)
200
600
1000
1400

Which conclusion is consistent with the data and with v = f λ?

choices.text: The tube is open at both ends with fundamental 200 Hz, so even harmonics should appear at 400 Hz and 800 Hz.
The tube is closed at one end with fundamental 400 Hz; 200 Hz is an artefact.
The tube is open at both ends with fundamental 100 Hz; the missing 100 Hz is below the speaker range.
The tube is closed at one end: f1 = v / (4L) = 200 Hz, and only odd harmonics 3f1, 5f1, 7f1 appear.

items.explanation: For a pipe closed at one end, L = λ/4 at the fundamental, so f1 = v / (4L) = 336 / (4 × 0.42) = 336 / 1.68 = 200 Hz. Allowed frequencies are the odd multiples 200, 600, 1000, 1400 Hz, matching the table and explaining the absent 400 Hz and 800 Hz. An open pipe with f1 = 200 Hz would have shown 400 Hz and 800 Hz. Treating 400 Hz as the fundamental contradicts both the 200 Hz peak and L = 0.42 m. An open-pipe fundamental of 100 Hz would produce 200, 300, 400, … including the missing even values. The missing even harmonics are therefore diagnostic of a closed pipe of this length.

distractorRationales.A: An open pipe would display the even harmonics 400 Hz and 800 Hz. The analyser found none of those peaks, so the open-pipe assignment is inconsistent with the table.
distractorRationales.B: A closed-pipe fundamental of 400 Hz would give L = v / (4 × 400) = 0.21 m, not 0.42 m, and would not produce a real 200 Hz resonance.
distractorRationales.C: An open pipe with f1 = 100 Hz would still produce 300 Hz, 400 Hz, 500 Hz and so on. The spectrum is only odd multiples of 200 Hz.

items.stem: In a Festinger and Carlsmith-style design, students complete a dull spool-turning task and then tell a waiting participant that the task was interesting. One group is paid $1 for the lie; another is paid $20. A control group does not lie. On a later private rating, which group should describe the original task as most enjoyable?

choices.text: The $20 group, because a larger reinforcer stamps in a new positive attitude
The $1 group: counterattitudinal speech with insufficient external justification creates dissonance, reduced by deciding the task really was enjoyable
Both lie groups equally, because any public statement rewires attitude regardless of pay
Neither lie group; cognitive dissonance theory predicts that behavior never feeds back on attitude

items.explanation: Cognitive dissonance theory says holding two inconsistent cognitions is aversive and motivates change. Saying a boring task was fun conflicts with the belief that it was boring. Twenty dollars is ample external justification for the lie, so little dissonance remains and the original attitude can stand. One dollar is insufficient justification, so people reduce dissonance by shifting the attitude: the task must have been somewhat interesting. Simple reinforcement would predict the opposite ($20 produces more liking). Dissonance theory is precisely a behavior-to-attitude path, not a ban on that path.

distractorRationales.A: Large payment supplies justification and should reduce, not increase, the need to change the attitude. Reinforcement is the competing prediction that the classic result contradicts.
distractorRationales.C: Pay magnitude matters; the theory’s point is that insufficient, not any, justification produces the attitude shift.
distractorRationales.D: Dissonance theory’s central claim is that counterattitudinal behavior can change attitude when justification is low.

items.stem: The potassium Nernst potential is EK = 60 log10([K+]o / [K+]i) mV. A neuron has [K+]i = 140 mM. Resting [K+]o = 5.0 mM. During ischaemia [K+]o rises to 10 mM. (log10 28 ≈ 1.45; log10 14 ≈ 1.15.) How does EK change?

choices.text: From about −87 mV to about −69 mV, a depolarising shift
From about −87 mV to about −105 mV, a hyperpolarising shift
EK remains −87 mV because [K+]i is unchanged
EK becomes positive because [K+]o doubled

items.explanation: At rest EK = 60 log10(5/140) = 60 log10(1/28) = −60 × 1.45 = −87 mV. After the rise, EK = 60 log10(10/140) = 60 log10(1/14) = −60 × 1.15 = −69 mV. Raising extracellular potassium therefore moves EK toward 0 mV (depolarisation), which is why ischaemic hyperkalaemia can inactivate sodium channels. The inward concentration ratio shrank, so the magnitude of the negative potential must fall, not increase. Doubling [K+]o does not reverse the gradient, which is still 14-fold inward.

distractorRationales.B: A more negative EK would require a steeper inward [K+] gradient, the opposite of raising [K+]o.
distractorRationales.C: EK depends on the ratio of concentrations, not on [K+]i alone.
distractorRationales.D: Even at 10 mM outside versus 140 mM inside the log argument is still <1, so EK stays negative.

items.stem: Three 6.0 Ω resistors are combined. Network X is all three in series. Network Y is all three in parallel. Network Z is one resistor in series with a parallel pair of the other two. A 12 V ideal battery is applied to each network in turn. What are the three currents drawn from the battery?

choices.text: X: 6.0 A; Y: 0.67 A (series/parallel reversed)
All three draw 2.0 A, because each network still contains three 6 Ω resistors

items.explanation: Series: Req = 18 Ω, I = 12/18 = 0.67 A. Parallel: 1/Req = 3/6.0, Req = 2.0 Ω, I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 A. For Z, the parallel pair is 3.0 Ω, plus 6.0 Ω in series gives 9.0 Ω, I = 12/9.0 = 1.33 A. Reversing series and parallel swaps 0.67 with 6.0. Identical resistor counts do not imply identical Req. A current of 2.0 A would be 12 V across a single 6 Ω resistor, not three in parallel. The three currents therefore rank Y > Z > X, matching decreasing equivalent resistance.

distractorRationales.A: Series adds resistance (small current); parallel cuts resistance (large current).
distractorRationales.B: Series and parallel equivalents of three 6 Ω resistors are 18 Ω versus 2 Ω, not the same.
distractorRationales.C: Y draws 6.0 A, not 2.0 A; 2.0 A would be a single 6 Ω across 12 V.

items.stem: In the phrase “confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology,” ontology most nearly means

choices.text: the cataloguing software used by university libraries.
what the art is taken to be, as opposed to what is easiest to store and grade.
the legal copyright in a composer's estate.
the physical weight of paper scores in an archive box.

items.explanation: The contrast is convenience (still paper, gradable seminars) versus what the work is in a tradition that treats the night’s playing as the work. Ontology here is the status of the object, not software, copyright, or mass. Context is the sentence about calling a living tradition incomplete because it will not sit still. Vocabulary-in-context items should prefer the contrast the author actually draws, which is ease of study versus the kind of thing music is.

distractorRationales.A: No library software is mentioned; archive here is the still, comparable paper object.
distractorRationales.C: Composer authority is a scholars' defense of the score, not the meaning of ontology in this sentence.
distractorRationales.D: Physical weight is not in play; stillness versus disappearance is.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

items.stem: Leaving the honest email in the outbox until morning assumes, in this story, that

choices.text: the supervisor has no internet
delay can be a way of knowing the right sentence while still not sending it — cowardice that can tell the two drafts apart
thank-you notes are illegal after midnight
the friend wrote both emails

items.explanation: The last sentence calls the overnight outbox a kind of cowardice that still knows the difference between I sounded like myself and I used your paragraph. The assumption is that unsent can be morally intelligible: he can distinguish the drafts and still not transmit. No claim about the supervisor's connection, law, or the friend's authorship. Unstated-assumption questions should name the psychology the ending needs, which is knowledge-without-sending.

distractorRationales.A: Nothing about connectivity; the delay is his.
distractorRationales.C: No legal frame is given.
distractorRationales.D: He writes and deletes and writes; the friend only mispraised him.

passage.title: The borrowed coat
passage.body:
He wore other people's sentences the way some men wear coats: against weather, and with the labels left in. At the seminar he began, "One might argue," and then produced, almost unaltered, a paragraph his supervisor had emailed at midnight to save him. The room nodded. He felt the coat settle on his shoulders, warm and slightly too large in the sleeves.

Afterward a friend said, "That was the first time you sounded like yourself." He laughed too quickly. In the bathroom mirror the coat was still on. He tried to take it off by telling the truth to the glass: I do not know whether I think this. The glass, being a glass, offered his mouth moving.

Ethics talks as if authenticity were a mineral you either contain or fake. The evening suggested something cheaper and more ordinary. A borrowed argument can keep you from freezing. It can also teach your arms the wrong length. The crime, if there is one, is not the borrowing. It is the nod you collect as if the sleeves had always been yours.

He sent the supervisor a note: Thank you. I sounded like myself. He deleted it. He sent: Thank you. I used your paragraph. He left that one in the outbox until morning, which is a kind of cowardice that still knows the difference.

items.stem: Ion flux versus external [ion] is measured on the same membrane. Without ATP the flux is linear through the origin with slope 0.80 nmol min−1 mM−1 and no plateau up to 50 mM. With ATP an additional saturable component appears (Km 0.80 mM, Vmax 12 nmol min−1) while the linear leak remains. At 50 mM external ion, which pathway carries more flux?

choices.text: The ATP-dependent pump, because 12 nmol min−1 is greater than zero.
The two pathways are equal (12 versus 40 nmol min−1).
Only the pump operates at high concentration; leak saturates and shuts off.
The linear leak (~40 nmol min−1) exceeds the saturable pump (~12 nmol min−1).

items.explanation: Leak flux at 50 mM is 0.80 × 50 = 40 nmol min−1. The pump is already near Vmax at this concentration (50 mM ≫ Km 0.80 mM), so it contributes about 12 nmol min−1. Forty is larger than twelve, so the unsaturable pathway dominates at high substrate even though ATP is present. A leak that is linear by description does not shut off at high concentration; that is the opposite of saturation. Being nonzero does not make the pump the larger term.

distractorRationales.A: Twelve is less than the leak’s 40 nmol min−1; nonzero is not the same as dominant.
distractorRationales.B: 12 and 40 are not equal.
distractorRationales.C: The leak was measured as linear to 50 mM; it does not saturate. The pump is the saturable term.

items.stem: In a lab shock-noise study, students wearing identical hoods in a dim room deliver longer white-noise bursts to a stranger than students who wear large name tags under bright lights, even though each student decides the burst length alone. Which process best explains the increase?

choices.text: Deindividuation: anonymity and reduced self-awareness disinhibit behavior that is usually constrained
Social loafing on a motor task whose output is individually recorded
Social facilitation of a well-learned skilled performance
Diffusion of responsibility for a medical emergency unfolding in another room

items.explanation: Deindividuation occurs when people are anonymous, aroused, and less self-aware, so personal standards exert less control and behavior can become more impulsive or aggressive. Hoods plus darkness are a standard anonymity manipulation; name tags plus lights restore identifiability. The dependent measure is disinhibited harm, not reduced effort on a pooled task (loafing) and not improved skilled performance (facilitation). Diffusion of responsibility is the bystander explanation for not helping when others are thought to be present; no emergency and no co-helpers are described.

distractorRationales.B: Burst length is an individual, recorded act, so loafing’s unidentifiable-pooled-effort logic does not apply.
distractorRationales.C: Delivering noise is not a well-learned skilled task being improved by an audience; it is disinhibited aggression.
distractorRationales.D: There is no emergency and no set of potential helpers among whom responsibility is split.

items.stem: A pain clinic places transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation pads over a painful lumbar dermatome and records a drop in reported intensity without a change in the noxious heat on the skin. Melzack and Wall’s gate-control theory locates the critical interaction where?

choices.text: Only in the anterior cingulate, because gating is purely a cognitive relabeling of heat
At the free nerve ending, where TENS chemically destroys C-fiber peptides
In the olivary cochlea, because pain and hearing share a single thalamic nucleus
In the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn, where large-fiber (Aβ) input can inhibit transmission of small-fiber nociceptive signals

items.explanation: Gate-control theory (Melzack and Wall) proposes that the spinal dorsal horn, especially substantia gelatinosa, is a gate: large-diameter Aβ activity can close it and reduce projection of C and Aδ nociceptive traffic, while small-fiber activity opens it. TENS is taught as a clinical use of that large-fiber inhibition. Anterior cingulate modulates affect but is not the named spinal gate. TENS does not ablate peripheral peptides as its primary mechanism. Hearing pathways are anatomically separate.

distractorRationales.A: Affective cortex can modulate pain, but Melzack and Wall located the gate in the dorsal horn, not only cingulate relabeling.
distractorRationales.B: TENS is not a chemical lesion of C-fiber terminals.
distractorRationales.C: Auditory olives are irrelevant to lumbar nociceptive gating.

items.stem: A neutralizing monoclonal IgG binds a repeating viral glycoprotein with Kd = 2 nM. Limited papain digestion yields Fab fragments that still bind the same epitope with a nearly identical Kd in a monovalent ELISA, yet they neither agglutinate virions nor fix C1q. Which conclusion is most consistent with antibody structure?

choices.text: Antigen specificity resides in the Fc domain, so an intact Fc is required for the observed nanomolar Kd.
Each Fab retains the original combining site, so monovalent affinity is largely unchanged, but bivalent avidity, agglutination, and Fc-dependent effector functions are lost.
Papain destroys complementarity-determining loops, so the Kd in the ELISA must have increased by several orders of magnitude.
C1q binds the antigen-combining site; without intact IgG the viral epitope itself is chemically altered and can no longer be recognized.

items.explanation: Papain cleaves IgG above the hinge, releasing two monovalent Fab fragments and an Fc fragment. The variable domains that form the paratope remain in each Fab, so the intrinsic Kd for a single epitope is essentially unchanged, matching the ELISA. What is lost is simultaneous engagement of two epitopes on one particle (avidity), lattice formation that produces agglutination, and Fc clustering that recruits C1q. Specificity is not encoded in Fc, an unchanged Kd shows that CDRs were not destroyed, and C1q binds Fc rather than the combining site or the viral antigen itself.

distractorRationales.A: The antigen-binding site is formed by VH and VL CDRs in Fab, not by Fc; Fc is dispensable for monovalent Kd.
distractorRationales.C: The stem states that monovalent Kd is nearly identical, so the combining site survived papain cleavage.
distractorRationales.D: C1q docks on clustered Fc regions; it does not occupy the paratope or chemically modify the viral epitope.

items.stem: Blindfolded participants pull a rope, believing they are alone or on a two- or six-person team. Force per person falls as believed team size rises. When a screen displays each person’s force in real time, the drop disappears. Which process is illustrated?

choices.text: Social facilitation of a complex novel task
Deindividuation that requires costumes and darkness
Normative peer pressure to pull harder in larger teams
Social loafing: effort drops when individual output is not identifiable, and identifiability restores effort

items.explanation: Social loafing is reduced individual effort on a collective task when contributions are pooled and hard to monitor. The rope-pull (Ringelmann) pattern—less force per person as the believed team grows—is the classic case. Making each person’s output identifiable removes the incentive to hide, so loafing shrinks. Facilitation would predict better performance of a simple, well-learned pull in front of others, not a drop. Deindividuation is about anonymity and disinhibition of usually restrained acts, not a dynamometer. Peer pressure to pull harder predicts the opposite slope.

distractorRationales.A: A simple maximal pull getting worse in a group is loafing, not facilitation of a complex skill.
distractorRationales.B: No costumes or darkness are required for loafing; the manipulation is identifiability of force.
distractorRationales.C: If peers pressured harder pulling, per-person force should rise, not fall, with team size.

items.stem:
A Task A set reads:
1. “We outsourced judgment to whoever had the thickest lamination on a name badge.”
2. “Ignorance is not a crime; pretending we do not need teachers is.”
3. “A society that cannot tell a specialist from a loud amateur will pay for the confusion in waiting rooms.”
4. “Democracy is not a refusal of knowledge.”
5. “Humility before evidence is not elitism.”
A student writes that the theme is “the importance of university.” Why is that identification weak, and which theme is tighter?

choices.text: It is weak because none of the comments mention universities; a tighter theme is the civic status of expertise versus the flattening of knowledge into mere opinion.
It is weak because Task A forbids any theme involving knowledge; the only legal theme is sport.
It is strong; “teachers” in comment 2 proves the set is about campus funding formulas.
It is weak because the real theme is name-badge stationery, which must be discussed as industrial design.

items.explanation: “University” is a nearby institution, not the shared object. The comments concern judgment, specialists, amateurs, democracy, evidence, and humility—expertise as a public good, not a budget line for campuses. Teachers appear as a figure for needed knowledge, not as a prompt to rehearse HECS policy. Theme identification fails when a student substitutes a familiar essay they have memorised. A is the correction. Sport as the only legal theme is invented; stationery is a metaphor in comment 1, not the issue.

distractorRationales.B: Task A has no banned-knowledge rule and no sport requirement; that answer invents exam law.
distractorRationales.C: One mention of teachers does not convert the set into a funding-formula essay; the other four comments would become decoration.
distractorRationales.D: Lamination is a metaphor for hollow credential theatre, not an industrial-design brief.

items.stem: Country X publishes vital statistics after a national vaccine and sanitation campaign. Crude death rate falls from 30 to 12 per 1,000 over twenty years, while crude birth rate stays near 40. The age pyramid is wide at the base and total population is rising fast. Which demographic-transition stage is this?

choices.text: Stage 2: mortality decline precedes fertility decline, producing rapid natural increase
Stage 1: high birth and high death rates in approximate equilibrium
Stage 4: low birth and low death rates with a stable size
Stage 3: fertility has already fallen to match the new death rate

items.explanation: In the demographic transition, stage 1 has high fertility and high mortality and little growth. Stage 2 begins when death rates fall—typically from public health—while birth rates remain high, so the population booms and the pyramid stays youthful. Stage 3 is when fertility falls in response to urbanization, education, and contraception. Stage 4 is the later low-low equilibrium. Country X has a mortality drop without a birth-rate drop, which is the definition of stage 2, not stages 1, 3, or 4.

distractorRationales.B: Stage 1 would still show a high death rate near 30, not a fall to 12, and would not produce a boom.
distractorRationales.C: Stage 4 requires low fertility as well as low mortality; CBR near 40 is incompatible.
distractorRationales.D: Stage 3 is the fertility decline; the stem says births remain high.

items.stem: A globular protein is unfolded in 8 M urea plus a thiol reductant so that all disulfides are broken and secondary structure is lost. Both urea and reductant are then removed by dialysis in air, and catalytic activity spontaneously returns to near-wild-type levels. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: Native tertiary structure can form only if ribosomes and chaperones remain present during dialysis
The native fold, including correct disulfides, is thermodynamically encoded in the primary sequence under these conditions
Urea covalently rearranges side chains, so the recovered activity belongs to a chemically new protein
Quaternary structure is the only level of structure that can reform after urea treatment

items.explanation: This experiment is the Anfinsen result: once the denaturant and reductant are gone, the polypeptide finds its free-energy minimum in solution, pairing cysteines correctly as air reoxidizes thiols. That outcome implies that the information for the native tertiary structure resides in the amino-acid sequence, not in a lingering cellular folding machine in the dialysis bag. Urea is a noncovalent denaturant and does not rewrite the covalent sequence. Activity return also shows that tertiary (and any required disulfides), not merely quaternary assembly of already-folded subunits, can be regenerated from the unfolded chain.

distractorRationales.A: The classic refolding is performed on purified protein without ribosomes; chaperones are not required for this demonstration.
distractorRationales.C: Urea disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic effect; it does not covalently remodel side chains in this protocol.
distractorRationales.D: Activity requires a correct tertiary active site. The experiment speaks to refolding of the chain, not only oligomer assembly.

items.stem: A cuvette of double-stranded DNA is heated through its melting transition while absorbance at 260 nm is recorded. Absorbance rises as the sample denatures. Which molecular explanation is best?

choices.text: Heat hydrolyzes phosphodiester bonds, releasing free nucleotides that absorb more strongly than polymers.
High temperature protonates the bases, increasing n→π* absorbance independently of strand status.
Unstacking of bases upon strand separation increases UV absorbance (the hyperchromic effect).
Hydrogen-bond donors on the bases absorb 260 nm light only when they are paired with a complement.

items.explanation: Stacked bases in a duplex have hypochromic UV absorbance relative to the same nucleotides in a random coil. When heat melts hydrogen bonds and stacking, the bases become more exposed to solvent and electronic coupling between stacked rings is lost, so A260 rises. That hyperchromic shift is the experimental readout of a melting curve and is reversible upon cooling if strands can reanneal. Melting temperatures used in the experiment are far below those needed to hydrolyze phosphodiesters, and pairing does not create a special 260 nm chromophore in the hydrogen-bond donors; unpaired bases absorb more, not less.

distractorRationales.A: Thermal melting at typical Tm values does not hydrolyze the backbone; oligonucleotides remain intact and can reanneal, which would be impossible if phosphodiesters were cleaved.
distractorRationales.B: The absorbance jump tracks the cooperative helix-to-coil transition, not a bulk protonation of bases as temperature rises.
distractorRationales.D: Paired, stacked bases absorb less at 260 nm than unpaired bases; hydrogen-bond donors do not become chromophores only when paired.

items.stem: A 20-residue alanine-based peptide that is highly α-helical in water is redesigned by placing proline at the central position. Far-UV circular dichroism then shows a marked loss of the 222 nm helical minimum. Which property of proline best accounts for the helix disruption?

choices.text: Proline’s side chain is positively charged at neutral pH and electrostatically breaks every helix dipole
Proline cannot form peptide bonds, so the chain is cleaved at the substitution site
Proline’s pyrrolidine ring constrains φ and its backbone nitrogen has no hydrogen-bond donor
Proline uniquely forms a disulfide that covalently kinks the helix

items.explanation: In an α-helix each carbonyl accepts a hydrogen bond from the amide NH of the residue four positions ahead. Proline’s cyclic side chain tethers the backbone nitrogen, restricting φ to values that are poorly compatible with helix geometry, and that nitrogen has no amide hydrogen, so it cannot donate the i→i+4 hydrogen bond. The combination makes proline a classic helix breaker in the middle of a helix and explains the loss of 222 nm ellipticity. Proline is not charged, does form peptide bonds (as an imide), and has no thiol for disulfide formation.

distractorRationales.A: Proline is not ionizable at neutral pH; helix breaking is steric and hydrogen-bonding, not a salt-bridge effect.
distractorRationales.B: Proline forms peptide (imide) bonds in proteins; the substitution does not hydrolyze the chain.
distractorRationales.D: Disulfides require cysteine thiols. Proline has no sulfur and cannot cross-link the helix that way.

items.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment the spacing between adjacent bright fringes on a distant screen is lambda L / d. That spacing increases if:

choices.text: the slit separation d is increased at fixed lambda and L
the wavelength lambda is decreased at fixed d and L
the slit separation d is decreased at fixed lambda and L
the screen distance L is decreased at fixed lambda and d

items.explanation: Fringe spacing Delta y = lambda L / d grows when the numerator grows or the denominator shrinks. Decreasing d therefore spreads the interference pattern. Increasing d or decreasing lambda or L all shrink Delta y. This is the small-angle geometry of two-source interference and does not require changing the brightness of the source.

distractorRationales.A: Larger d reduces lambda L / d, packing fringes closer together rather than spreading them.
distractorRationales.B: Shorter wavelength reduces spacing. That is why blue fringes sit closer than red fringes in the same apparatus.
distractorRationales.D: A closer screen reduces L and therefore reduces linear fringe spacing, even though the angular spacing is unchanged.

items.stem: A light ray in air (n = 1.00) strikes glass (n = 1.50) at 30° to the normal. Snell’s law: n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2. sin 30° = 0.50. The critical angle for glass → air satisfies sin θc = 1.00/1.50 = 2/3. Which pair is correct? (arcsin(1/3) ≈ 19.5°; arcsin(2/3) ≈ 42°.)

choices.text: Refracted angle in glass ≈ 19.5°; light in glass incident at 42° to the normal is at the critical angle
Refracted angle ≈ 45°; critical angle 30°
Refracted angle ≈ 19.5°; critical angle 60°, from n_g sin 60° = 1
The ray cannot enter the glass because 30° exceeds the critical angle

items.explanation: sin θ2 = (1.00/1.50) × 0.50 = 1/3, so θ2 ≈ 19.5°. Light bends toward the normal on entering glass, so the angle must drop below 30°, not rise to 45°. The critical angle is measured inside glass: sin θc = n_air/n_glass = 2/3, θc ≈ 42°. Using sin 60° = √3/2 with n_g would not equal 1. The critical angle applies to the dense-to-rare direction; a 30° air ray is well able to enter. Total internal reflection is not an issue on this first interface.

distractorRationales.B: 45° would be a larger angle in the denser medium, violating Snell; 30° is the air incidence, not θc.
distractorRationales.C: The 19.5° refraction is right, but sin θc = 2/3, not a 60° guess from n sin 60° = 1 (that would need sin 60° = 2/3, which is false).
distractorRationales.D: Critical-angle physics applies when the ray is already in glass heading toward air; here the ray starts in air.

items.stem: Which statement best captures the dispute between the two letters?

choices.text: They disagree about whether underserved clinics currently lack staff.
They disagree about whether the graduate's obligated time, rather than the state's furnishing of the posting, is the proper site of the remedy.
They disagree about whether the editor should have printed both letters.
They disagree about whether nurses and radiographers exist.

items.explanation: Both letters treat underserved rooms as understaffed. A locates justice in recouping a public wager from the graduate's years; B locates justice in making the posting liveable and treats the bond as a cheap substitute that spares the budget. That is a dispute about the site of remedy and about what counts as a ledger. Neither argues about the editor's choice to print, and B mentions other professions to generalise the staffing problem, not to deny they exist. Comparing competing arguments means finding the fork, which is whose body or whose budget must move first.

distractorRationales.A: A's ledger and B's empty clinics both presuppose a staffing lack; that is shared ground.
distractorRationales.C: The editor's note is framing, not a point of controversy between A and B.
distractorRationales.D: B invokes nurses and radiographers as fellow absences; A does not deny those occupations.

passage.title: Return-of-service bond: two letters
passage.body:
Two letters appeared in the same metropolitan daily after the health minister proposed a "return-of-service" bond: new doctors whose training was publicly subsidised would owe three years in designated underserved clinics before they could take an unrestricted urban post.

Letter A
A public scholarship is not a gift ribbon. It is a wager the public makes on a scarce skill. If the graduate then sells that skill immediately to the densest private market, the wager has been privatised without a receipt. Three years is not indenture; it is the time in which a clinic learns a name and a name learns a clinic. Those who call the bond a "mobility tax" speak as if mobility were a natural right unpolluted by the taxes that built the teaching hospitals. Rights that forget their invoices are just appetites with better stationery. Underserved towns are not a lifestyle choice the profession may decline, like a sport. They are the other half of the ledger.

Letter B
The minister has misdiagnosed a staffing failure as a character failure in the young. Clinics are empty of doctors for the same reasons they are empty of radiographers and nurses: housing costs, school deserts, professional isolation, and locum markets that pay more for a weekend than a bonded year pays for a winter. A bond does not staff a town; it parks a resentful beginner there and calls the parking "justice." Meanwhile the budget that should have made the posting liveable is spared the embarrassment of being seen. Coercion is cheaper than housing. If the public wants doctors in those rooms, it should furnish the rooms, not hostage the people it trained. A ledger that counts only the graduate's debt, and never the state's, is not a ledger. It is a sermon.

Editor's note: Letter A was signed by a retired regional physician; Letter B by a recent graduate now in a metropolitan hospital.

items.stem: A chemist needs one enantiomer of 2-phenylpropanoic acid from a racemate. Which procedure can produce an enantioenriched free acid?

choices.text: Simple distillation, because the R and S acids have different boiling points
Treat the racemate with enantiopure (S)-1-phenylethanamine, crystallize one diastereomeric salt, and regenerate the acid by aqueous HCl
Pass plane-polarized light through the melt so that only one enantiomer crystallizes
Extract with achiral diethyl ether and water, because enantiomers have different partition coefficients

items.explanation: Enantiomers are identical in an achiral environment, so they share boiling point, ordinary solubility, and ether/water partition. They cannot be separated by simple distillation or by achiral extraction, and a polarimeter measures rotation rather than physically sorting molecules. Reaction with an enantiopure amine creates two diastereomeric salts, which differ in lattice energy and solubility. Crystallizing one salt and then protonating the carboxylate returns an enantioenriched acid. This is classical resolution via diastereomers.

distractorRationales.A: Enantiomers have identical boiling points. Distillation does not resolve a racemate.
distractorRationales.C: Polarized light is an analytical tool for optical rotation; it does not selectively crystallize one enantiomer under ordinary laboratory conditions.
distractorRationales.D: Partition coefficients in achiral solvent pairs are identical for enantiomers, so the extraction does not enrich either isomer.

items.stem: A vestibular lab spins a seated patient at constant angular velocity about a vertical axis for 30 seconds, then stops the chair abruptly. For several seconds the patient reports rotation in the opposite direction and shows post-rotary nystagmus. Which receptors, and which physical lag, produce that after-sensation?

choices.text: Otolith organs of the utricle and saccule detecting linear acceleration of the chair rails
Cochlear inner hair cells, because angular motion is encoded as a Doppler shift on the basilar membrane
Cristae in the horizontal semicircular canals, because endolymph inertia keeps the cupula deflected after the canal itself has stopped
Muscle spindles in the neck, because they are the only sensors that fire after motion ceases

items.explanation: Semicircular-canal cristae encode angular acceleration via cupula deflection. During a sudden stop, the canal wall halts but endolymph continues, bending the cupula opposite the original spin and driving a false sense of counter-rotation plus nystagmus. Otolith maculae sense linear acceleration and head tilt, not this angular after-effect. Cochlear hair cells encode sound. Neck spindles contribute to proprioception but are not the mechanism of post-rotary nystagmus in this chair test.

distractorRationales.A: Otoliths detect linear acceleration and gravity, not the angular after-sensation of a stopped yaw spin.
distractorRationales.B: The cochlea is not a gyroscope; it does not encode chair yaw as a traveling-wave Doppler shift.
distractorRationales.D: Cervical proprioception is not the generator of classic post-rotary nystagmus after an abrupt stop.

items.stem: An α-helix in a soluble protein is probed by mutating a solvent-exposed internal alanine to proline. The magnitude of the negative circular-dichroism band at 222 nm decreases, while the peptide covalent mass is unchanged. The most direct structural interpretation is that:

choices.text: Proline increases helical hydrogen bonding, so the CD change must reflect aggregation rather than helix loss
The mutation oxidizes nearby cysteines and the CD change reports new disulfides
Helical secondary structure is reduced because proline kinks the helix and cannot donate an amide hydrogen bond
Alanine cannot occur in helices, so the starting protein had no helix and the mutation has no structural meaning

items.explanation: Far-UV ellipticity at 222 nm is a standard reporter of α-helix content. Proline’s pyrrolidine ring constrains the backbone and removes the amide NH that would donate a hydrogen bond to the carbonyl four residues earlier, so an internal proline typically breaks or kinks a helix. Loss of helix is therefore the most parsimonious reading of a smaller 222 nm signal at constant covalent mass. Alanine is in fact helix-favoring, proline does not create disulfides, and increased helix would deepen—not shrink—the 222 nm minimum.

distractorRationales.A: Proline is a helix breaker, not a helix stabilizer; a smaller 222 nm signal is the opposite of increased helicity.
distractorRationales.B: Proline has no thiol. Disulfide formation is a cysteine chemistry and is not implied by this substitution.
distractorRationales.D: Alanine has high helix propensity and is common in helices; the starting CD signal already indicated helix.

items.stem:
An asynchronous culture has a measured generation time of 20.0 h. A snapshot of 360 cells shows:
interphase 324, prophase 18, metaphase 12, anaphase 4, telophase 2.
The duration of a phase is (fraction of cells in that phase) × generation time.
How long is metaphase?

choices.text: 12 h, reading the metaphase cell count as hours
20.0 h, the full generation time
40 min

items.explanation: The metaphase fraction is 12/360 = 1/30. Multiplied by a 20.0 h cycle that is 20/30 h = 2/3 h = 40 min. The cell count 12 is a number of cells, not a time. The whole cycle is 20 h, which would apply only if every cell were in metaphase. Using 60 h or treating 12/360 as a 2 h interval is an arithmetic mix-up. As a check, interphase is 324/360 × 20 = 18 h, the expected long gap phase, and prophase is 18/360 × 20 = 1.0 h.

distractorRationales.A: Twelve is the head-count in metaphase, not a duration in hours.
distractorRationales.B: 20 h is the entire cycle; only 12 of 360 cells are in metaphase.
distractorRationales.D: 12/360 × 20 h is 0.67 h, not 2 h; there is no 60 h generation time in the stem.

items.stem: A CpG island at a tumor-suppressor promoter is densely methylated on cytosine. A DNA methyltransferase inhibitor reduces 5-methylcytosine at this island, increases local histone acetylation, and restores mRNA. Which mechanism is most consistent?

choices.text: Cytosine methylation is required for RNA polymerase II binding at CpG islands, so removing it should silence rather than activate the gene.
Methylated CpG is recognized by complexes that recruit histone acetyltransferases, so demethylation would decrease acetylation.
Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases and compacting factors; demethylation releases this silencing, permitting HAT activity and transcription-factor access.
DNA methylation in animals occurs only on adenine; the drug must therefore be acting on contaminating bacteria rather than the tumor-suppressor gene.

items.explanation: In vertebrates, methylation of cytosine in promoter CpG islands is a stable silencing mark. Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases and other corepressors, compacting chromatin and blocking transcription-factor and polymerase access. Inhibiting DNA methyltransferase allows passive loss of 5-methylcytosine through replication, dissociation of the silencing complex, histone acetylation by HATs, and restoration of tumor-suppressor mRNA, matching the experiment. Methylation does not promote Pol II recruitment at these promoters, and it does not primarily recruit HATs. Cytosine, not adenine, is the predominant DNA methylation target in mammalian genomes.

distractorRationales.A: Promoter CpG methylation correlates with silencing, not with obligatory Pol II recruitment; demethylation restored mRNA in the stem.
distractorRationales.B: Methyl-CpG readers typically recruit deacetylases, not acetyltransferases; acetylation rose after demethylation, the opposite of this prediction.
distractorRationales.D: Mammalian DNA methylation is primarily 5-methylcytosine at CpG dinucleotides, not N6-methyladenine as the dominant gene-silencing mark.

items.stem: Marmot’s Whitehall studies found a stepwise gradient in coronary mortality across British civil-service grades, even though all groups had access to the National Health Service. Which conclusion about class and health is most justified?

choices.text: Only the unemployed are unhealthy; employed grades should be identical
Weber denied that status can affect the body, so Whitehall refutes Weber
The gradient proves Davis–Moore meritocracy causes infarctions by justice
A socioeconomic gradient in health can persist above poverty and despite universal access, implicating status, control, and related class-linked conditions—not access alone

items.explanation: The socioeconomic gradient in health is the graded, not binary, association of SES with morbidity and mortality. Whitehall is famous because it appears among employed, NHS-covered civil servants, so “no insurance” and “absolute destitution” cannot be the whole story. Control, hierarchy, and other class-linked exposures are implicated. Weber actually made status a distinct stratification dimension, compatible with a gradient. Davis–Moore does not claim justice of infarcts as functional necessity.

distractorRationales.A: Whitehall’s point is the gradient among the employed, not a healthy-worker plateau.
distractorRationales.B: Weber included status and life chances; Whitehall does not refute him.
distractorRationales.C: Functional meritocracy is not the cardiologic mechanism Marmot described.

items.stem: A city has a large 0–14 population and relatively few 15–64 workers after a baby boom, straining pediatric clinics. Forty years later the same boom cohort is 65+, pension outlays spike, and the youth share is smaller. Which demographic-structure claim is best?

choices.text: Sex ratio, not age structure, explains both clinic crowding and pensions
Only international immigration can change a population’s age distribution
Birth cohorts move through the age pyramid, so a high youth-dependency ratio can later become a high aged-dependency ratio
Gender identity determines how many pediatric versus geriatric beds are needed

items.explanation: Age is a core axis of demographic structure. A birth cohort is a set of people born in the same interval; they occupy successive bands of the pyramid as they age. Dependency ratios compare non-working-age groups (children, elderly) to working-age adults. A baby boom therefore presents first as youth dependency and later as old-age dependency without any change in the identity of the cohort. Sex ratio and gender identity do not replace that age-cohort mechanism. Fertility, mortality, and migration all can reshape age structure; immigration is not the only path.

distractorRationales.A: The timeline is an aging cohort, not a change in males per females.
distractorRationales.B: Fertility waves change age structure even with zero migration, which is the baby-boom story.
distractorRationales.D: Need for pediatric versus geriatric services tracks age composition, not gender identity.

items.stem: Chloroquine is used to raise the pH of macrophage lysosomes. Acid hydrolases in the lysosomal lumen are expected to:

choices.text: become more active, because they are optimized for alkaline pH
relocate to the nucleus and degrade genomic DNA as their primary effect
lose activity, because they are adapted to an acidic lumen
synthesize ATP by running the vacuolar ATPase in reverse as a synthase

items.explanation: Lysosomal hydrolases have acidic pH optima matching the V-ATPase-acidified lumen. Raising pH moves them off their optimum, impairing degradation of endocytosed cargo (the basis of chloroquine's effect in this assay). They are not alkaline enzymes, they are not nuclear DNases as a first consequence of chloroquine, and the vacuolar ATPase is a proton pump that consumes ATP; it is not an ATP synthase in this setting.

distractorRationales.A: Lysosomal enzymes are acid hydrolases. Alkalinization reduces, not increases, their activity.
distractorRationales.B: These enzymes are sequestered in lysosomes. Raising luminal pH does not retarget them to chromatin as the primary mechanism.
distractorRationales.D: V-ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to pump H+ in. Uncoupling or pH collapse does not turn it into the cell's ATP source.

items.stem:
Two isomers of octahedral [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ are isolated.

Isomer | colour | measured dipole moment | Cl–Co–Cl angle from diffraction
Violet | polar (μ > 0) | 90°
Green | μ = 0 | 180°

MA4B2 octahedra have a cis isomer (adjacent X ligands) and a trans isomer (opposite X ligands). Which assignment follows?

choices.text: Green is cis because a 180° angle means the chlorides are neighbours
Both must be the same isomer because the formula is [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ in each case
Violet is tetrahedral CoCl2(NH3)2, which is why it is polar
Violet is cis (90° Cl–Co–Cl, net dipole); green is trans (180° Cl–Co–Cl, dipoles cancel)

items.explanation: Adjacent chlorides in cis-[Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ give a 90° Cl–Co–Cl angle, so the Co–Cl bond dipoles cannot cancel and the ion is polar: the violet isomer. Opposite chlorides in the trans isomer sit 180° apart, the dipoles cancel (μ = 0), and that is the green isomer. A 180° angle is the definition of trans, not of neighbouring (cis) ligands. The same formula with two geometries is stereoisomerism, not identity. Four ammines plus two chlorides is coordination number 6, octahedral Co(III), not a tetrahedral CoCl2(NH3)2 species.

distractorRationales.A: Neighbouring chlorides are 90° apart (cis). 180° is trans.
distractorRationales.B: Cis and trans share a formula by definition; polarity and the Cl–Co–Cl angle distinguish them.
distractorRationales.C: The formula [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ already contains six ligands, so the geometry is octahedral.

items.stem: A landlord privately endorses hostile stereotypes about a tenant group (prejudice) but, fearing a fair-housing suit, rents to the first qualified applicant. Merton’s typology of prejudice and discrimination would call this person which type?

choices.text: A timid bigot (prejudiced non-discriminator), whose behavior does not match the negative attitude
An all-weather bigot, who both hates and discriminates
An all-weather liberal, who has neither prejudice nor discrimination
A fair-weather liberal, who is unprejudiced but discriminates under social pressure

items.explanation: Prejudice is an attitude (often with affective and cognitive components); discrimination is unequal treatment. They can dissociate. Merton’s timid bigot holds the prejudice but does not discriminate when situational costs are high—the lawsuit-fearing landlord. The all-weather bigot would also refuse to rent. The all-weather liberal has neither. The fair-weather liberal discriminates despite lacking prejudice, under pressure. The stem is attitude without the behavior.

distractorRationales.B: An all-weather bigot would act on the hostility, not comply with fair housing.
distractorRationales.C: Hostile stereotypes mean prejudice is present.
distractorRationales.D: A fair-weather liberal lacks prejudice and still discriminates; this landlord has prejudice and does not discriminate.

items.stem:
Two cell types are characterised:
Cell P: ribosomes sediment at 70S; 100% of 3H-thymidine autoradiographic grains over a nucleoid with no nuclear envelope; internal membrane area 0.2 µm² per cell; diameter 1.2 µm.
Cell E: cytoplasmic ribosomes 80S, plus 70S ribosomes inside double-membrane organelles; 94% of DNA grains inside a nuclear envelope; internal membrane area 48 µm² per cell; diameter 18 µm.
Which classification is supported?

choices.text: Cell P is prokaryotic: 70S ribosomes, nucleoid DNA, and almost no endomembrane.
Cell E is prokaryotic, because some of its ribosomes are 70S.
Cell P is eukaryotic, because a diameter of 1.2 µm is typical of animal cells.
Both are eukaryotic, because both contain DNA.

items.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear envelope, use 70S ribosomes, and have little internal membrane; those are exactly the measurements for cell P (nucleoid grains 100%, 0.2 µm² membranes, 1.2 µm diameter). Cell E has a nucleus, 80S cytosolic ribosomes, and extensive endomembrane (48 µm²), so it is eukaryotic. The 70S ribosomes inside E’s organelles are the bacterial-descended mitochondrial or chloroplast ribosomes, not evidence that E itself is a prokaryote. DNA is present in both domains.

distractorRationales.B: 70S ribosomes inside organelles of a nucleated 80S cell are expected in eukaryotes; they do not make E prokaryotic.
distractorRationales.C: 1.2 µm is bacterial-scale; typical animal cells are an order of magnitude larger, matching E at 18 µm.
distractorRationales.D: Prokaryotes also contain DNA; the distinguishing features are the nucleus and endomembrane system.

items.stem: A neuronal membrane is modeled as a K+ concentration cell. Extracellular K+ is raised tenfold (for example 5 mM to 50 mM) while intracellular K+ is unchanged. The K+ Nernst potential EK:

choices.text: Shifts in the positive direction by about 61 mV (depolarizes), because EK = (RT/F) ln([K+]o/[K+]i) and the concentration ratio falls tenfold
Shifts negative by about 61 mV (hyperpolarizes), because more external K+ increases the outward driving force
Is independent of [K+]o and remains at the sodium Nernst potential
Reverses the sign of ENa without affecting EK

items.explanation: The Nernst equation for a monovalent cation is E = (RT/zF) ln(out/in), about 61 mV * log10(out/in) at mammalian temperature with z = +1. Increasing [K+]o tenfold multiplies the argument of the log by 10, adding +61 mV to EK regardless of the starting ratio. EK therefore becomes less negative. Resting membranes are largely K+-permeable, so Vm follows EK and the cell depolarizes (the basis of hyperkalemic excitability changes). Raising external K+ decreases, not increases, the outward chemical gradient. ENa depends on sodium concentrations and is not slaved to this K+ change.

distractorRationales.B: A smaller out-to-in K+ gradient reduces the magnitude of the negative EK; the shift is depolarizing.
distractorRationales.C: EK is defined by the K+ gradient; it is not a constant and is not ENa.
distractorRationales.D: Changing only K+ concentrations moves EK, not ENa.

items.stem: In 3-methyl-2-pentene the double-bond carbons are C2 (attached to CH3 and H) and C3 (attached to CH2CH3 and CH3). If the C2 methyl and the C3 ethyl group lie on the same side of the double bond, the isomer is designated:

choices.text: Z
E
R
meso

items.explanation: E/Z assignment uses CIP priorities at each alkene carbon, not whether the identical-looking alkyl groups happen to be trans in a casual sense. At C2, CH3 outranks H. At C3, CH2CH3 outranks CH3 because the first point of difference is a carbon versus hydrogen. The two higher-priority groups are therefore the C2 methyl and the C3 ethyl. When those two groups are on the same side, the isomer is Z (from zusammen). E would require those higher-priority groups on opposite sides. R/S and meso do not describe this alkene geometry.

distractorRationales.B: E means the two higher-priority groups are on opposite sides. Same-side higher-priority groups are Z.
distractorRationales.C: R/S labels tetrahedral stereocenters, not the cis/trans relationship of an alkene.
distractorRationales.D: Meso refers to an achiral member of a set of stereoisomers that also includes chiral diastereomers, typically with two stereocenters; it is not an alkene configuration label.

items.stem: A buffer is prepared from acetic acid (pKa = 4.74) with [CH3CO2−] = 0.30 M and [CH3CO2H] = 0.030 M. What is the pH?
items.explanation: Henderson–Hasselbalch gives pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]). The ratio 0.30/0.030 = 10, and log10(10) = 1, so pH = 4.74 + 1 = 5.74. Equal concentrations would have given pH = pKa = 4.74. The value 3.74 would correspond to inverting the ratio (tenfold excess acid). Neutrality (pH 7) is not required for a buffer; this acetate buffer is mildly acidic, as expected near pKa 4.74 with excess conjugate base pulling the pH one unit above pKa.

distractorRationales.A: 3.74 is pKa − 1, which would apply if [HA]/[A−] were 10 rather than [A−]/[HA] = 10. The logarithm was inverted.
distractorRationales.B: 4.74 is the pKa and is the pH only when [A−] = [HA], which is not the case here.
distractorRationales.D: pH 7 is neutrality of pure water, not the pH of a carboxylate buffer with pKa 4.74.

items.stem: The oscillation “between the venue and the ruin” is presented as the result of

choices.text: an inability to hold the thought that a park can be both non-innocent and still not for sale to the highest bidder.
a shortage of metronomes in urban planning departments.
too many toilets.
developers suddenly denying that parks have a price.

items.explanation: The last sentence says that if politics cannot hold “that thought”—the preceding honesty about rents, displacement, and kindness as display—it will oscillate between venue and ruin. The structure is: failure to hold a complex defense yields two crude policies already named. B is noise. C inverts the maintenance list. D contradicts the opening grant. Logic questions should tie the closing consequence to the thought the previous paragraph asked the city to hold.

distractorRationales.B: Metronomes belong to another argument; they are not in this passage.
distractorRationales.C: Toilets are listed as how openness lasts, not as a cause of ruin.
distractorRationales.D: Developers' price claim is granted at the start; the oscillation is a political failure among park policies.

passage.title: The ledger of the commons
passage.body:
When a city puts a park on a map, it appears to have given something away: land that could have been lots, hours that could have been tolls. Developers are not wrong that the gift has a price. They are wrong when they treat the price as a leak from an otherwise watertight private order. The private order is already subsidized by streets, courts, pipes, and the patience of people who do not sue every time a stranger walks past a porch. A park is not the exception to property. It is one of the ways a dense city remains inhabitable enough for property to be worth wanting.

Accountants prefer a ledger in which every square metre has a named owner and a yield. Parks embarrass the ledger because their yield is a crowd that does not pay at the gate, a cooling that does not send an invoice, a child who learns a city can include her without a purchase. The embarrassment produces two crude policies. One is to fence and ticket until the park behaves like a venue. The other is to neglect the park until the crowd looks like a problem that only private security can solve. Both policies claim to be realistic. Both are ways of refusing to count the effects that made the park rational in the first place.

Friends of the park sometimes answer with a poetry of the unowned. The poetry is moving and strategically weak. A commons that cannot speak in maintenance budgets will lose to a spreadsheet that can. The more adult defense is to insist that the ledger is incomplete, not that ledgers are evil. Planting, lighting, toilets, and a gardener who is paid in winter are not betrayals of openness. They are how openness lasts past a ribbon-cutting.

There is a further honesty. Parks are not innocent. They have been used to raise adjacent rents, to move unhoused people out of sight, to display a city’s kindness to visitors who will never need the toilets. Naming those uses does not hand the land to the highest bidder. It prevents the park’s defenders from pretending that green on a map is already justice. Justice would be a park whose ledger includes the people who were priced off the blocks around it.

If urban politics cannot hold that thought, it will keep oscillating between the venue and the ruin, and calling the oscillation pragmatism.

items.stem:
At the experimental temperature the Nernst equation is given as E = (58 mV / z) log10([ion]out / [ion]in). Concentrations (mM) are:
K+: out 4, in 140 (z = +1).
Na+: out 145, in 12 (z = +1).
Cl−: out 116, in 4 (z = −1).
If the membrane were permeable only to K+, the resting potential would be closest to which value?

choices.text: 0 mV, because unequal concentrations cannot produce a voltage until pumps run.
+90 mV, using log10(140/4) with a positive sign.
+58 mV, assuming a ten-fold K+ gradient.
−90 mV

items.explanation: For K+, z = +1 and [out]/[in] = 4/140 = 0.0286. log10(0.0286) ≈ −1.54, so E_K = 58 × (−1.54) ≈ −89 mV, about −90 mV.
