distractorRationales.B: Q’s increased K_m at fixed V_max steepens the slope and moves the x-intercept; competitive lines share a y-intercept, not a slope.
distractorRationales.C: Uncompetitive inhibition is the standard reversible case that leaves K_m/V_max unchanged; Table 1 shows R doing exactly that.

passage.title: Reversible inhibitors of a cytosolic dehydrogenase
passage.body:
Investigators purified a cytosolic NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase that oxidizes a small-molecule metabolite S. Initial velocities were measured at 25 °C by following NADH formation in 1.00 mL assays. Nonlinear fits of v versus [S] produced the apparent Michaelis constants and maximal velocities in Table 1. When an inhibitor was present, its concentration was 2.0 μM in the assay mix. Dialysis that removed unbound compound restored full catalytic activity after incubation with P, Q, or R, indicating reversible binding rather than covalent inactivation. Active-site titration with a tight-binding stoichiometric inactivator found 4.0 nmol of catalytic sites per milligram of protein.

Table 1. Apparent kinetic parameters from initial-rate fits

| Condition | Apparent K_m (mM) | Apparent V_max (nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1}) |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|
| No inhibitor | 0.50 | 80 |
| Compound P (2.0 μM) | 0.50 | 40 |
| Compound Q (2.0 μM) | 1.50 | 80 |
| Compound R (2.0 μM) | 0.25 | 40 |

In a separate progress-curve experiment, 25 μg of the same enzyme protein was mixed with 0.50 mM S and no inhibitor in a 1.00 mL reaction. Product concentration was recorded as a function of time (Table 2).

Table 2. Product appearance at [S]_0 = 0.50 mM without inhibitor

| Time (s) | [Product] (μM) |
|----------|----------------|
| 0 | 0.0 |
| 10 | 9.9 |
| 20 | 19.6 |
| 30 | 29.1 |
| 60 | 56.2 |
| 120 | 102.4 |

items.stem: Glycerol (HOCH2CH(OH)CH2OH) is a viscous liquid with a boiling point near 290 °C, far above that of 1-propanol (bp 97 °C). What is the best explanation?

choices.text: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups, so it forms an extensive hydrogen-bond network; 1-propanol has only one hydroxyl group.
Glycerol is a salt; 1-propanol is a molecular liquid.
Glycerol has a much smaller molar mass, so it should be a gas; viscosity is unrelated to intermolecular forces.
Only London forces operate in glycerol because the OH groups are intramolecularly satisfied.

items.explanation: Each glycerol molecule can donate three hydrogen bonds and accept several more, producing a three-dimensional hydrogen-bond network in the liquid. That network both raises the enthalpy of vaporization (high boiling point) and resists flow (high viscosity). 1-Propanol, with a single OH, forms only linear or loosely associated hydrogen-bonded chains and is far less associated. Glycerol is a neutral triol, not a salt, and its molar mass is larger than 1-propanol’s, not smaller. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds, if present, do not eliminate the many remaining intermolecular OH contacts.

distractorRationales.B: Glycerol is a covalent polyol, not an ionic compound.
distractorRationales.C: Glycerol’s molar mass is higher than 1-propanol’s, and viscosity is a direct macroscopic consequence of strong intermolecular attractions.
distractorRationales.D: The three OH groups are the hydrogen-bond sites; they are not “used up” intramolecularly to the exclusion of intermolecular bonding.

items.stem: The weakest point in Upper Shore’s reasoning is that it

choices.text: mentions relatives at all.
assumes the pictured disorder of time is caused by patient behaviour, which the drawing locates in institutional devices instead.
uses a suburb as a signature.
fails to praise the gold frame.

items.explanation: Even granting staff dedication, the letter’s causal story (late people and relatives make clocks diverge) does not meet the image, where clocks are assigned per person, the public clock is blank, triage is privatised, and a clock is hidden. The argument is weak because it changes the subject to manners. A and C and D pick surface features. Evaluating strength means asking whether the reply addresses the cartoon’s evidence.

distractorRationales.A: Relatives could be relevant in some waiting-room arguments; here they are a dodge.
distractorRationales.C: A pen-name is not the logical failure.
distractorRationales.D: The gold frame is the cartoonist’s irony, not a premise Upper Shore must praise.

passage.title: Cartoon: Clinic time
passage.body:
A single-panel cartoon, unsigned, published on a letters page.

Foreground: a waiting-room bench. Four people sit. Above each head a small clock; the hands are at 1:10, 2:40, 4:15, and 9:50. None of the clocks match the large wall clock, which has no hands.

On the wall, a framed motto: WE VALUE YOUR TIME. The frame is gold. The glass is cracked.

To the right, a receptionist window. The receptionist smiles with many teeth and holds a clipboard titled TRIAGE (PRIVATE). On the clipboard the only visible line is: “Can they still sit up?” A potted plant on the sill is fake; its price tag remains.

Under the bench, a fifth clock, face-down.

Caption, in small type: “The system is coping.”

A letter printed beneath, from “Concerned, Upper Shore”: “Cartoons like this undermine dedicated staff. If people arrived on time and did not bring relatives, clocks would match.”

items.stem: Using only the L = 0.400 m and L = 0.800 m rows of Table 1, the gradient of a graph of T² against L is closest to
items.explanation: Gradient is Δ(T²)/ΔL. Table 1 gives T² = 3.220 s² at 0.800 m and 1.610 s² at 0.400 m, so Δ(T²) = 1.610 s² and ΔL = 0.400 m. The ratio is 1.610/0.400 = 4.025 s² m^{-1}, which is closest to 4.03 s² m^{-1}. Using the full span of L as the denominator (dividing by 0.800 m rather than by the difference) halves the gradient to about 2.01 s² m^{-1}. Dividing by 0.200 m doubles it. Reporting Δ(T²) itself as if it were a slope leaves the 1.61 s² figure with the wrong units. The numerical value cannot be obtained without those two tabulated T² entries.

distractorRationales.A: 2.01 s² m^{-1} is (3.220 − 1.610)/0.800, which uses the larger length instead of the change in length as the denominator.
distractorRationales.C: 8.05 s² m^{-1} would follow if ΔL were taken as 0.200 m rather than the 0.400 m interval between the two chosen rows.
distractorRationales.D: 1.61 s² is the difference in T², not a gradient; a slope of T² versus L must be divided by the 0.400 m change in length.

passage.title: Period of a simple pendulum and the value of g
passage.body:
A student determines the gravitational field strength g from the small-angle period of a simple pendulum. Length L is measured from the support to the centre of a spherical bob of diameter 3.0 cm. For each length the student times 20 oscillations and divides by 20 to obtain the period T; the procedure is repeated three times and the mean is recorded. The timing uncertainty on each 20-oscillation interval is estimated as ±0.20 s from reaction time, so the uncertainty in a single mean T is about ±0.010 s. All runs in Table 1 used a maximum angular displacement of about 5°. Take 4π² = 39.48. For an ideal simple pendulum, T² = (4π²/g) L, so a graph of T² against L should be a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π²/g.

Table 1. Mean period versus length (θ ≈ 5°)

| L (m) | Mean T (s) | T² (s²) |
|-------|------------|---------|
| 0.400 | 1.269 | 1.610 |
| 0.500 | 1.419 | 2.012 |
| 0.600 | 1.554 | 2.415 |
| 0.700 | 1.678 | 2.817 |
| 0.800 | 1.794 | 3.220 |

The student then holds L fixed at 0.600 m and varies the release angle (Table 2).

Table 2. Period versus amplitude at L = 0.600 m

| Maximum angular displacement θ (°) | Mean T (s) |
|------------------------------------|------------|
| 5 | 1.554 |
| 10 | 1.557 |
| 20 | 1.571 |
| 30 | 1.595 |

items.stem: A real gas is compressed to moderate pressure at a temperature near but above its boiling point. The compressibility factor Z = PV / nRT is less than 1. The dominant reason is:

choices.text: finite molecular volume, which makes the measured volume larger than the ideal prediction
inelastic collisions that permanently lower the kinetic temperature of the sample
attractive intermolecular forces, which pull molecules closer together than the ideal model assumes
complete conversion of the sample to a solid, so that Z is identically zero

items.explanation: Z < 1 means the product PV is smaller than nRT, so the gas is more compressible than ideal. Attractive forces (the van der Waals a term) reduce the pressure (or the volume at a given P) relative to the non-interacting model and are the usual cause of Z dipping below 1 at moderate density. Finite molecular volume (the b term) has the opposite sign and drives Z above 1 at very high density. Inelastic collisions do not steadily drain thermal energy from an isolated equilibrium sample, and a true solid would not be described as a compressed gas with a modest Z deficit.

distractorRationales.A: Excluded volume increases the effective volume and tends to make Z > 1, the opposite of the observation.
distractorRationales.B: Equilibrium molecular collisions are elastic in the kinetic-theory energy-bookkeeping sense; they do not provide a continuing heat sink that would redefine T in PV = nRT.
distractorRationales.D: Z slightly below 1 is a real-gas correction, not evidence that the entire sample has frozen into a solid with vanishing gas volume.

items.stem: On the question of public money and professional mobility, the letters most clearly

choices.text: agree that invoices exist and disagree about which unpaid bill—the graduate's or the state's—should be presented as the moral centre.
agree that three years is indenture and disagree only about the size of urban salaries.
have no shared vocabulary, because one writes about clinics and the other about hospitals.
agree that coercion is cheaper than housing and disagree about whether locums should exist.

items.explanation: A speaks of rights that forget their invoices and of the other half of the ledger. B says a ledger that counts only the graduate's debt and never the state's is a sermon. Shared: public money, debt imagery, underserved work. Conflict: whose unpaid bill is the scandal. Paired-prose comparison should not flatten A into B's indenture language (A denies indenture) or invent a locum-existence dispute. Purpose differs too: A defends the bond as recoupment; B unmasks it as cheaper than housing. A is the comparison that keeps the shared ledger metaphor and the forked addressee of the bill.

distractorRationales.B: A explicitly says three years is not indenture; that word is B's charge, not common ground.
distractorRationales.C: Both write about publicly trained doctors and underserved rooms; clinic/hospital is not a vocabulary rupture.
distractorRationales.D: “Coercion is cheaper than housing” is B's line; A does not grant it, and locum existence is not the fork.

passage.title: Return-of-service bond: two letters
passage.body:
Two letters appeared in the same metropolitan daily after the health minister proposed a "return-of-service" bond: new doctors whose training was publicly subsidised would owe three years in designated underserved clinics before they could take an unrestricted urban post.

Letter A
A public scholarship is not a gift ribbon. It is a wager the public makes on a scarce skill. If the graduate then sells that skill immediately to the densest private market, the wager has been privatised without a receipt. Three years is not indenture; it is the time in which a clinic learns a name and a name learns a clinic. Those who call the bond a "mobility tax" speak as if mobility were a natural right unpolluted by the taxes that built the teaching hospitals. Rights that forget their invoices are just appetites with better stationery. Underserved towns are not a lifestyle choice the profession may decline, like a sport. They are the other half of the ledger.

Letter B
The minister has misdiagnosed a staffing failure as a character failure in the young. Clinics are empty of doctors for the same reasons they are empty of radiographers and nurses: housing costs, school deserts, professional isolation, and locum markets that pay more for a weekend than a bonded year pays for a winter. A bond does not staff a town; it parks a resentful beginner there and calls the parking "justice." Meanwhile the budget that should have made the posting liveable is spared the embarrassment of being seen. Coercion is cheaper than housing. If the public wants doctors in those rooms, it should furnish the rooms, not hostage the people it trained. A ledger that counts only the graduate's debt, and never the state's, is not a ledger. It is a sermon.

Editor's note: Letter A was signed by a retired regional physician; Letter B by a recent graduate now in a metropolitan hospital.

items.stem:
A resonance tube open at both ends is driven by a loudspeaker. Sound speed in the laboratory air is 340 m s−1. Intensity versus driving frequency shows peaks at:

Frequency of intensity peak (Hz)
200
400
600
800

For an open pipe, standing-wave frequencies are n v / (2L) with n = 1, 2, 3, … . For a pipe closed at one end they are the odd multiples (2n − 1) v / (4L). What is the length of the tube?

choices.text: 0.85 m, an open pipe whose fundamental is 200 Hz.
0.43 m, an open pipe whose fundamental is 400 Hz.
0.43 m, a closed pipe whose fundamental is 200 Hz.
1.70 m, a closed pipe whose fundamental is 100 Hz.

items.explanation: The spectrum contains 200, 400, 600, 800 Hz, i.e. consecutive integer multiples of 200 Hz, including the even harmonics. That pattern is an open pipe with f1 = 200 Hz, so L = v / (2 f1) = 340 / 400 = 0.85 m. A closed pipe of fundamental 200 Hz would show 200, 600, 1000 Hz and would miss 400 and 800. Taking 400 Hz as the fundamental would ignore the observed 200 Hz peak and would give L = 340 / 800 = 0.43 m. A 1.70 m closed pipe would have f1 = v / (4L) = 50 Hz, which is not the observed spacing. The even-harmonic presence is the diagnostic that the tube is open.

distractorRationales.B: 0.43 m would be L = v / (2 × 400). That treats 400 Hz as the fundamental and cannot account for the 200 Hz peak.
distractorRationales.C: A closed pipe with f1 = 200 Hz has L = v / (4 × 200) = 0.43 m, but then 400 Hz and 800 Hz would be absent. The table includes those even harmonics.
distractorRationales.D: 1.70 m is v / (200 Hz), which is 2L for an open pipe, not L, and a closed pipe of that length would not produce this harmonic list.

items.stem:
Period-3 atomic radius and first ionisation energy:

Element | radius (pm) | IE1 (kJ mol−1)
Na | 186 | 496
Mg | 160 | 738
Al | 143 | 577
Si | 118 | 787

Which statement is consistent with both columns?

choices.text: Al has a higher IE1 than Mg because it has more protons
Na has the smallest radius, which is why its IE1 is the lowest
Radius falls Na→Si as Zeff rises, but Al’s IE1 dips below Mg because Al loses a 3p electron that is higher in energy and more shielded than Mg’s 3s electron
Radius increases across the period, matching the IE1 dip at Al

items.explanation: Radius decreases steadily from 186 to 118 pm as nuclear charge rises while the valence shell stays n=3, so Zeff climbs. IE1 generally climbs too (496 → 738 → 787) but Al is the well-known exception (577): the electron removed is 3p1, not 3s2, so it is easier to remove than Mg’s paired 3s electron despite Al’s extra proton. The radius column does not increase, Al’s IE1 is not higher than Mg, and Na has the largest, not smallest, radius.

distractorRationales.A: The table shows Al IE1 = 577, lower than Mg 738, so extra protons do not dominate here.
distractorRationales.B: Na has the largest radius (186 pm); a large radius and low Zeff together explain the low IE1.
distractorRationales.D: Radius falls from 186 to 118 pm; it does not increase.

items.stem: A city closes bilingual clinics and posts English-only wayfinding so that “everyone uses the same system.” Advocates of multiculturalism object. Which contrast is most accurate?

choices.text: The policy is culture shock, a legal term for bilingualism
The policy is a subculture of hospital engineers, which is the definition of assimilation
Sapir–Whorf linguistic determinism requires English-only signs for thought to occur
The policy is assimilation (melting-pot pressure toward a dominant pattern); multiculturalism would maintain legitimate cultural pluralism in institutions

items.explanation: Assimilation is the process of taking on the dominant group’s language and institutions, historically imaged as a melting pot. Multiculturalism (cultural pluralism) values persistence of distinct cultural streams within a shared polity. English-only clinics are assimilationist. Culture shock is individual strain abroad. A subculture is a group with distinct norms inside a larger culture, not the definition of this city policy. Sapir–Whorf concerns language shaping thought, not a requirement for monolingual signage to think.

distractorRationales.A: Culture shock is not the name of an English-only ordinance.
distractorRationales.B: Subculture ≠ assimilationist city policy.
distractorRationales.C: Whorf does not legislate English-only wayfinding as a condition of thought.

items.stem: A chromosomal domain is marked by histone H3 lysine-9 trimethylation, HP1 binding, late replication, and low RNA polymerase II occupancy. Forced histone hyperacetylation of the same domain increases DNase I sensitivity and nascent transcription. Which statement best describes the original state?

choices.text: The domain is euchromatin packaged with acetylated histones that recruit HP1 to activate transcription.
The domain is a nucleosome-free enhancer; H3K9me3 is a canonical mark of active promoters.
The domain is a prokaryotic nucleoid region, and HP1 functions there as a sigma initiation factor.
The domain is heterochromatin; H3K9me3 and HP1 compact chromatin and silence transcription, whereas acetylation loosens histone–DNA contacts and favors expression.

items.explanation: Constitutive and many facultative heterochromatic regions carry H3K9me3, which is read by HP1 proteins that oligomerize, compact chromatin, delay replication timing, and exclude RNA polymerase II. Histone acetylation neutralizes lysine charge, weakens histone–DNA interaction, and correlates with DNase-sensitive euchromatin and transcription. Forced hyperacetylation therefore switches the domain toward an open, transcribed state, matching the experiment. HP1 is not recruited by acetylation as an activator, H3K9me3 is a silencing mark rather than an active-promoter modification, and this histone code is a feature of eukaryotic nuclei, not of a bacterial nucleoid.

distractorRationales.A: Acetylated euchromatin is transcriptionally permissive and does not use H3K9me3–HP1 as an activation module.
distractorRationales.B: H3K9me3 is associated with compact, late-replicating heterochromatin, not with nucleosome-free active enhancers or promoters.
distractorRationales.C: HP1 and histone octamers are eukaryotic; bacteria lack this chromatin-silencing system and do not use HP1 as sigma factor.

items.stem: Monochromatic light illuminates a single slit. The angular width of the central diffraction maximum increases when the experimenter:

choices.text: narrows the slit
widens the slit
switches to a shorter wavelength at the same slit width
moves the viewing screen closer, which changes the diffraction angles themselves

items.explanation: Single-slit minima satisfy a sin theta ≈ m lambda. The angular half-width of the central peak therefore scales as lambda / a. Decreasing slit width a increases that angle, spreading the central maximum. Shorter wavelength or a wider slit both narrow the angular pattern. Distance to the screen changes the linear size of the pattern but not the diffraction angles set by a and lambda.

distractorRationales.B: A wider slit decreases lambda/a and therefore narrows the central peak, the opposite of the asked change.
distractorRationales.C: Smaller lambda decreases the angular width. This is how a diffraction-limited spot shrinks at shorter wavelength.
distractorRationales.D: Diffraction angles are set at the aperture. Screen distance maps those angles onto a larger or smaller spatial pattern without rewriting theta.

items.stem: In a Sperry–Gazzaniga split-brain examination, a key is flashed briefly in the left visual field of a patient with complete callosotomy. Speech is left-lateralized. Which outcome is expected?

choices.text: She cannot name the key, but her left hand can select the key from a hidden tray
She names the key immediately, because the left hemisphere saw it first
She cannot name the key, and neither hand can select it, because all vision is lost
She names the key only if it is also spoken by the examiner, illustrating Wernicke’s area as a callosal relay

items.explanation: Left visual field projects to right striate cortex. After callosotomy the speaking left hemisphere does not receive that percept, so naming fails. The right hemisphere can still guide the left hand to the matching object. The left hemisphere sees the right visual field, not the left. Vision is not lost; it is disconnected from speech. Wernicke’s area is a language-comprehension region, not the explanation of this field-to-hand dissociation.

distractorRationales.B: LVF information does not reach the speaking hemisphere after callosal section.
distractorRationales.C: The right hemisphere still sees the LVF and can steer the left hand.
distractorRationales.D: Naming does not require the examiner to speak the word; the issue is interhemispheric transfer, not Wernicke as a callosal relay.

items.stem: A cell-free liver extract can synthesize glucose from several precursors. Avidin is added to inactivate biotin-dependent carboxylases, including pyruvate carboxylase. Which 14C-labeled precursor can still yield [14C]glucose in this system?

choices.text: [14C]pyruvate
[14C]lactate
[14C]glycerol
[14C]alanine

items.explanation: Gluconeogenesis from pyruvate, lactate, or alanine all funnel through pyruvate and therefore require pyruvate carboxylase to form oxaloacetate before PEPCK can make PEP. Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin; avidin binds biotin extremely tightly and blocks that step. Glycerol is phosphorylated to glycerol-3-phosphate and oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which enters the pathway at the triose-phosphate level, bypassing the pyruvate carboxylase/PEPCK bypass of pyruvate kinase. From DHAP, aldolase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase can still produce glucose. Hence only labeled glycerol remains a competent glucogenic precursor in the avidin-treated extract.

distractorRationales.A: Pyruvate must be carboxylated by the biotin enzyme pyruvate carboxylase before it can form PEP.
distractorRationales.B: Lactate is oxidized to pyruvate and then faces the same biotin-dependent carboxylation block.
distractorRationales.D: Alanine transaminates to pyruvate and likewise requires pyruvate carboxylase.

items.stem: The talkback host’s dismissal is weakest because it

choices.text: uses the word grow up.
treats the verbs as interchangeable labels, while the table’s divergent profiles are exactly what would be unlikely if they were mere synonyms without selection.
mentions politics.
speaks at night rather than Monday morning.

items.explanation: If the verbs were idle synonyms, four papers covering one statement would not show such specialised stacks (said versus claimed/insisted versus admitted versus revealed). The host asserts synonymy without meeting that pattern. Rudeness and time of day are not the logical failure. Evaluating reasoning means testing the synonym claim against the evidence the researcher offered.

distractorRationales.A: Tone is blunt but not the core gap.
distractorRationales.C: Politics is the researcher’s point; mentioning it is not a fallacy.
distractorRationales.D: When the host spoke is irrelevant to the inference.

passage.title: Table: Verbs in the morning
passage.body:
A media researcher counts finite verbs in the first paragraphs of four papers on the same Monday, all covering the same ministry announcement.

Paper | “said” | “claimed” | “admitted” | “revealed” | “insisted” | Other verbs of speaking
North Evening | 12 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 2
Civic Daily | 3 | 8 | 1 | 0 | 4 | 1
Harbour Post | 7 | 1 | 6 | 0 | 0 | 3
The Signal | 2 | 2 | 0 | 9 | 1 | 2

Caption under the table, written by the researcher: “Speaking is never only speaking. The ministry released one statement. The city woke in four grammars.”

A talkback host that night: “This is just synonyms. Nobody is doing politics with a verb chart. Grow up.”

items.stem: A soil isolate forms colonies in an anaerobic jar but dies within an hour when the same medium is shaken in air. Enzyme assays detect neither superoxide dismutase nor catalase. The isolate is best classified as:

choices.text: An obligate aerobe that requires O2 as its only terminal electron acceptor
A facultative anaerobe that grows faster in air than without oxygen
An obligate anaerobe that cannot detoxify reactive oxygen species generated in air
A microaerophile that requires 21% oxygen and lacks anaerobic metabolism

items.explanation: Obligate anaerobes are inhibited or killed by oxygen, often because they lack superoxide dismutase and catalase (or equivalent peroxidases) and therefore cannot dispose of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide formed when O2 oxidizes cellular reductants. Growth in an anaerobic jar plus rapid death in air matches that physiology. Obligate aerobes and microaerophiles require oxygen, and facultative organisms grow with or without it, typically better with respiration in air. The enzyme profile is the mechanistic reason for the oxygen-sensitive growth pattern, not a side detail.

distractorRationales.A: Obligate aerobes need oxygen and would not thrive in an anaerobic jar.
distractorRationales.B: Facultative anaerobes grow in air; this isolate is killed by air.
distractorRationales.D: Microaerophiles need low oxygen, not strict anaerobiosis, and 21% oxygen is atmospheric, which kills this isolate.

items.stem: Which paraphrase of “A borrowed argument can keep you from freezing. It can also teach your arms the wrong length.” stays inside the passage?

choices.text: Help can prevent collapse and also habituate you to a shape of thought that is not yours
Cold rooms in universities should be illegal
Physical coats always damage the rotator cuff
Arguments should never be written down

items.explanation: The two sentences pair survival-function and deformation-function of a borrow. Paraphrase without over-reading keeps both and does not legislate heating policy, medicine, or a ban on writing. The coat-sleeves image is already glossed as taught arm-length, i.e. habituation. Over-reading would drop the first sentence's charity or inflate the second into a campus by-law.

distractorRationales.B: Freezing is metaphorical for being without an argument in the seminar weather.
distractorRationales.C: Arms and sleeves are figurative for fit of thought.
distractorRationales.D: The paragraph is about credit and habituation, not about prohibiting text.

passage.title: The borrowed coat
passage.body:
He wore other people's sentences the way some men wear coats: against weather, and with the labels left in. At the seminar he began, "One might argue," and then produced, almost unaltered, a paragraph his supervisor had emailed at midnight to save him. The room nodded. He felt the coat settle on his shoulders, warm and slightly too large in the sleeves.

Afterward a friend said, "That was the first time you sounded like yourself." He laughed too quickly. In the bathroom mirror the coat was still on. He tried to take it off by telling the truth to the glass: I do not know whether I think this. The glass, being a glass, offered his mouth moving.

Ethics talks as if authenticity were a mineral you either contain or fake. The evening suggested something cheaper and more ordinary. A borrowed argument can keep you from freezing. It can also teach your arms the wrong length. The crime, if there is one, is not the borrowing. It is the nod you collect as if the sleeves had always been yours.

He sent the supervisor a note: Thank you. I sounded like myself. He deleted it. He sent: Thank you. I used your paragraph. He left that one in the outbox until morning, which is a kind of cowardice that still knows the difference.

items.stem:
A double heterozygote AaBb produces 160 scored gametes:
AB 38; Ab 42; aB 41; ab 39.
Which genetic conclusion do the counts support?

choices.text: The loci are completely linked in cis, which would yield only AB and ab, each near 80.
The loci assort independently: the four gamete classes are statistically indistinguishable from 1:1:1:1.
AB gametes are lethal, because 38 is effectively zero.
Only Ab and aB appear, so the loci are completely linked in trans.

items.explanation: Independent assortment of two heterozygotes predicts four equally frequent gametes, 40 each in a sample of 160. The observed 38, 42, 41, and 39 sit on that expectation (each is 40 ± 2). Complete linkage would collapse the table to two parental classes of about 80. All four classes are present and large, so neither cis nor trans complete linkage fits, and 38 is not a lethal zero. First-year Mendelian reasoning plus the counts is sufficient; no map distance near zero is implied.

distractorRationales.A: All four classes are occupied near 40, not two classes near 80.
distractorRationales.C: 38/160 is ~24%, not a missing class.
distractorRationales.D: AB and ab are present (38 and 39) at the same level as the ‘recombinant’ pair.

items.stem:
A dynamics trolley starts from rest. Students plot v^2 (vertical axis, m^2 s−2) against s (horizontal axis, m). The kinematic relation from rest is v^2 = 2 a s, so the graph should be a straight line through the origin with slope 2a. Data with vertical error bars of ±0.4 m^2 s−2 are:

s (m) | v^2 (m^2 s−2)
0.50 | 3.1 ± 0.4
1.00 | 5.9 ± 0.4
1.50 | 9.0 ± 0.4
2.00 | 12.1 ± 0.4

A least-squares line through the origin has slope 6.0 s−2. What acceleration does that slope imply?

choices.text: 6.0 m s−2, reading the slope as a rather than as 2a.
3.0 m s−2, because slope = 2a so a = 3.0 m s−2.
12 m s−2, doubling the slope instead of halving it.
0.17 m s−2, taking a = 1 / slope.

items.explanation: The given relation is v^2 = 2 a s, so the plotted slope equals 2a. With slope = 6.0 s−2, a = 3.0 m s−2. Checking a point: at s = 2.00 m, 2 a s = 2 × 3.0 × 2.00 = 12.0, which lies on 12.1 ± 0.4. Identifying a with the slope itself (6.0) forgets the factor of 2. Doubling the slope would be appropriate only if someone wrote a = 2 × slope. The reciprocal of the slope is not acceleration. All four tabulated points lie on v^2 = 6.0 s to within the stated error bars, so the line is a fair summary of the experiment.

distractorRationales.A: The slope of v^2 versus s is 2a, not a. Using 6.0 m s−2 as the acceleration double-counts nothing; it simply forgets to divide by 2.
distractorRationales.C: Doubling 6.0 would be 2 × (2a) = 4a. The algebra requires dividing the slope by 2.
distractorRationales.D: 1/slope has units of seconds squared, not m s−2. Acceleration is not the reciprocal of this graph’s slope.

items.stem: A patient with right-sided heart failure has elevated central venous pressure. Capillary hydrostatic pressure in dependent tissues rises. According to Starling forces, net filtration at those capillaries should:

choices.text: Decrease, dehydrating the interstitium because plasma oncotic pressure must rise in parallel
Stop entirely, because lymphatics reverse and empty into arterioles
Increase, producing edema as Pc more strongly favors filtration over oncotic reabsorption
Depend only on interstitial PCO2, which Starling listed as the filtration driving force

items.explanation: Net fluid flux is k * [(Pc - Pi) - sigma(pi_c - pi_i)]. Raising venous pressure is transmitted retrograde into capillaries, increasing Pc. Filtration therefore exceeds downstream reabsorption and lymph drainage capacity, and dependent edema forms. Plasma oncotic pressure does not automatically rise enough to cancel the hydrostatic change. Lymphatics return interstitial fluid to veins; they do not reverse into arteries. Carbon dioxide partial pressure is not a Starling force. This is the same hydrostatic logic as standing still or venous obstruction.

distractorRationales.A: Oncotic pressure does not obligately climb in step with venous hypertension to dehydrate tissues.
distractorRationales.B: Lymph flow may increase but does not reverse into arterioles or zero filtration.
distractorRationales.D: Starling forces are hydrostatic and oncotic pressures, not PCO2.

items.stem: In Ainsworth’s Strange Situation, a 12-month-old plays using the parent as a base, cries at separation, and is readily comforted at reunion, then returns to play. This pattern is which attachment classification?

choices.text: Insecure-avoidant (Type A): little distress, avoidance at reunion
Insecure-resistant/ambivalent (Type C): distress not soothed, angry clinging
Secure (Type B)
Disorganized (Main and Solomon): freeze/collapse as the only possible secure pattern

items.explanation: Ainsworth’s secure infants use the caregiver as a secure base, protest separation, and settle at reunion. Avoidant infants show muted distress and avoid contact on return. Resistant/ambivalent infants are distressed and not easily soothed, often with anger. Disorganized infants show contradictory or freezing behavior and were added later by Main and Solomon; they are not the secure pattern. Bowlby’s attachment theory supplies the evolutionary-ethological frame for why a secure base matters.

distractorRationales.A: Avoidant reunion behavior is avoidance, not ready comfort and return to play.
distractorRationales.B: Resistant infants do not soothe readily; the stem’s child does.
distractorRationales.D: Disorganized is not the definition of secure attachment.

items.stem: Infrared and X-ray data show that the two C–O bonds of the acetate anion, CH3CO2−, are equal in length and intermediate between a typical C–O single bond and a C=O double bond. Which bonding description accounts for that observation?

choices.text: The anion contains one C–O single bond and one C=O double bond that rapidly tautomerize by proton transfer.
Both oxygens are sp3 hybridized and form only sigma bonds to carbon, so the lengths must be identical single bonds.
The methyl carbon conjugates with the carboxylate, giving three equivalent C–C bonds.
The negative charge is delocalized by resonance over both oxygens, so each C–O bond has a bond order of 1.5.

items.explanation: Acetate is described by two equivalent resonance structures in which the C=O double bond and the negative charge swap between the two oxygen atoms. The actual ion is a hybrid: the π electrons are delocalized, each C–O bond order is 1.5, and the bond lengths are equal and intermediate. There is no proton on the carboxylate oxygens to tautomerize, the carbonyl carbon is sp2 with a π system, and the methyl group is not part of that delocalized π system. Equal bond lengths are the structural signature of that resonance hybrid.

distractorRationales.A: Acetate is not a rapidly tautomerizing mixture of localized single and double C–O bonds; spectroscopy sees one averaged structure, not two isomers exchanging by proton transfer.
distractorRationales.B: If both C–O links were ordinary single bonds, the carbon would not have a π system and the C–O lengths would match alcohols, not the intermediate carboxylate length.
distractorRationales.C: The methyl carbon is sp3 and is not conjugated into the carboxylate π system, so it does not equalize C–C bonds.

items.stem:
E. coli is grown for many generations in 15N so that all DNA is heavy–heavy (HH). Cells are then switched to 14N. Density-gradient fractions after the switch are:

Generations in 14N | % HH | % hybrid HL | % light LL
0 | 100 | 0 | 0
1 | 0 | 100 | 0
2 | 0 | 50 | 50
3 | 0 | 25 | 75

Which replication model do the percentages support?

choices.text: Conservative replication: each generation a fully new LL duplex is made and the original HH duplex is preserved, so generation 1 would still show 50% HH.
Semiconservative replication: each daughter duplex keeps one parental strand, producing only HL at generation 1 and then diluting HL with LL.

Dispersive replication: every duplex is a patchwork, so generation 1 DNA would band at a single intermediate density that then shifts continuously toward light, not a 50:50 HL/LL split at generation 2.
End-to-end ligation of an HH chromosome to an LL chromosome, which cannot produce a hybrid-density band.

items.explanation: After one replication in light nitrogen every duplex is one 15N strand plus one 14N strand, so 100% HL and 0% HH, ruling out conservative synthesis (which would retain HH). At generation 2 the two hybrid templates yield two HL and two LL molecules (50:50). Generation 3 keeps the original two hybrid molecules among eight duplexes (25% HL, 75% LL). Dispersive replication would not split into two discrete bands with those exact 1:1 then 1:3 ratios. The table is the Meselson–Stahl signature of semiconservative replication.

distractorRationales.A: Conservative replication predicts persistent HH DNA (the original duplex) at generation 1; the table shows 0% HH.
distractorRationales.C: A dispersive mechanism yields one migrating intermediate peak, not a 50% HL plus 50% LL pair of bands at generation 2.
distractorRationales.D: Concatemer ligation would not convert 100% of molecules to a single hybrid density in one generation.

items.stem: Aspirin acetylates a serine in cyclooxygenase, blocking the enzyme’s cyclooxygenase activity. In platelets, production of thromboxane A2 from membrane phospholipid-derived arachidonic acid is therefore expected to:

choices.text: Increase, because COX inhibition shunts arachidonate into TxA2 synthase only
Remain constant, because thromboxanes are steroids made from cholesterol, not from arachidonic acid
Fall, because COX converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2, the precursor of TxA2
Fall only if vitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase is also acetylated, because TxA2 is a secosteroid

items.explanation: Arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2 is oxygenated by cyclooxygenase (COX) to PGH2. Tissue-specific synthases then make prostaglandins, prostacyclin, or thromboxane A2. Aspirin’s covalent COX blockade therefore cuts the PGH2 supply and lowers platelet TxA2, which is why aspirin reduces platelet aggregation. Thromboxanes are eicosanoid lipids, not cholesterol-derived steroids or vitamin D-like secosteroids. Inhibiting COX does not selectively force residual arachidonate into TxA2; the shared precursor is reduced.

distractorRationales.A: Without COX, PGH2 is not made; TxA2 cannot rise by a COX-independent synthase route from arachidonate in this pathway.
distractorRationales.B: TxA2 is an arachidonic-acid metabolite, not a steroid.
distractorRationales.D: Vitamin D chemistry is irrelevant to COX-dependent thromboxane synthesis.

items.stem: Decay constant λ = ln 2 / T½. Take ln 2 = 0.693. For T½ = 2.0 h, λ = 0.347 h−1. A = λ N. At t = 0, N = 800, so A0 = 0.347 × 800 ≈ 278 h−1 (decays per hour). After 2.0 h, what is A, and how many nuclei decay in a short 0.010 h interval right after t = 2.0 h if A is approximately constant over that interval?

choices.text: A = 0 after one half-life
A ≈ 139 h−1; about 1.4 decays in 0.010 h
A ≈ 278 h−1 still; 2.8 decays
A ≈ 139 h−1; 1390 decays in 0.010 h

items.explanation: One half-life cuts N and therefore A in half: 139 h−1. In a 0.010 h window, decays ≈ A Δt = 139 × 0.010 ≈ 1.4. Activity is not still A0. Multiplying 139 by 10 h instead of 0.010 h inflates the count. Activity is halved, not destroyed, after one T½. The small-interval approximation A Δt is the definition of activity as a rate. Units of h−1 times hours cancel to a pure count of decay events.

distractorRationales.A: Half the nuclei remain, so half the activity remains.
distractorRationales.C: After one half-life both N and A are half of the t = 0 values.

items.stem:
20.0 mL of 0.10 M weak acid HA (pKa = 5.00) is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. Approximate pH landmarks:

Volume NaOH (mL) | composition | pH
0.0 | 0.10 M HA | ~3 (not needed)
10.0 | equimolar HA/A− | 5.00
20.0 | equivalence, 0.050 M A− | >7
30.0 | excess strong base | ~12

Which statement is justified?

choices.text: Equivalence is at 10.0 mL, because that is where pH = pKa
The equivalence pH is 5.00, the pKa of HA
After 30.0 mL the solution is a buffer at pH 5
The half-equivalence pH equals pKa (5.00); the equivalence point is basic because A− hydrolyses; a strong-acid analogue would be pH 7 at 20.0 mL

items.explanation: Equal moles of HA and NaOH meet at 20.0 mL (0.0020 mol each), the equivalence point. At 10.0 mL half of HA is converted, so [HA]=[A−] and pH=pKa=5.00, which is half-equivalence, not equivalence. The salt A− is a weak base, so equivalence pH > 7, unlike a strong acid–strong base titration. At 30.0 mL there is 0.0010 mol of leftover OH− in 50 mL, a strongly basic unbuffered solution, not a pH 5 buffer.

distractorRationales.A: 10.0 mL is half-equivalence; stoichiometric completion is 20.0 mL.
distractorRationales.B: pKa describes the half-equivalence buffer, not the A− solution at equivalence.
distractorRationales.C: Excess strong base destroys the buffer; pH is near 12, as tabulated.

items.stem: A 21-nucleotide DNA probe hybridizes to a wild-type allele through a fully matched duplex that includes a central G–C pair. A disease-associated SNP replaces that pair with A–T. Hybridization is performed at a temperature 2 °C below the melting temperature of the wild-type duplex. Which outcome is most likely?

choices.text: The probe remains bound to the wild-type allele but largely dissociates from the SNP allele.
The probe binds more tightly to the SNP allele because A–T pairs stack more strongly than G–C pairs.
Both duplexes remain equally hybridized because oligonucleotide Tm depends only on length, which is unchanged.
The SNP duplex has the higher Tm because adenine presents a larger hydrophobic surface than guanine.

items.explanation: Short DNA duplex stability, and therefore melting temperature, increases with GC content because G–C pairs contribute three hydrogen bonds and more favorable base stacking than A–T pairs. Replacing a central G–C pair with A–T therefore lowers the Tm of that hybrid by several degrees even though length is identical. A wash or hybridization temperature just below the wild-type Tm leaves the perfectly matched duplex largely double-stranded while the weaker SNP hybrid is substantially melted. That differential occupancy is the physical basis of allele-specific hybridization. Length-only or A–T-is-stronger arguments contradict measured nearest-neighbor thermodynamics used to design probes.

distractorRationales.B: A–T pairs are thermodynamically weaker than G–C pairs, not stronger; they form two hydrogen bonds and stack less favorably, so they lower rather than raise Tm.
distractorRationales.C: For oligonucleotides of fixed length, sequence composition and mismatches dominate Tm; a GC-to-AT substitution is enough to shift melting by several degrees.
distractorRationales.D: Adenine’s size does not make A–T duplexes more stable; G–C pairing and stacking are the main stabilizers of short DNA hybrids.

items.stem: Relative to the poem, Okonkwo's commentary mainly

choices.text: translates images into an argument about what official forms can and cannot rent
accuses the poet of not understanding kettles
provides the missing census data the poem omitted
agrees with the radio host that objects should vote

items.explanation: The commentary reads the coat and the kettle as figures for surplus and for proxy, and it names the census's decisions about what may stand for a life. That mapping turns images into an argument. She does not fill census numbers or repeat the radio host's slogan about objects voting.

distractorRationales.B: She defends the kettle image as showing proxy, not as a mistake.
distractorRationales.C: She does not fill in census numbers; the table is about gallery visitors.
distractorRationales.D: She refuses the host's flattening.

passage.title: Two ways of hearing a census
passage.body:
Poem (untitled, 2019)

We counted rooms as if rooms were people.
The spare one kept its coat on.
In the column for language we wrote the kettle.
Nobody asked the stairs their age.

Commentary by L. Okonkwo, catalogue essay for an exhibition of household inventories:
The poem is easy to misread as anti-data. It is not. It notices that a census already poetizes: it decides what may stand for a life (rooms, language, age) and what must remain downstairs, unasked. The coat on the spare room is not a joke about furniture. It is a figure for surplus — the part of a household that official forms cannot rent. When the poem puts a kettle in the language column, it is not claiming kettles speak. It is showing how quickly a form will accept a proxy if the proxy is small and warm.

A table printed beside the poem in the gallery listed visitors by hour and by whether they photographed the stairs:
Hour 10: 14 visitors, 2 photographed stairs
Hour 11: 31 visitors, 18 photographed stairs
Hour 12: 9 visitors, 0 photographed stairs (docent talk in progress)
The curator captioned the table: Attention is not the same as attendance.

A radio host later called the exhibition “political because it made a kettle into a citizen.” Okonkwo's essay had already refused that flattening. The political cut, for her, is not enfranchising objects. It is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss.

items.stem: A mixture of a 180 kDa homotetramer, a 25 kDa monomer, and free tyrosine is loaded onto a size-exclusion (gel-filtration) column whose fractionation range is 3–80 kDa. The column is eluted isocratically with buffer. What is the elution order (first to last)?

choices.text: Tyrosine, then 25 kDa, then 180 kDa, because small molecules travel fastest through the beads
25 kDa, then 180 kDa, then tyrosine, because only proteins in the middle of the range can enter pores
180 kDa, then 25 kDa, then tyrosine, because larger species are excluded from the internal pore volume and travel a shorter path
All three emerge together in the void volume, because gel filtration does not resolve by mass

items.explanation: Size-exclusion beads contain pores accessible to molecules below a cutoff. The 180 kDa tetramer exceeds the 80 kDa upper limit, is confined to the interstitial (void) volume, and therefore elutes first. The 25 kDa monomer explores a fraction of the internal pore volume and is delayed. Tyrosine enters essentially all pores and has the longest path, so it elutes last. This order is the opposite of SDS-PAGE, where small proteins migrate faster through a mesh. Gel filtration does resolve by hydrodynamic size when the species span the fractionation range and the void.

distractorRationales.A: That order confuses gel filtration with SDS-PAGE. In a porous bead column, small solutes take the long path through the pores and elute late.
distractorRationales.B: The 180 kDa species is fully excluded and must precede, not follow, the 25 kDa protein.
distractorRationales.D: Only fully excluded species share the void. The 25 kDa protein and tyrosine are included to different extents and separate.

items.stem: Furosemide inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb. After the medullary interstitial gradient has run down, the kidney's ability to produce concentrated urine in the presence of ADH is expected to:

choices.text: Increase, because more salt is delivered to the collecting duct for osmotic water reabsorption
Be unchanged, because concentrating ability depends only on urea transporters in the bladder
Decrease, because the countercurrent multiplier can no longer add NaCl to the medullary interstitium
Increase, because furosemide inserts extra AQP2 independently of V2 receptors

items.explanation: The thick ascending limb is water-impermeable and pumps NaCl into the interstitium via NKCC2, creating the corticomedullary osmotic gradient that the countercurrent multiplier and vasa recta maintain. ADH then inserts AQP2 in collecting-duct principal cells so water can flow toward that hypertonic medulla. Blocking NKCC2 dissipates medullary hypertonicity; even with ADH and aquaporins, the driving force for water reabsorption is reduced, so urine cannot be concentrated normally. Furosemide does not insert AQP2, and the bladder is a storage organ, not the multiplier.

distractorRationales.A: Salt remaining in the lumen osmotically holds water; it does not steepen medullary interstitial tonicity.
distractorRationales.B: Medullary interstitial osmolarity, not bladder urea transporters, sets concentrating ability.
distractorRationales.D: AQP2 trafficking is ADH/V2/cAMP-dependent, not a loop-diuretic action.

items.stem:
pKb values (smaller = stronger base) in water:

Compound | pKb
Ethanamine | 3.4
Ammonia | 4.8
Aniline | 9.4
Acetamide | ~14 (no measurable protonation of N in dilute acid)

Which order of basicity, and which structural reason, match the numbers?

choices.text: Aniline is stronger than ethanamine because it is aromatic
All four have the same basicity because each has a nitrogen lone pair
Ethanamine > NH3 > aniline >> acetamide; alkyl donation raises amine basicity, the phenyl ring delocalises the lone pair, and the amide lone pair is tied up in the carbonyl
Acetamide is the strongest base because pKb 14 is the largest number

items.explanation: Basicity decreases as pKb increases: 3.4 < 4.8 < 9.4 << 14, so ethanamine is strongest and acetamide weakest. An alkyl group is electron-releasing relative to hydrogen, making aliphatic amines stronger than ammonia. In aniline the nitrogen lone pair conjugates with the ring, lowering availability. In acetamide the lone pair is delocalised onto oxygen of the carbonyl, so the nitrogen is not a practical aqueous base. Large pKb means weak base. Aromaticity of aniline reduces, rather than increases, basicity relative to ethanamine. A lone pair is necessary but not sufficient; its availability differs.

distractorRationales.A: Aniline’s pKb 9.4 versus ethanamine 3.4 shows aniline is weaker by six log units.
distractorRationales.B: A 10-unit pKb spread is ten orders of magnitude in Kb, not sameness.
distractorRationales.D: The largest pKb is the weakest base; acetamide is essentially non-basic at nitrogen.

items.stem: Two coherent waves of amplitude 4.0 cm and 3.0 cm occupy the same region. Superposition adds displacements. In phase, the resultant amplitude is 7.0 cm; exactly out of phase it is 1.0 cm. Intensities scale as amplitude squared. What is the ratio I_max / I_min?
items.explanation: I_max is proportional to (4.0 + 3.0)² = 49 and I_min to (4.0 − 3.0)² = 1, so the ratio is 49. Intensity does not scale with amplitude linearly, so 7 is only the amplitude ratio. 16/9 is the intensity ratio of the two separate sources. 25/7 would mix A² sums in an unmotivated way (16+9 over 7). Completely constructive versus completely destructive interference of unequal amplitudes therefore gives a large but finite intensity contrast, not zero minima.

distractorRationales.A: Seven is A_max/A_min, not I_max/I_min; intensity goes as amplitude squared.
distractorRationales.B: 16/9 = A1²/A2² compares the two waves one at a time, not the interference extremes.
distractorRationales.C: 25/7 has no standing in (A1±A2)²; those squares are 49 and 1.

items.stem:
A sample of 800 nuclei has half-life 2.0 h. Remaining number N = N0 (1/2)^{t/T}. Activity A is proportional to N. Complete:

Time (h) | N | relative A
0 | 800 | 1.00
2.0 | 400 | 0.50
6.0 | ? | ?

What belongs in the 6.0 h row?

choices.text: N = 100; relative A = 0.125
N = 200; relative A = 0.25
N = 100; relative A = 1.00, because activity is a constant for a given isotope
N = 0 after three half-lives

items.explanation: 6.0 h is three half-lives, so N = 800 / 8 = 100. Activity tracks N, so it also falls to 1/8 = 0.125 of the t = 0 value. Two half-lives would leave 200 and 0.25, the 4.0 h row, not 6.0 h. Activity is not an immutable isotope property; it is λN and falls as the nuclei disappear. Exponential decay never strictly hits zero at a finite number of half-lives; 100 nuclei remain at 6.0 h on this accounting. The table’s 2.0 h row already illustrates the halving rule to be reapplied twice more.

distractorRationales.B: N = 200 is the 4.0 h (two-half-life) value, not 6.0 h.
distractorRationales.C: N = 100 is right, but A ∝ N, so relative activity is 100/800 = 0.125, not 1.
distractorRationales.D: Three half-lives leave one-eighth, not zero; 100 nuclei are still there.

items.stem: Mammalian phosphofructokinase-1 uses ATP as a phosphoryl donor yet is inhibited by high ATP at a second site. AMP relieves that inhibition even though AMP is not a substrate. This pattern is best described as:

choices.text: Competitive inhibition by AMP at the catalytic ATP site
Irreversible covalent adenylation of a catalytic lysine by ATP
Uncompetitive inhibition by AMP that binds only the fructose-6-phosphate complex
Allosteric feedback in which cellular energy charge tunes glycolytic flux at a regulatory site

items.explanation: PFK-1 is a major control point of glycolysis. ATP binds both the active site (as substrate) and an inhibitory allosteric site that signals high energy charge. AMP, which rises when ATP is depleted, binds a distinct regulatory site (or shifts the T/R equilibrium) to oppose ATP inhibition and restore activity. That is reversible allosteric feedback, not covalent inactivation. AMP is an activator here, not a competitive dead-end inhibitor versus ATP at the catalytic site, and the vignette does not match uncompetitive kinetics. Energy charge therefore sets glycolytic rate independently of simple Michaelis saturation by fructose-6-phosphate.

distractorRationales.A: AMP relieves inhibition; it is not acting as a competitive blocker of the catalytic ATP site in this description.
distractorRationales.B: The ATP effect is rapid and reversible allostery, not a stoichiometric covalent modification required by the vignette.
distractorRationales.C: AMP is described as relieving ATP inhibition, which is activation, not uncompetitive inhibition.

items.stem: In a Cherry dichotic-listening setup, a student shadows a surgical podcast in the left ear and ignores a word list in the right. Afterward she cannot report the ignored list’s content, but she did notice her own name when it occurred once on the right (a Moray-type breakthrough). Which filter model best accommodates both results?

choices.text: Broadbent’s early, all-or-none filter based only on physical channel, which predicts the name cannot be identified
Deutsch and Deutsch late selection only, which predicts full semantic analysis of every ignored word and thus full report of the list
Treisman’s attenuation model, in which unattended input is turned down but highly primed items (one’s name) can still exceed threshold
Kahneman’s capacity model, which claims there is no filter and therefore both ears are shadowed equally

items.explanation: Broadbent’s filter drops the unattended channel before meaning, which fits poor list report but not name breakthrough. Treisman proposed attenuation: unattended signals are weakened, yet items with very low thresholds (own name) can still be perceived. Late-selection models expect more semantic report of the ignored list than the stem allows. Capacity models address resource limits in divided attention; they do not by themselves explain a selective name pop-out with otherwise empty report.

distractorRationales.A: An uncompromising early filter cannot explain identifying the unattended name.
distractorRationales.B: Late selection overpredicts memory for ignored semantic content relative to the sparse report described.
distractorRationales.D: Equal shadowing of both ears is not what dichotic shadowing tasks produce.

items.stem: Ethnographers film posed and spontaneous faces of anger, fear, disgust, happiness, sadness, and surprise in a highland community with little exposure to global media. University students on another continent label still frames at well above chance, although they mis-rank how intense the sitters felt. Which conclusion is most justified?

choices.text: Display rules are identical worldwide, so intensity rankings should have matched as well as category labels
The result shows that language, not biology, creates the six categories, because the raters used English emotion words
Only happiness is conserved; the other five expressions must have been taught by outsiders
A small set of facial emotion signals is recognized across cultures, consistent with a universal-emotions account, while judged intensity may still be culturally scaled

items.explanation: Cross-cultural recognition of a small set of facial configurations is the core evidence associated with Ekman’s universal-emotions claim. Above-chance labeling by distant raters of faces produced in an isolated community supports conservation of those signals. Display rules and scaling of intensity can still differ by culture, so mismatched intensity rankings do not cancel the categorical recognition result. Use of English response options is a measurement detail, not proof that the facial signals themselves are linguistic inventions. Restricting universality to happiness alone contradicts the six-category recognition pattern described.

distractorRationales.A: Universal recognition of categories does not imply identical display rules or identical intensity scales; those can vary even when the facial prototypes are shared.
distractorRationales.B: Raters must use some lexicon; that does not show the facial configurations are created by English rather than being widely recognizable signals.
distractorRationales.C: The data cover six categories above chance, not happiness alone, so a happiness-only universality claim is too narrow.

items.stem: A linear eukaryotic chromosome is replicated in a telomerase-null cell. After the terminal RNA primer on the extreme 5′ end of a newly made lagging strand is removed, conventional DNA polymerases cannot fill the resulting gap. Which statement best describes why, and the long-term consequence?

choices.text: DNA polymerases synthesize 3′→5′ when dNTP concentrations are high, so the gap is filled and ends do not shorten.
The parental 3′ overhang is used as a primer that extends the recessed 5′ end, lengthening the chromosome each S phase.
RNA primers on the leading strand cannot be replaced, so both ends grow until the cell senesces from excess telomeric DNA.
DNA polymerases require a primer and add nucleotides only to a 3′-OH, so they cannot fill a 5′-terminal gap after primer removal; repeated cycles shorten the chromosome.

items.explanation: Replicative DNA polymerases cannot initiate chains de novo and add dNTPs only onto an existing 3′-OH in the 5′→3′ direction. Removal of the terminal lagging-strand RNA primer leaves a 5′ gap with no downstream primer terminus to extend. Each S phase therefore shortens chromosome ends unless telomerase, a specialized reverse transcriptase, extends the 3′ G-overhang using its internal RNA template. Polymerases never synthesize 3′→5′, the parental overhang is not a primer for the recessed 5′ end, and leading-strand priming is not the source of progressive end erosion in this end-replication problem.

distractorRationales.A: Template-dependent DNA polymerases elongate exclusively 5′→3′; raising dNTPs does not reverse polarity or fill a 5′ terminal gap.
distractorRationales.B: A 3′ overhang cannot prime DNA synthesis on the recessed 5′ end; polymerases need a 3′-OH on the strand being extended.
distractorRationales.C: The unreplicated terminus is a lagging-strand 5′ gap after primer removal; ends shorten rather than grow in telomerase-null cells.

items.stem: The radio host's remark is politically flattened, according to Okonkwo, because it

choices.text: treats the exhibit as giving objects the vote instead of asking which human details the state misses
correctly restates her essay
focuses on the table's hour 12 talk
denies that any exhibition can be political

items.explanation: The host says the show is political because it made a kettle into a citizen. Okonkwo refuses enfranchising objects; the political cut is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss. The host does not restate her, does not discuss the table, and does call the show political.

distractorRationales.B: The passage says the essay had already refused that flattening.
distractorRationales.C: The host is not described as talking about hour 12.
distractorRationales.D: The host does call it political; the dispute is about why.

passage.title: Two ways of hearing a census
passage.body:
Poem (untitled, 2019)

We counted rooms as if rooms were people.
The spare one kept its coat on.
In the column for language we wrote the kettle.
Nobody asked the stairs their age.

Commentary by L. Okonkwo, catalogue essay for an exhibition of household inventories:
The poem is easy to misread as anti-data. It is not. It notices that a census already poetizes: it decides what may stand for a life (rooms, language, age) and what must remain downstairs, unasked. The coat on the spare room is not a joke about furniture. It is a figure for surplus — the part of a household that official forms cannot rent. When the poem puts a kettle in the language column, it is not claiming kettles speak. It is showing how quickly a form will accept a proxy if the proxy is small and warm.

A table printed beside the poem in the gallery listed visitors by hour and by whether they photographed the stairs:
Hour 10: 14 visitors, 2 photographed stairs
Hour 11: 31 visitors, 18 photographed stairs
Hour 12: 9 visitors, 0 photographed stairs (docent talk in progress)
The curator captioned the table: Attention is not the same as attendance.

A radio host later called the exhibition “political because it made a kettle into a citizen.” Okonkwo's essay had already refused that flattening. The political cut, for her, is not enfranchising objects. It is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss.

items.stem: The letter from Upper Shore is best described as

choices.text: sharing the cartoon’s satire of triage.
reassigning blame to patients’ punctuality and relatives, missing the cartoon’s target.
a statistical study of waiting times.
an admission that the motto is cracked glass.

items.explanation: The letter defends staff by scolding arrivals and relatives so that clocks would match. That accepts clock-matching as the patients’ duty and treats the cartoon as an attack on dedication. The cartoon’s target is the system’s self-description, not nurses’ souls. Tone is earnest, slightly stung, not satirical. C invents data. D would require the letter to notice the cracked motto, which it does not.

distractorRationales.A: The letter says the cartoon undermines staff, so it does not share the satire.
distractorRationales.C: No figures are offered, only a counterfactual about punctuality.
distractorRationales.D: The cracked glass is in the drawing; the letter does not mention it.

passage.title: Cartoon: Clinic time
passage.body:
A single-panel cartoon, unsigned, published on a letters page.

Foreground: a waiting-room bench. Four people sit. Above each head a small clock; the hands are at 1:10, 2:40, 4:15, and 9:50. None of the clocks match the large wall clock, which has no hands.

On the wall, a framed motto: WE VALUE YOUR TIME. The frame is gold. The glass is cracked.

To the right, a receptionist window. The receptionist smiles with many teeth and holds a clipboard titled TRIAGE (PRIVATE). On the clipboard the only visible line is: “Can they still sit up?” A potted plant on the sill is fake; its price tag remains.

Under the bench, a fifth clock, face-down.

Caption, in small type: “The system is coping.”

A letter printed beneath, from “Concerned, Upper Shore”: “Cartoons like this undermine dedicated staff. If people arrived on time and did not bring relatives, clocks would match.”

items.stem: A 2.0 kg block is launched up a frictionless incline at 10 m s−1. g = 10 m s−2. Mechanical energy is conserved: (1/2) m v² = m g h at the highest point. What maximum vertical height does it reach, and if a constant 8.0 N kinetic-friction force later acts on the level return path, how much extra distance is needed to stop it from the same 10 m s−1?

choices.text: h = 5.0 m; extra stopping distance 12.5 m
h = 10 m; extra stopping distance 25 m
h = 5.0 m; extra stopping distance 2.5 m
h = 0.50 m; extra stopping distance 12.5 m

items.explanation: Initial KE = (1/2)×2.0×100 = 100 J. Height: 100 = 2.0×10×h, so h = 5.0 m. On the level, friction does −8.0 s = −100 J to cancel that KE, hence s = 12.5 m. Using mgh with g omitted or v² = 100 as h would give 10 m. Dividing 100 J by 40 N (perhaps mg) gives 2.5 m, ten times too short for an 8 N force. h = 0.50 m would be 100 / (2×10×10) with an extra factor of 10. Energy accounting therefore separates the vertical climb from the later dissipative stop.

distractorRationales.B: h = v²/g = 10 m forgets the 1/2 in KE, or uses h = v²/g instead of v²/2g.
distractorRationales.C: The 5.0 m height is right, but 100 J / 8.0 N = 12.5 m, not 2.5 m.
distractorRationales.D: 0.50 m is a factor-of-ten error in mgh; 100 J / 20 N = 5.0 m.

items.stem: Human erythrocytes are suddenly suspended in distilled water. The most likely immediate outcome is:

choices.text: crenation from net water efflux
no volume change, because water cannot cross plasma membranes
swelling and possible lysis from net water influx
Na+/K+ ATPase pumping water out fast enough to hold volume exactly constant

items.explanation: Distilled water is profoundly hypotonic to cytoplasm. Water moves by osmosis (largely through aquaporins) toward the higher osmolarity inside the cell, so the erythrocyte swells and may lyse. Crenation is the hypertonic response. Plasma membranes are not water-impermeable, and the sodium pump transports Na+ and K+, not water as a primary substrate, so it cannot osmotically clamp a cell dropped into pure water.

distractorRationales.A: Crenation occurs in hypertonic medium, when water leaves the cell. Distilled water is hypotonic.
distractorRationales.B: Erythrocyte membranes are highly water-permeable. Osmotic swelling is the classic demonstration.
distractorRationales.D: Na+/K+ ATPase moves ions, not bulk water, and cannot outrun osmotic influx from an infinite hypotonic bath.

items.stem: After a failed organic-chemistry exam, Student X says “I’m a worthless person” but still enrolls in tutoring because “I can learn this if I drill mechanisms.” Student Y says she still likes herself as a person but that “no amount of work will change my organic score.” Which pairing is correct?

choices.text: X has high self-esteem and low self-efficacy; Y is the reverse
Both quotations measure only locus of control, so self-esteem cannot differ
X shows low self-esteem but relatively high self-efficacy; Y shows higher self-esteem but low self-efficacy for this task
Self-efficacy and self-esteem are the same construct, so the reports cannot diverge

items.explanation: Self-esteem is global (or domain-general) evaluation of worth. Self-efficacy is a task-specific belief that one can execute the actions needed to produce an outcome. X’s “worthless” is low self-esteem; signing up because practice will work is relatively high efficacy. Y’s intact liking of the self with a belief that work is useless is higher esteem plus low efficacy. The two constructs can move separately, which is why MCAT items treat them as distinct from each other and from locus of control (who or what is seen as the cause of outcomes).

distractorRationales.A: This swaps the labels: X’s global worth statement is low, not high, esteem; Y’s “work will not matter” is low, not high, efficacy.
distractorRationales.B: Locus of control is about internal versus external causes; the stem also contrasts worth versus capability.
distractorRationales.D: The educational point of the pair is that esteem and efficacy are not identical.

items.stem: A spanner of length 0.25 m applies a force of 40 N to a nut. Torque τ = F d sin θ, with θ the angle between the force and the spanner. Compute τ for θ = 90° and for θ = 30° (sin 30° = 0.50). Which pair is correct, and which orientation tightens more effectively?

choices.text: 10 N m at both angles, because F and d are unchanged
5.0 N m at 90°; 10 N m at 30°
100 N m at 90°; 50 N m at 30° (using 2.5 m as the length)
10 N m at 90°; 5.0 N m at 30°; perpendicular is more effective

items.explanation: At 90°, sin θ = 1, so τ = 40 × 0.25 = 10 N m. At 30°, sin θ = 0.50, so τ = 5.0 N m. Only the perpendicular component of the force produces rotation, so the 90° pull is twice as effective. Angle independence would contradict the sin θ factor. Swapping the two values inverts that geometry. Using 2.5 m instead of 0.25 m inflates both torques by ten. Maximum torque at a given F and d is always the perpendicular case.

distractorRationales.A: τ includes sin θ, which halves when θ goes from 90° to 30°.
distractorRationales.B: sin 90° = 1 > sin 30° = 0.50, so the 10 N m value belongs to 90°.
distractorRationales.C: The length is 0.25 m, not 2.5 m; 40 × 0.25 = 10, not 100.

items.stem: An Atwood machine has masses 3.0 kg and 1.0 kg joined by a light inextensible string over a light frictionless pulley. g = 10 m s−2. The acceleration of the system is a = (m1 − m2)g / (m1 + m2), and the tension is the same throughout the string. What are a and T?

choices.text: a = 10 m s−2; T = 0, as in free fall of both masses

items.explanation: a = (3.0 − 1.0) × 10 / (3.0 + 1.0) = 20/4 = 5.0 m s−2. For the 1.0 kg mass, T − 10 = 1.0 × 5.0, so T = 15 N. Checking the 3.0 kg mass: 30 − T = 15, T = 15 N. Both masses cannot be in free fall while linked by a taut string; T is not zero. T = 30 N would be the 3.0 kg weight with no acceleration. a = 2.5 m s−2 would follow from dividing by 8 kg or using g/4 without the mass difference of 2.0 kg over 4.0 kg.

distractorRationales.A: The string constraint couples the masses, so neither falls at g and the string carries tension.
distractorRationales.B: T = 30 N is the weight of the heavy mass; a non-zero acceleration requires T < m1 g.
distractorRationales.C: The factor (m1 − m2)/(m1 + m2) is 2/4 = 1/2, so a = 5.0 m s−2, not 2.5.

items.stem: A sprinter moving at a constant 10 m/s begins to slow with uniform acceleration and comes to rest after covering 20 m. The sprinter's acceleration during the slowing interval is:
items.explanation: The time-independent kinematic relation is v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a x. With v = 0, v0 = 10 m/s, and x = 20 m this is 0 = 100 + 2 a (20), so 40 a = -100 and a = -2.5 m/s^2. The negative sign means the acceleration is opposite the original velocity. The same result follows from v_avg = 5 m/s, t = 20/5 = 4 s, and a = Delta v / t = -10/4 = -2.5 m/s^2.

distractorRationales.A: This is -v/x = -10/20. Acceleration is Delta v / t, not Delta v / x; you need the factor of 2 in v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a x.
distractorRationales.C: This is -v^2 / x = -100/20, which drops the 2 in 2 a x. That overstates the magnitude of the deceleration.
distractorRationales.D: This is simply -v0 with the units changed, or -v^2 / (2 x) evaluated with x = 5 m. It does not satisfy the kinematic equation for a 20 m stop from 10 m/s.

items.stem: Two point charges in vacuum exert a repulsive force of 16 N when they are 1.0 m apart. If the same charges are moved to 2.0 m apart, the force is:

choices.text: 4 N
8 N

items.explanation: Coulomb's law is F = k |q1 q2| / r^2, so force scales as the inverse square of separation. Doubling r multiplies F by 1/4: 16 N / 4 = 4 N. The force remains repulsive because the product q1 q2 does not change sign. Inverse-linear scaling (halving to 8 N) would apply to electric potential, which goes as 1/r, not to force. Increasing the force when charges move apart would violate the inverse-square dependence.

distractorRationales.B: This halves the force, as if F were proportional to 1/r (the scaling of potential V). Force and field scale as 1/r^2.
distractorRationales.C: This doubles the force. Separating like charges reduces the repulsive force; it does not increase it.
distractorRationales.D: This multiplies by 4, inverting the inverse-square law (using r^2 in the numerator). Doubling distance must quarter the Coulomb force.

items.stem: Which of the following would the author be most likely to treat as conversion misdescribed as rescue?

choices.text: A philologist who publishes a critical edition of a widely copied legal code and notes the manuscript variants.
A gallery caption that praises curators for saving a household altar from a condemned apartment by placing it in a climate-controlled case, presented as a continuation of the altar’s original life.
An oral historian who leaves a narrator’s refusal on the transcript so that a later reader can see where questioning was resisted.
A municipality that demolishes a merchant townhouse in order to build housing and does not retain the blueprints.

items.explanation: The author locates the objectionable piety in museum language that treats moving an object into a case as a continuation of its first life rather than as a conversion into evidence. A caption that calls the transfer a saving and implies unbroken life is exactly that misdescription: conversion is real, but rescue-talk hides the historian’s or curator’s power. Editing a legal code is ordinary documentary work the author does not condemn; keeping a refusal visible is what the oral-history paragraph praises; demolition without files is the civic problem of missing cartons, not the rescue-rhetoric problem. The inference depends on the attic-and-glass-case example, not on a general hostility to museums.

distractorRationales.A: Critical editing is the ordinary conversion the author says historians must do; nothing in the passage tags scholarly apparatus as fake rescue.
distractorRationales.C: Leaving a refusal audible is the visibility the author wants in the making of an interview, the opposite of concealing power.
distractorRationales.D: Demolition that leaves fewer boxes is the author’s civic illustration of undocumented loss, not an instance of rescue language covering conversion.

passage.title: The archive and the street
passage.body:
Historians often speak as if the past were a reluctant witness who can be coaxed into testimony if only the right box is opened. The letter, the minute-book, the trial transcript, and the parish register are treated not as remnants but as the event itself, patiently waiting to be interviewed. The metaphor is professionally convenient. It locates virtue in attentiveness and implies that an archive, handled without aggression, will speak of its own accord. Archives do not speak. They are offices that decide, usually long before a scholar arrives, which traces of life will be kept, numbered, and thereby made eligible for later recovery. To mistake a folder for a microphone is to forget that someone built the studio, invited some guests, and switched the machine off when the conversation became inconvenient.

This is not a case for abandoning documents. It is a case against a piety now common in public history: the belief that proximity to a primary source is itself a moral credential. Museum captions announce that an object was found in an attic or rescued from a demolition site, as if its later career in a glass case were a continuation of its first life rather than a conversion into evidence. Conversion is what historians do. Trouble begins when conversion is narrated as rescue, because that narration conceals the historian's power and, more consequentially, conceals the people who never generated a paper trail to be rescued.

Oral historians have pressed this objection for decades, sometimes with more hope than caution. They have offered the recorded interview as a democratic patch, a way of admitting those whom the file forgot. The patch is real; it is not automatic. An interview is also a document, made under conditions of prompting, recording, transcription, and later cutting. It can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette. What distinguishes a responsible oral history is not orality as such, but the historian remaining visible in the manufacture of the record—visible enough that a later reader can see where a question steered, where a narrator pushed back, and where a silence was not a hole but a refusal.

The sharper problem is civic rather than technical. If the only past that can be cited is the past that was filed, public memory will go on over-representing those who employed clerks. Cities make the point more bluntly than seminars do. A demolished neighborhood deposits fewer cartons than a merchant's townhouse; a street seller deposits fewer than a chartered company. When a preservation trust then campaigns to save the townhouse because it is richly documented, the trust is not merely selecting architecture. It is ratifying a distribution of paperwork as a distribution of historical weight. The house is asked to stand for an age, and the undocumented street is invited, if at all, to supply atmosphere.

Honesty does not require the fantasy that every life can be reconstructed with equal density. Some absences are final. The decent procedure is to treat those absences as facts about power rather than as temporary vacancies that a more heroic search will fill. A history that admits what cannot be known is more public-minded than a history that performs completeness by adding still more pages to an already thick dossier. The archive will remain necessary. It need not remain innocent.

items.stem: A 17-year-old patient has switched intended majors three times, dropped two friend groups, and says “I still don’t know who I am supposed to be.” According to Erikson’s psychosocial stages, this crisis is which stage, and which nearby stage is not yet the central task?

choices.text: Industry versus inferiority (school age); identity is already finished
Generativity versus stagnation, because career indecision is a midlife problem by definition
Identity versus role confusion (adolescence); intimacy versus isolation is the subsequent young-adult task that presupposes a clearer identity
Trust versus mistrust, because all identity problems reduce to oral feeding

items.explanation: Erikson placed identity versus role confusion in adolescence: integrating values, occupations, and groups into a coherent self, or remaining diffuse. Intimacy versus isolation is the young-adult stage that, in his sequence, is harder without a prior identity. Industry versus inferiority is the school-age competence stage. Generativity is midlife care for the next generation. Trust versus mistrust is infancy. The named 17-year-old presentation is the identity crisis, not those others.

distractorRationales.A: Industry/inferiority is earlier; the stem is an adolescent identity problem.
distractorRationales.B: Generativity is not the adolescent identity stage.
distractorRationales.D: Infant trust is not the developmental task described.
